Workers at Grand Theft Auto VI developer Rockstar Games won’t unionize, after the vote for a formal recognition agreement failed, with only 25 percent of votes in favor of unionization. The Independent Workers Union of Great Britain (IWGB) said that Rockstar workers in the union will continue organizing even without formal recognition.

Voting ran from November 12th through 26th, covering the launch of GTA VI. If successful, the vote would have established a formal framework for collective negotiation with the studio over pay, overtime, bonuses, leave, and pensions, along with a right to consultation over future changes including AI implementation and layoffs. Without it, Rockstar won’t have an obligation to meet union representatives, though workers and union members can still lobby for change informally.

“For anyone at Rockstar who believes in a fairer workplace, a fairer sector and a fairer society - this isn’t a sign to retreat, it’s a sign to double down on what we stand for,” IWGB said in a statement sent to The Verge. “Hundreds of our coworkers voted in favour of our union at Rockstar, yet sadly we recognise we have more work to do to build understanding and win the trust of more of our colleagues. We’re ready to put in the effort to make that happen.”

When Rockstar fired 31 IWGB members last year, the union accused it of “the most blatant and ruthless act of union busting in the history of the games industry.” That case has gone to a UK employment tribunal, with a judgment still pending.

“We are extraordinarily proud of our team, the culture we’ve built together and the launch of Grand Theft Auto VI,” Rockstar head of publishing Jennifer Kolbe told Bloomberg News. “This result reflects our team’s strong support for continuing the direct relationships, collaboration and open dialogue that have helped make Rockstar Games so innovative and strong. As we look ahead, we’re excited to build on all we’ve accomplished together.”

The Acer Nitro VG270K is a 27-inch dual-mode 4K gaming monitor. It operates at a 160 Hz refresh rate at its native 4K resolution, but dropping down to FHD resolution boosts that figure to 320 Hz.

The 32-inch 4K segment of the gaming monitor market is quite popular these days, and we can understand why. Not only do you get a large screen, but you can enjoy your favorite games at 4K resolution, as long as you have the graphics horsepower to back it up. If you’re in the market, the ASUS ROG PG32UCDMR is ringing up with a 32% discount at Amazon, taking its price down to $899. However, Amazon is sweetening the deal with an additional $20 coupon, which brings the final price to $879.

The Asus ROG PG32UCDMR is a 32-inch 4K QD-OLED gaming monitor with a 240 Hz refresh rate and VESA DisplayHDR 400 True Black compliance.

The PG32UCDMR features a native refresh rate of 240 Hz, uses a QD-OLED panel, and has a 0.03 ms response time (GtG). You’ll also get VESA DisplayHDR 400 True Black compliance, 99.3 percent coverage of the DCI-P3 color space, and the Asus Neo Proximity Sensor, which turns the screen black when you’re not sitting in front of the monitor to help prevent premature burn-in on the QD-OLED panel.

Asus also has you covered on the connectivity front, as the PG32UCDMR includes two HDMI 2.1 ports, one DisplayPort 2.1 port, and USB-C with DisplayPort Alt-Mode support.

As someone who uses a 49-inch DQHD QD-OLED monitor daily, I won’t settle for anything less. I love having the wide expanse of screen real estate, along with the rich colors and deep blacks that OLED technology brings. If you’re looking for some big-screen OLED love and don’t want to spend upwards of $1,000, take a look at the Samsung 49-inch Odyssey OLED G9 (G91SD), which is discounted by 39 percent at Amazon, bringing the price down to just $790.27.

The Samsung Odyssey OLED G9 (G91SD) is a massive 49-inch QD-OLED monitor with a DQHD resolution (5120 x 1440). It offers a 144 Hz refresh rate and AMD FreeSync Premium Pro support.

You’ll get DQHD resolution, or 5120 x 1440, along with a 144 Hz refresh rate, 0.03 ms response time, 250 nits typical brightness, and VESA DisplayHDR True Black 400 certification. The monitor is NVIDIA G-SYNC compatible and supports AMD FreeSync Premium Pro.

As for connectivity, you’ll get two HDMI ports, one DisplayPort 1.4 port, three USB-C ports, and a 3.5 mm headphone jack. — Brandon Hill

If you’re an eSports junkie who is always craving pumping out as many frames per second as possible, it’s hard to find anything as bonkers as the Acer Nitro XV273U F5, which reaches the 1,000 Hz refresh rate threshold. It's on sale right now with a 14 percent discount, taking the price to $599.99 at Amazon.

Now we have to add a bit of levity to that 1,000 Hz figure. The XV273U F5 only reaches 540 Hz at its native QHD resolution (2560 x 1440). That's still a lofty figure for today's IPS monitors and is nothing to scoff at. To reach the 1,000 Hz refresh rate, you'll need to lower the resolution to 1280 x 720. However, for gamers looking for any kind of edge when it comes to performance, it doesn't get any better than this.

The Acer Nitro XV273U F5 is an insane gaming monitor, with a native refresh rate of 540 Hz at QHD resolution. However, if you drop down to 720p, the monitor can refresh at up to a crazy 1,000 Hz.

And it's not just raw performance where the XV273U F5 excels; the monitor has a claimed contrast ratio of 1,000:1, which is about average for an IPS monitor. However, our testing measured an incredible 2,003.4, putting it more in line with IPS Black panels.

The XV273U F5 also has plenty of video inputs, including two DisplayPort 1.4 and two HDMI 2.1. You won't find speakers or USB ports on this monitor, but there is a 3.5mm headphone jack.

Be sure to check out our full review of the Acer Nitro XV273U F5. — Brandon Hill

This portable monitor from KYY is a great choice if you're traveling but still need that extra screen real estate to fall back on. The KYY K3 is down to a record-low $55.99, and it includes a 15.6-inch 1080p IPS panel with a 60 Hz refresh rate and an anti-glare coating over the display. We've tested the slightly more expensive but almost physically identical KYY K3-3 model and found it to have excellent build quality.

The KYY K3 is a 15.6-inch portable monitor with a 1080p resolution. It features two USB-C ports, one HDMI port, and a screen cover that doubles as a stand.

You'll find two USB-C ports, including one offering DisplayPort Alt-Mode connectivity, along with a mini-HDMI. You'll find that this display is compatible with almost any system, from smartphones and tablets to a PC, laptop, or game console.

Despite the budget price, this laptop has two built-in speakers and an audio jack. There's no integrated kickstand, but for the price, you can always pick one up for a few dollars. As a cheap second monitor for your bag, or as a quick-and-easy second display for messages, this KYY K3 option will do the job well for less than $60. — Brandon Hill

Here’s an unbeatable Black Friday deal: the Samsung Odyssey OLED G6 is 58% off at Woot, plus an extra $60 off for new customers. That slashes this 240Hz OLED display from its original list price down to just $279.99 ($339.99 without the new customer bonus).

The Samsung Odyssey OLED G6 offers a 2560 x 1440 resolution, 240Hz refresh rate, 1x HDMI 2.1 port, 1x DisplayPort 1.4, a 3.5mm headphone jack and USB Type-A port, with additional built-in speakers.

Featuring a 1440p resolution and a refresh rate reaching 240Hz, this OLED panel delivers up to 400 nits of peak brightness in HDR mode. It includes complete G-Sync and FreeSync Premium Pro support, delivering all the high-end capabilities expected from a top-tier gaming monitor without demanding a high-end price tag.

The display is equipped with integrated Samsung OLED safeguard technology, a height-adjustable stand, and compatibility with 100 x 100 mm VESA mounting arms. As one of the standout Black Friday offers so far, this OLED display is worth grabbing before stock runs out. — Sayem Ahmed

The ZenScreen OLED (MQ16FC) is a fresh portable monitor from Asus, and it’s a great all-arounder. The best thing about it is that it features a gorgeous OLED panel that is not only vibrant and colorful, but also has the inky blacks that we expect from the panel technology. You'll also find a smidge more vertical resolution than most portable monitors thanks to its 1920 x 1200 resolution (FHD+). And you can get the monitor now for $199, a 29% discount off its usual asking price at Amazon.

The ASUS ZenScreen MQ16FC is a 16.1-inch portable monitor with an FHD+ OLED panel. Color performance is excellent, and it includes some nice touches like an aluminum unibody and a built-in kickstand.

The MQ16FC has excellent build quality, with an aluminum unibody design and integrated kickstand. Asus has you covered on connectivity as well, with two USB-C ports, a micro-HDMI port, and a 3.5 mm headphone jack. There's even a 1/4-inch tripod socket if that's a buying consideration for you.

In my testing, I found color performance to be excellent compared to its peers. While maximum brightness wasn't quite as high as the competition, it was perfectly acceptable in my home office testing environment.

Snag an awesome after-the-sales bargain on a new OLED monitor upgrade with a delicious 36% off deal on the 32-inch ROG PG32UCDP for $799. Now's the perfect time to upgrade your gaming setup to a WOLED panel whilst it's on sale. You can find this superb deal on Amazon, where the original list price of this screen was $1,199, so you're looking at savings of $400. That's nothing to be sniffed at in the current climate for PC gaming prices.

The Asus ROG PG32UCDP is a flat-panel gaming monitor with a 4K resolution along with a super-fast native refresh rate of 240Hz. However, it’s also a dual-mode monitor, meaning that if you drop the resolution down to FHD (1920 x 1080), the refresh rate jumps to 480Hz. As with the majority of OLED monitors, the technology allows for a rapid response time of just 0.03ms; this provides an incredibly smooth gaming experience and eliminates ghosting from fast-motion gameplay.

The Asus ROG PG32UCDP is a great all-around gaming monitor, offering a 32" WOLED that is dual-mode capable. It'll operate at up to 240 Hz at its native 4K resolution, or at up to 480 Hz at 1080p resolution.

The WOLED panel sports VESA DisplayHDR 400 True Black compliance, 99% DCI-P3 color gamut, true 10-bit color, and a Delta E <2 color difference for astonishing HDR performance in your games.

Asus' superb WOLED monitor also comes with plenty of connectivity options for connecting to your PC and other computing hardware. You can hook up your game consoles like the Xbox Series X, Switch 2, and PlayStation 5, or maybe even your laptop for work or school, or anything else with a compatible video port. There are 2x HDMI 2.1 ports, 1x DisplayPort 1.4, and 1x USB port. — Brandon Hill

The Samsung Odyssey OLED G5 G50SF 27-inch, 1440p gaming monitor has hit an all-time low of just $299 with a coupon at Amazon. Sporting a modest 180Hz refresh rate, in addition to a 0.03ms GtG response time, this gaming monitor might not be the fastest, but it'll certainly look fantastic on your desk.

The Samsung Odyssey OLED G50SF is a 27-inch 1440p QD-OLED gaming monitor that offers up to 180 Hz refresh rate, 99% coverage of DCI-P3, 0.03ms of response time, a heap of features to prevent OLED burn-in. Just remember to use the coupon at checkout to slice $20 off its listed price.

This display hits 99% of the DCI-P3 color gamut and supports HDR10 for those bright highlights and inky clacks. Samsung has also added a glare-free finish to this panel, in addition to several anti-burn-in safeguards to ensure the longevity of the monitor. The Odyssey OLED G50SF sports DisplayPort 1.2 for your PC, in addition to an HDMI 2.0 input for any additional consoles you may have lying around. Do note the lack of HDMI 2.1, meaning that VRR is off the table for this particular panel for console gaming, but at under $300 for an OLED display, it's difficult to complain. — Sayem Ahmed

If you're looking for an even bigger upgrade this Black Friday, look no further than LG's C6 OLED Evo TV. While it's not, strictly speaking, a gaming monitor, more than a few folks at Tom's Hardware towers use televisions as gaming displays, especially if said PC also happens to be conveniently located in a living room. LG's lineup of OLED televisions has been a go-to for years, and Amazon is offering up the latest model, LG's C6 Evo, at a staggering 48% off right now.

The LG C6 OLED TV comes equipped with a massive 65-inch OLED panel, heaps of gaming-focused features like Nvidia G-Sync, FreeSync Premium Pro, and a refresh rate of up to 165Hz.

Now just $1399.99 at Amazon, the LG C6 OLED TV ships with some impressive features, like WebOS support for plenty of apps, as well as Dolby Vision, a brilliantly bright screen, support for HDR10, HDMI 2.1 for VRR gaming at up to 165Hz, and, of course, an unmatched contrast ratio when compared to any other panel type out there. A television might be an unconventional choice to run as your main gaming monitor, but if your PC already lives in your living room, or another space where a TV naturally fits, you can't do much better than the LG C6 OLED Evo at this price point. — Sayem Ahmed

The Acer Predator X27U W1 features a 26.5-inch QD-OLED Penta Tandem panel. Acer claims that the Penta Tandem panel boosts luminous efficiency, doubles panel life, and allows for peak brightness of up to 1,000 nits (although typical brightness is closer to 200 nits).

As is typical for most 27-inch monitors these days, you get 2560x1440 or QHD resolution. You also get a 240 Hz refresh rate with support for AMD FreeSync Premium, 0.03 ms GtG response time, 99 percent coverage of the sRGB color space, an anti-glare coating over the display panel, and dual 3-watt speakers. On the connectivity front, you get two HDMI 2.1 ports, two DisplayPort 1.4 ports, and a single 3.5 mm headphone jack.

The Acer Predator X27U W1 is a 27-inch gaming monitor with a QHD resolution, 240 Hz refresh rate, and a QD-OLED panel. It supports AMD FreeSync Premium and includes two HDMI 2.1 and two DisplayPort 1.4 ports.

The Predator X27U W1 is also adjustable for height, pivot, tilt, and swivel. The monitor rings up with a 14 percent discount at Amazon, bringing its final price to $269.99. — Brandon Hill

We’ve seen quite a few monitors on sale so far for Black Friday week, and we have another solid deal for a WOLED panel in Gigabyte’s MO27Q28G. This 27-inch monitor uses Tandem OLED technology, which, according to our review (which earned 4.5 stars) on this monitor, is “... two layers of light-emitting diodes stacked together…” Essentially, light output increases, power decreases, and burn-in risk is lower as more diodes do less work. Anything that helps to mitigate one of OLED's biggest drawbacks is always welcomed, especially if your workflow consists of a lot of static on screen items (think icons, taskbars, tickers).

Save big on this awesome 27-inch Tandem OLED 280Hz gaming monitor from Gigabyte. Originally priced at $600, this deal is hard to pass up for a premium OLED monitor and a excellent option to make the jump to OLED without going 4K.

The QHD (2560x1440) panel sports a 280Hz refresh rate, adaptive-sync, and DisplayHDR500. It covers over 99% of DCI-P3 color gamut and 84% of BT.2020 (90/75/95% for R/G/B) and 1,500 cd/m2 brightness. It comes with two HDMI (v2.1) ports and one DisplayPort (v1.4). It also has USB passthrough with two USB 3.2 Gen 1 (5 Gbps) ports. As the review states, if gaming is your primary focus, the MO27Q28G has few, if any, equals, which says a lot. And now that it’s discounted $250 (33%), it’s a steal compared to the MSRP.

This is one of the better Black Friday deals for monitors. Samsung's Odyssey OLED G6's price has dropped precipitously at Woot, with 57% off its list price and an additional $60 off for new Woot customers. If you're a new customer at Woot, that makes this monitor an incredible $279.99, otherwise, it's still a great deal at $339.99.

Get an additional $60 off for new Woot customers.

The Samsung Odyssey OLED G6 offers QHD 2560 x 1440 resolution, fast 240Hz refresh rate, 1x HDMI (v2.1), 1x DisplayPort (v1.4), a 3.5mm headphone jack and USB Type-A port. It also has built in speakers.

This QHD 1440p OLED display sports a refresh rate of up to 240Hz, with 400 nits of peak brightness when in HDR. It fully supports FreeSync Premium Pro and G-Sync support, and offers all of the premium fixings of a fully-featured gaming monitor, without the premium price point.

Expect Samsung's OLED safeguard features built straight into the panel, with a height-adjustable stand, and support for a 100 x 100 mm VESA mount, in case you want to mount it up on an arm. This OLED panel is one of the best deals that we've seen on Black Friday so far, so be sure to pick it up before it sells out. — Joe Shields

Dell's range of Alienware gaming monitors has been a mainstay on Tom's Hardware for years. Above average build quality and excellent performance has made them a great choice for gamers looking for an upgrade. Today you can snag a swift 280Hz 34-inch Dell Alienware AW3426DW ultrawide for $649.99 in this awesome Amazon Black Friday deal.

This 34-inch, 3440 x 1440 panel can hit 280 Hz and is brighter than its predecessor, thanks to its five-layer tandem tech. Our reviewer praised it for its colorful image and low input lag with "perfect motion resolution."

We reviewed the Alienware AW3426DW, with the monitor earning an Editor's Choice award for its solid value in the 34-inch curved ultra-wide genre due to its premium imagery and performance. The size and shape are also a good balance between gaming immersion and workday utility.

From our color testing in the review, we found the panel was colorful and well-balanced out of the box, but you can achieve 105% DCI-P3 coverage with couple of minor calibration adjustments.

This is a curved gaming monitor with a smooth 1800R curve that wraps around your peripheral vision. The mix of the low 0.03 response time and rapid 280Hz refresh rate makes for an incredibly smooth gaming experience with zero ghosting in fast-moving games. — Joe Shields

From what we've seen of the sales so far during this Black Friday event, the real winners so far have been the fantastic discounts on OLED monitors. In this instance, it's Gigabyte's 27-inch MO27Q28G OLED gaming monitor that has dipped $200 to just $399. That's a heck of a good price for a Tandem OLED display with these specifications.

The MO27Q28G sports a crisp 2560 x 1440 (QHD) pixel resolution on a flat panel, a superfast 0.03ms gray-to-gray response time, and an even faster 280Hz refresh rate. That alone is a great start for a monitor, but add adaptive sync, DisplayHDR 500 certification, and color coverage of 99% of the DCI-P3 color gamut, and you have a gaming monitor that can display your games and media with beautiful inky blacks and eye-popping color.

Save big on this awesome 27-inch Tandem OLED 280Hz gaming monitor from Gigabyte. Originally priced at $600, this deal is hard to pass up for a premium OLED monitor and a excellent option to make the jump to OLED without going 4K.

The screen has super-thin bezels around the edge to maximise the screen real estate, and for connectivity, there are two HDMI 2.1 ports, one DisplayPort 1.4, and two USB 3.2 Gen 1 (5 Gbps) ports.

In our review of the Gigabyte MO27Q28G, we awarded the monitor 4.5 stars and an Editor's Choice Award for the amazing value for money for such a feature-rich OLED gaming monitor. We loved the build quality, super-low input lag, and out-of-the-box color calibration, although for the best color settings, you will want to further calibrate the screen. — Stewart Bendle

If our last Samsung Odyssey deal didn't grab your attention, this one certainly will. The Samsung Odyssey OLED G8 monitor is 36% off at Woot, pushing the price down to $699.99. New customers get that extra $60 discount, meaning you can save heaps on a flagship-level 4K display without breaking the bank entirely.

The Samsung Odyssey OLED G8 offers a 3840 x 2160 resolution, 240Hz refresh rate, 1x HDMI 2.1 port, 1x DisplayPort 1.4, 1x USB-C (DP Alt Mode with 98W PD), 2x USB-A 3.2 downstream ports, and a 3.5mm headphone jack.

Getting a 4K OLED display with as many features as this, and at this price point, doesn't come around too often. Sporting up to 1000 nits of peak brightness, this 4K display has almost everything you could want out of an OLED monitor. The only thing missing in its feature set is built-in speakers, but that's nothing a set of cheap freestanding desktop speakers can't fix.

Expect Samsung OLED Safeguard+ to prevent burn-in, in addition to a height-adjustable swivel stand, VESA mount, and all of the gaming features you want, like VRR support, as well as FreeSync Premium Pro and G-Sync compatibility. This should be your next main monitor upgrade, if you've got the cash to spare. — Sayem Ahmed

If you're looking for a panel that doesn't compromise on pure refresh rates, Innocn's GA27M1Q QD-OLED display might be just the panel you're after. Sporting a 27-inch size, QHD resolution, and a blisteringly fast 500Hz refresh rate, this display's got heaps of gaming performance under the hood, especially if you play esports-focused titles like Valorant or Counter-Strike 2.

Offering a 2560 x 1440p resolution, in addition to dual HDMI 2.1 ports and DisplayPort 1.4, as well as 1x USB-B upstream and 2x Type-A downstream ports, this panel offers performance without the premium price, thanks to its rapid 500Hz refresh rate and support for FreeSync and G-Sync.

Expect a sweet spot between performance and resolution here. With the display's 256 x 1440p resolution and refresh rate, you'll want a fairly powerful system with a decent CPU under the hood to reliably saturate the monitor here. One important note is that the semi-gloss display isn't actually all that bright when compared to more expensive competitors. While you do get a 0.03ms GtG response time, the GA27M1Q's SDR brightness tops out at 300 nits. However, considering the wealth of other features on offer here, it might be a fine trade for a very well rounded panel that's almost garaunteed to look fantastic with deep blacks and a near-infinite contrast ratio. — Sayem Ahmed

Buying a monitor over Black Friday could be one of the best ways to elevate your gaming setup. In 2026, PC component pricing means that upgrades to RAM, SSDs, and GPUs are much more expensive than they used to be. Monitors, by contrast, are cheaper. So, you could spend less and upgrade your viewing experience in a number of different ways. You could get a larger monitor for more immersive viewing and multitasking, upgrade to a higher refresh rate for more frame headroom, or increase your resolution for more detail. Of course, you could also make the leap to OLED, one of the biggest upgrades you can make to gaming right now.

Black Friday has begun and we're tracking all the very best deals on OLED gaming monitors, productivity monitors, and more!

#10329. Hands-on: Sony’s Walkman-revival USB-C headphones are back in stock and worth a look

Sony’s iconic Walkman headphones are back in the USB-C MDR-3R and, after quickly selling out on launch day, they’ve now been restocked. And, after using them, I can see why they sold out so quickly.

The MDR-3R are Sony’s revival of the wired over-ear headphones that many used with a classic Walkman player. The retro style still looks great in 2026, but using an original pair is a bit of a headache in today’s age of headphone jack-less smartphones. So it was nice to see Sony give this a revival with USB-C.

Update 11/24: After we first published our hands-on with MDR-3R last week, Sony’s USB-C headphones sold out pretty quickly again. As of today, though, they’re back in stock and still shipping in early December – don’t miss out!

While the style won’t be for everyone, I think these work brilliantly. The sound quality is excellent and having a pair of headphones that doesn’t fully enclose my ears is pretty refreshing. There’s no noise cancellation, but with open-ear earbuds becoming more popular, I actually really like these as a similar solution (though high volumes will definitely be heard by those around you). I’m not fully cut off from the world around me, but I’m also able to get good sound quality. Lows are the weakness here, with unimpressive bass drops, but the sound quality is crisp and clear and pretty neutral, and the open-ish style makes it feel like the room around me is filled with music.

The physical hardware is great. While a plastic and metal build is objectively not as comfy as a premium pair of ANC headphones, the extremely light weight helps MDR-3R become an afterthought. You simply forget you’re wearing them after a few minutes.

The earpads are swappable, with orange and blue options included in the box.

As for the USB-C cable, it’s fully plug-and-play. No app needed and it worked across every device I tested (including Pixel, which doesn’t work with all USB-C audio output). I do wish the cable was perhaps a few inches longer, but it’s long enough to wear the headphones with my phone in my front pocket. There’s a remote along the cable for play/pause and volume adjustments, though I think it’s a little too high on the cable.

For $59.99, these are a fun pair of USB-C headphones to have on hand. They sound good, work great, and don’t cost an arm and a leg. I can see why they sold out so quickly on launch day – in just 10 hours, Sony told me.

Sony MDR-3R are back in stock now and shipping in early December. If you want a pair, I say don’t wait. They’re well worth at least trying if you can get them for retail price – please don’t give in to the scalpers selling these at double, they’re not worth that.

#10328. Grand Theft Auto VI is a different kind of GTA — so it needed a different kind of ending

Posts from this topic will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Posts from this topic will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Posts from this topic will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

GTA VI producer Rob Nelson explains Rockstar’s approach to letting players explore Vice City after the main story.

GTA VI producer Rob Nelson explains Rockstar’s approach to letting players explore Vice City after the main story.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

In most Grand Theft Auto games, and most open-world games for that matter, the world is left open for you to explore once the credits roll. It could be Los Santos or a twisted take on Manhattan, but the idea is that the main story is just one part of the experience. After that’s done, there are usually still places you haven’t explored or side missions you left lingering. But Grand Theft Auto VI doesn’t work quite the same way. Because of its storyline, which involves a couple trying to get out of the criminal life for good, that kind of ending didn’t really fit.

“In this one it didn’t make sense,” Rob Nelson, producer on GTA VI and co-studio head at developer Rockstar North, told me ahead of the game’s launch. “Their story needed to end and have some kind of conclusion.”

This story contains light spoilers for the ending of Grand Theft Auto VI, along with a key plot point from chapter 1.

To be clear, you can still play GTA VI after the main storyline wraps up. But in order for that to happen, you have to zip back in time to a moment before a pivotal decision — I won’t spoil it for you — that alters the lives of main characters Jason and Lucia, along with their young son Tomás, who they’re attempting to get custody of. Nelson says the team tried “all sorts of things” but soon realized that “in no way did it make sense” to have the game end like a traditional GTA experience.

“Their story needed to end and have some kind of conclusion.”

“You go back and have this open time again where you have the best single-player safehouse you’ve ever had in a GTA, with a garage full of supercars, a helipad, a gym, and all of the stuff you could ever want,” he says of the solution the studio landed on. “And you can spend as long as you want there. But you don’t have Tommy. So the characters don’t have the one thing that they wanted at the start. There’s the tension where you have to spend some extra time grinding to make some more money without knowing what it’s going to get you, and it plays out differently if you get that money.”

One advantage of this structure is that it lets you try out different endings. GTA VI’s story can wrap up in multiple ways based on a variety of factors: how much money you have saved up, what kind of criminal you were throughout the game, and some key decisions you’re forced to make in the final moments. The new postgame structure creates an opportunity to see some of the alternate ways the story can go. “There’s a large number of potential outcomes based on how you played it,” Nelson says.

#10326. Build Live Video Chat With WebRTC: From First Call to Production Debugging

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Adding real-time video to a web app used to mean plugins, proprietary SDKs and a lot of money. Today every modern browser ships with WebRTC, a set of APIs that lets two browsers exchange audio, video and data directly. The catch is that WebRTC gives you building blocks, not a finished feature. This guide walks through those blocks in the order you actually need them, with the exact API calls you need, and then covers the production issues that tutorials usually skip.

A browser-to-browser call has four moving parts:

Start with the local preview. Browsers only allow camera access on HTTPS or localhost, so serve your page accordingly.

1.     Request a stream with navigator.mediaDevices.getUserMedia(), passing video constraints (an ideal width of 1280 and height of 720 is a sensible default) and audio constraints with echoCancellation and noiseSuppression enabled.

2.     Assign the returned MediaStream to the srcObject property of your local video element.

3.     Keep a reference to the stream, because you will add its tracks to the peer connection later.

Set the muted and playsinline attributes on the local video element. Without muted users hear themselves, and without playsinline iOS Safari opens the video full screen.

The peers need a way to find each other. A tiny Node.js server using the ws package is enough for development. Its whole job is to relay messages between the peers in a room:

1.     Create a WebSocket server (for example with the ws package) listening on its own port.

2.     Keep a map of room names to the set of sockets in each room.

3.     When a client sends a join message, store the room name on the socket and add it to that room's set.

4.     For every other message type, forward the raw message to the other sockets in the same room, and never echo it back to the sender.

5.     On disconnect, remove the socket from its room so stale peers do not receive messages.

In production you would add authentication, limit room size to two for one-to-one calls, and validate message types, but the shape stays the same.

Both sides create an RTCPeerConnection, add their local tracks and listen for the remote ones:

1.     Create a new RTCPeerConnection with an iceServers list that contains at least one STUN server.

2.     Loop over the local stream's tracks and call addTrack() for each one.

3.     In the ontrack handler, attach the first remote stream to your remote video element.

4.     In the onicecandidate handler, send every new candidate to the other peer through your signalling channel as a candidate message.

One peer creates an offer, the other answers, and both apply each other's descriptions. Candidates arrive asynchronously in the background.

1.     The caller runs createOffer(), applies it with setLocalDescription() and sends the description as an offer message.

2.     The callee applies the offer with setRemoteDescription(), runs createAnswer(), applies it locally and sends it back as an answer.

3.     The caller applies the answer with setRemoteDescription().

4.     Both sides pass every incoming candidate message to addIceCandidate().

If both peers might start a call at the same time, look up the "perfect negotiation" pattern on MDN. It assigns one side as polite and resolves offer collisions cleanly instead of leaving both peers stuck.

On a home network, STUN alone often works. On corporate Wi-Fi, mobile carriers and symmetric NATs it frequently does not, and the call silently fails to connect. A TURN server relays media when a direct path is impossible. The open-source coturn server is the usual choice.

In practice, your iceServers list should contain your own STUN URL plus a TURN URL with a username and credential, so the browser can fall back to the relay automatically when direct connectivity fails.

Generate short-lived TURN credentials on your backend rather than hard-coding them, and budget for bandwidth: relayed calls pass every frame through your server.

Users deny camera access, unplug headsets and switch from Wi-Fi to 4G mid-call. Catch NotAllowedError and show a clear explanation, listen for devicechange events, and use RTCRtpSender.replaceTrack() to swap cameras without renegotiating the whole call.

Listen to pc.onconnectionstatechange. When the state becomes disconnected, wait a few seconds before giving up, because it often recovers. On failed, call pc.restartIce() to try new network paths.

Use RTCRtpSender.setParameters() to cap the bitrate on weak connections, and read pc.getStats() to monitor packet loss and round-trip time. Showing a small "poor connection" indicator does more for perceived quality than any codec tweak.

Mesh calls, where every participant connects to every other, work for two or three people. Beyond that, upload bandwidth explodes. Group calls need a Selective Forwarding Unit (SFU) such as mediasoup, LiveKit or Janus, which receives each stream once and forwards it to the others.

Tutorials end at a working demo, but the fastest way to understand what production WebRTC looks like is to watch a real call from the inside. Chrome ships an internal diagnostics page that shows every peer connection the browser opens, and it works on any site that uses WebRTC.

1.     Open chrome://webrtc-internals in one tab and keep it open.

2.     In another tab, start a call on your own demo and find its RTCPeerConnection entry.

3.     Expand that entry and look at the ICE candidate pairs: you will see whether the call went direct (host or srflx) or through a TURN relay (relay).

4.     Open the stats graphs for the outbound video stream and watch the bitrate, frame rate and resolution adapt when you throttle the network in DevTools.

5.     Check the negotiated codec and how quickly the connection recovers when you switch Wi-Fi off and back on.

Once you can read your own call, repeat the exercise on a production service. Any browser-based product works, whether a meeting tool or a live video chat that pairs two visitors, because webrtc-internals shows the same data for every site. Expect differences from your demo: more candidate pairs, a relay candidate in the list and a bitrate that adapts faster. Seeing them makes the earlier sections concrete, from why TURN matters to how bandwidth estimation reacts to packet loss.

The one-to-one call above is the core of many products, from telehealth consultations and tutoring to customer support. The engineering challenges grow with the use case: random matching needs queueing and presence on the signalling server, public platforms need moderation and reporting, and global audiences need TURN servers in several regions.

Start with the minimal version, get it working across Chrome, Firefox and Safari on both desktop and mobile, and add TURN before real users arrive. Once the call is reliable, every other feature becomes a much easier problem.

Its first home is the GP2 SSD, rated for more than 18 million random reads per second.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The Kioxia Corporation showcased a prototype of its new XL-Flash Generation 3 technology, next-generation low-latency, high-performance flash memory, at its KIOXIA Forum in Tokyo. The flash, which uses CMOS directly Bonded to Array, or CBA, for better power efficiency and storage density, is about 135% more efficient with 70% higher bit density than Gen 2, and its 3 µs average read latency is less than 10% of that of Kioxia’s standard BiCS8 TLC. Samples are due March 2027, and Kioxia named its GP2 enterprise SSDs, rated for more than 18 million 512-byte random read IOPS, as its first product using it.

The low-latency XL-Flash fills “a new memory tier” to bridge the gap between DRAM and regular flash memory, in a way that can complement or replace some DRAM to help drive down costs, especially in AI servers and data centers. This has some similarities to Optane, which used 3D XPoint instead, as a storage class memory (SCM) option to reach higher IOPS. Intel and Micron’s 3D XPoint stored bits as changes in the cell material’s resistance rather than as trapped charge like NAND, and Intel exited the Optane business in 2022. The XL-Flash NAND is built on BiCS flash technology, but it’s tuned for low read latency and high write endurance.

The first generation was SLC with under-5 µs reads, arriving in 2019. By 2022, Gen 2 added 2-bit MLC as an option for lower bit cost, trading some like-for-like performance for better price-to-density. Gen 3 is reported to use SLC, and its 3 µs average read latency challenges the first gen’s sub-5 µs rating while being more than ten times faster than the 40 µs of standard BiCS8 TLC. This is within the same ballpark as Optane SSDs. The flash also reportedly has SLC endurance at 150,000 to 250,000 P/E cycles, at least 50x standard TLC, running at a 4.8 Gb/s interface speed.

XL-Flash achieves lower latency, in part, by using more, smaller planes (16 per die, with a 4KB page, on earlier generations), which is common with SLC and low-latency flash, and especially helps with smaller I/O. Kioxia’s GP drives target 512B accesses rather than the typical 4KB, a pattern that matches developments in enterprise storage requirements for AI and other emerging workloads that involve constant fine-grained memory lookups. 3D XPoint would outmatch it for write performance, though, due to not needing to erase for new data.

The newer gen is able to maintain high levels of performance at much higher density thanks to CBA bonding, where Kioxia makes the logic CMOS wafer and flash memory-cell wafer separately and later bonds them. This technology also improves the efficiency of 512-byte reads, by Kioxia’s own tests, which matches the design intention of the forthcoming GP2. Kioxia hasn’t disclosed full details on the flash, such as layer count.

The GP2 Super High IOPS SSD will be Kioxia’s first product to use the new flash, promising high levels of performance, including up to 28 GB/s sequential reads, if it can saturate PCIe 6.0 x4 as expected. Kioxia’s 2.5x IOPS number, versus “typical TLC-based SSDs,” comes from a comparison to its own CM10 drives, for 512B I/O. Endurance will also be excellent at up to 50 drive writes per day, which is within the ballpark of Optane storage.

Kioxia is considering E1.S and E3.S form factors, and the drive will support direct liquid cooling, which is increasingly necessary for certain data centers, including GPU-heavy ones where the GP2 is likely to operate.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

These drives will serve as a flash tier to help get more out of a GPU’s HBM, and Kioxia first showed the GP series with Nvidia earlier this year. Offloading memory by any means possible is becoming a strategy with AI, even at the enthusiast level, due to high memory demands and how the technology and its KV caching work.

While the flash should sample to select customers before the end of the first quarter of 2027, Kioxia only promises GP2 evaluation samples to select customers by the end of that year. Exact specifications for the drive may differ, but what is clear is that later GP drives will target up to 100 million random-read IOPS that Kioxia and Nvidia have been working toward for AI servers. Kioxia announced its XL1 series of CXL memory expansion modules on XL-Flash in August, and it “will continue to leverage the speed, power efficiency, and endurance of XL-FLASH” for emerging data center needs.

#10324. Safetensors is Joining the PyTorch Foundation

Today, we're announcing that Safetensors has joined the PyTorch Foundation as a foundation-hosted project under the Linux Foundation, alongside DeepSpeed, Helion, Ray, vLLM, and PyTorch itself.

Safetensors started as a Hugging Face project born out of a concrete need: a way to store and share model weights that couldn't execute arbitrary code. The pickle-based formats that dominated the ecosystem at the time meant that there was a very real risk you’d be running malicious code. While this was an acceptable risk when ML was still budding, it would become unacceptable as open model sharing became central to how the ML community works.

The format we built is intentionally simple: a JSON header with a hard limit of 100MB, describing tensor metadata, followed by raw tensor data. Zero-copy loading that maps tensors directly from disk. Lazy loading so you can read individual weights without deserializing an entire checkpoint.

What we didn't fully anticipate was how broadly it would be adopted. Today, Safetensors is the default format for model distribution across the Hugging Face Hub and others, used by tens of thousands of models across all modalities in ML. It has become the preferred way for the open source ML community to share models.

We want Safetensors to truly belong to the community. The project has always been open source, but code contributions are just one part of its evolution. By bringing more companies and contributors into the governance of the project, we make sure that progress reflects the breadth of the community building on top of it. Joining the PyTorch Foundation means Safetensors now has a vendor-neutral home. The trademark, the repository, and the governance of the project sit with the Linux Foundation rather than any single company. Hugging Face's two core maintainers, Luc and Daniel, remain on the Technical Steering Committee and continue to lead the project day-to-day, but Safetensors now formally belongs to the community that depends on it.

We believe safety is best guaranteed when every contributor can build on what already exists; a principle now embedded in the project's governance itself.

For the vast majority of users, nothing changes. The format is the same, the APIs are the same, the Hub integration is the same: no breaking changes. Models stored in Safetensors format today will continue to work exactly as they do now.

For contributors, the path to becoming a maintainer is now formally documented and open to anyone in the community. The project's governance lives in GOVERNANCE.md and MAINTAINERS.md in the repository. For organizations building on top of Safetensors, neutral governance under the Linux Foundation provides a stable, long-term foundation, entirely community-driven.

Safetensors is a well-established project, adopted by the ecosystem at large, but we're still convinced we're at the very beginning of the project.

We're working with the PyTorch team so that Safetensors may be used within PyTorch core as a serialization system for torch models.

The coming months will see significant growth, and we couldn't think of a better home for that next chapter than the PyTorch Foundation. The roadmap ahead includes device-aware loading and saving, so tensors can load directly onto CUDA, ROCm, and other accelerators without unnecessary CPU staging.

We're also building first-class APIs for Tensor Parallel and Pipeline Parallel loading, so each rank or pipeline stage loads only the weights it needs. And as the ecosystem's quantization landscape continues to evolve, we'll be formalizing support for FP8, block-quantized formats like GPTQ and AWQ, and sub-byte integer types.

These are problems the whole ecosystem has a stake in solving, and being inside the PyTorch Foundation means we can work on them in collaboration with the other hosted projects rather than in parallel.

Safetensors is open source and contributions are welcome at every level, from bug reports and documentation to new features and participation in governance.

If you're a developer, researcher, or organization that builds on Safetensors and want to be more involved in shaping its direction, open an issue, start a discussion, or reach out to the maintainers directly. The project has always belonged to the community that uses it. The governance now reflects that too.

Will there be a concerted effort now to get newer (and older) LLM models to adopt the more secure safetensors format rather than allowing AI developers to continue with pickle files as they did in the past? And what would some of the objections be, if any, for a developer to not transition to safetensors format?

#10323. This gaming mouse should be a Logitech-killer, but it has one big flaw

Keychron’s G6 HE uses magnetic switches like Logitech’s Superstrike mice, but the clicks are all off.﻿

Keychron’s G6 HE uses magnetic switches like Logitech’s Superstrike mice, but the clicks are all off.﻿

When Keychron announced its $90 G6 HE gaming mouse, I immediately thought, “Cool! A cheaper alternative to the pricey $180 Logitech G Pro X2 Superstrike.” Logitech’s innovation with the Superstrike is using magnetic Hall effect switches for a user-adjustable mouse click depth, with haptic vibrations mimicking the tactile click feel. The Keychron G6 HE, as its name indicates, also uses Hall effect switches for that same kind of customization. But something felt immediately off as I began testing it.

The mouse’s shape and design are very reminiscent of Logitech G Pro models, with more colorful flair. The magnetic switches are there and easily customizable (through a browser-based app, no less). But the clicks? The clicks are all wrong.

The left and right mouse buttons on the G6 HE use Keychron’s MagOptic switches, which are both magnetic Hall effect and optical. They click just like any standard mouse, regardless of where you set the actuation point. There are no fancy haptics on the Keychron. If you set the buttons to a shallow hair-trigger depth, you’ll register a press before you actually feel or hear any click. Set the depth for a very heavy press, and the mouse clicks before it actually registers. That… kind of defeats the purpose here.

There’s not much point in tuning the actuation depth of the G6 HE’s buttons if the click feel doesn’t match it. I suppose it’s still nice to have a hair-trigger-like setting for taking faster single shots in an FPS, but not feeling anything when you shoot is weird. And it gets frustrating when using the G6 HE as a regular mouse for productivity — like you’re getting phantom clicks as you mouse around your computer. At least I can feel my accidental clicks when using a Logitech Superstrike with the action set too high, and I know I’m to blame for leaving the mouse on my try-hard settings.

I reached out to Keychron for the reasoning behind the G6 HE’s magnetic-but-not-haptic setup, and cofounder Fab Chan said, “There are two reasons for this design. First, many users still prefer the feel of a traditional click over haptics. Second, a haptic motor adds weight, and for this model we prioritized a lighter design. That said, we’re planning a model with haptic feedback. It will be slightly heavier than the G6 HE, and we’ll share more details soon.”

The G6 HE is a lightweight mouse. It’s only 49g with its battery, or 40g in wired mode with the battery removed. The Logitech X2 Superstrike is 60g, and the newer X3 Superstrike is 59g — each still pretty light. If you ignore all the Hall effect stuff and just use the G6 HE as a regular mouse, it has some things going for it over the Superstrikes. In addition to its lighter build and much lower price, it feels a tiny bit comfier in my hand, thanks to its side walls that curve slightly inward at the bottom.

One of its best features is hot-swappable batteries. From my time testing Angry Miao’s AM Infinity Mouse, I know that once you can pop out a magnetic battery pack and quickly swap it, you never want to go back to plugging in your mouse to charge. You can also get the G6 HE in black with a standard built-in rechargeable battery for $15 less, but I don’t think that’s enough savings to forgo the convenience of hot-swap batteries.

The G6 HE’s charging base doubles as the wireless receiver, and of course it’s lit up with customizable RGB lighting. It has four programmable buttons for on-the-fly changes to things like DPI, lighting, mouse profiles, or just about anything else you want to program. The browser-based Keychron Launcher software is robust and makes tinkering with the G6 HE or its base very easy. And for some reason, the receiver / charging base is designed like a vacuum tube, which is fun, but it means you’re unscrewing its clear housing to access the battery — a little tedious.

I can’t shake my disappointment with the G6 HE’s lackadaisical magnetic switch implementation. Keychron seems proud of the fancy MagOptic Switch it put into the G6 HE, even going so far as to call it “next gen,” but this mouse seems a jack of all trades and master of none. The G6 HE is cheaper than most other mice with hot-swap batteries — which can still make it worthwhile if you don’t care about all the Hall effect stuff — but that is its lone saving grace.

We’ll have to wait and see if Keychron’s follow-up model with haptics can properly compete with the Superstrike mice and their hallmark feature. I’m excited to see where Hall effect tech goes in mice, and how more companies can evolve it, but the G6 HE is a half-measure.

#10322. Google Messages replacing old Gemini with new ‘tasks’ chat, and it’s very proactive

Last week, Google announced that Gemini tasks (previously called Spark) is now available to free users in the US, along with an integration in Google Messages. In testing, I’ve found this instance of Gemini to be proactive and feel more like an assistant than the Gemini app does.

The original Gemini integration in Google Messages dates back to 2024 with a dedicated FAB (floating action button) above Start chat. It lets you have a straightforward conversation with Gemini.

This updated experience makes use of the “Channels” feature introduced last week that allows you to Text or Email with Gemini to accomplish tasks.

With the latest Google Messages beta (version 20261120_01_RC00), we’re seeing the Gemini FAB (or top-right corner icon with the homepage redesign) open gemini.google.com/channels on a fresh install. If you’ve already set up the new integration, the shortcut takes you to the new chat, which uses RCS Business Messaging behind the scenes.

After using it for the past few days, the proactive nature of Gemini tasks in Google Messages has really stood out. Every morning, Gemini messages me about what’s on my schedule or what should be on my radar. Examples include:

While this instance of Gemini is ostensibly for tasks, I’ve been able to ask general knowledge questions, like about the weather, similar to the old experience. Additionally, you can upload attachments like images and files.

This new Google Messages integration is currently available in the US and requires that you have tasks enabled in the Gemini app.

Laptop prices have been a hot-button topic all year long thanks to RAMageddon. We’ve seen existing models get more expensive and new models arrive at higher prices than last-gen — sometimes with lower specs, too. 2026 in general has been a bad time to buy a computer. But thankfully, Black Friday can offer a tiny bit of respite.

If the computer you currently use is working well for you, good. Happy for you. But if you’re in the market for something more powerful, bigger, smaller, thinner, etc. — and you prefer new over used — you can currently save some decent dough on MacBooks, Windows notebooks, and gaming laptops.

The big, multi-hundred-dollar savings are typically reserved for higher-end models with bigger specs, like Windows models running Nvidia’s new Arm-based RTX Spark platform — which are getting their first major discounts. More budget-friendly laptops are also receiving decent discounts right now, though, including the MacBook Neo. The current $100 discount on Apple’s budget laptop might seem like small potatoes considering it’s just a return to its original price, but it’s the best you can do for now (if you can’t hold out for a rumored new one in 2027).

As always, the deals below are for laptops we’ve reviewed or tested firsthand in some way at The Verge — either that exact model or a similar one we expect to be equally good. There are many laptops out there and myriad deals running now through Cyber Monday, but if any of these fit your needs, you can’t go wrong.

Apple’s most affordable laptop uses the same A18 Pro chip found in the iPhone 16 Pro. It features a vibrant 13-inch display, surprisingly good speakers, and 8GB of RAM, making it a solid option for students and anyone who needs a laptop for everyday tasks. Read our review.

Apple’s latest MacBook Air features an M5 chip and starts with 512GB of storage, with significantly faster performance than prior generations. It’s still an excellent machine despite the higher base price, especially given the battery life and speakers. Read our review.

Apple gave its base model MacBook Pro an upgrade to a 12-core M6 chip for 2026, and not a whole lot else. Read our review.

The non-OLED M5 Pro and M5 Max versions of the MacBook Pro deliver exceptional power and speed, making them ideal for creative work while offering best-in-class battery life. Read our review.

Apple’s latest (and priciest) MacBook Pro is its first with a touchscreen. The new PROLED models pack familiar M5 Pro and M5 Max chips into a thinner and lighter chassis. Read our review.

The best XPS 13 in years. It doesn’t have a headphone jack and starts with only 8GB of RAM but it’s an excellent thin-and-light with a great screen, a solid Intel chip, and speedy storage.

An incredibly nice feeling laptop with great battery life and a love-it-or-hate-it latticeless keyboard. Read our review.

The latest 13-inch Surface Laptop has lower starting specs than the 2025 model, with 8GB of RAM, but it’s still a well put together laptop that now feels better to use after some notable Windows 11 updates. Read our review.

The IdeaPad Slim 3x offers a 15.3-inch touchscreen and a comfortable keyboard. It runs a base Snapdragon X chip, making it well-suited for the basics. The real highlights are battery life and port selection. The speakers, however, are terrible. Read our review.

One of Lenovo’s new alternatives to the MacBook Neo, with an Intel Wildcat Lake chip, 8GB of RAM, and plenty of ports.

A great convertible Chromebook with fantastic battery life. Read our review.

A 16-inch laptop that’s as light as a 13-inch MacBook Air, packing a powerful Snapdragon X2 Elite Extreme chip and 48GB of RAM.

Asus’s Zenbook A14 is a bit of a MacBook Air wannabe, but it’s a compelling alternative if you value a superlight Windows laptop with long battery life. The 2025 model sports an Arm-based Qualcomm Snapdragon X Plus chip, a nice 14-inch OLED display, and a sleek textured beige finish.

An expensive but excellent dual-screen laptop with a powerful Intel Panther Lake chip. The only thing better than a lovely OLED display is having two of them. Read our review.

An affordable laptop with a large 16-inch display, plenty of ports, and a solid Intel Core 7 350 chip. Read our review of the Snapdragon model.

The Omen 15 isn’t as affordable as its previous generations, but its upgrade to an RTX 50-series GPU means access to Nvidia’s latest DLSS game enhancements. Read our review.

Our favorite do-it-all gaming laptop for everyday use and portability got a nice upgrade for 2026: a faster Intel chip, better battery life, and a full-size SD card slot. It also got much more expensive than its previous generation. Read our review.

A nice OLED, 16GB of RAM, and marathon battery life in a travel-friendly laptop with an affordalbe price. Build quality is only okay. Read our review.

Acer’s answer to the MacBook Neo, with an Intel Core 5 processor, 8GB of RAM, 120Hz display, and speedy Thunderbolt 4 ports. We’re still testing this one, but it’s showing promise for an affordable choice.

#10319. Motorola Signature 27 delivery dates slip ahead of launch as it expands to more regions

Motorola and Best Buy websites are now showing an early December shipping date, despite at least one customer already receiving tracking info.

Tons of excitement surrounds Motorola’s upcoming release of the Signature 27, and now retail websites are showing that new preorders won’t be arriving until early December. The original announcement in early November proclaimed a November 19 release date, but Motorola tells 9to5Google:

We’re excited by the strong consumer response of the new motorola signature 27, with demand exceeding our initial expectations. As a result, some orders may experience updated shipping timelines. Our teams are working to meet demand and get devices to customers as quickly as possible.

Motorola and Best Buy websites are still showing “Pre-order” buttons, so while you can order one right now, December 8 and December 11 are the current ship dates. Motorola also just announced that the Motorola Signature 27 will be officially available in India starting December 9 (via GSMArena), further complicating the supply chain.

Despite this, one Redditor who preordered says they received a tracking number for the Signature 27 and the free Motorola Watch Ultra preorder, and it’s scheduled to arrive on November 25. The Motorola Signature 27 has been available in Europe since November 16, so it’s clear demand is quite high for Motorola’s biggest premium launch in a long time.

The Motorola Signature 27 is the most premium phone Motorola has possibly ever launched in North America. The company has shied away from releasing flagship phones here for years, although Motorola’s Razr line of foldable phones often blends premium specs with more mid-range ones. The excitement for the Signature 27 is completely understandable in this case, especially now that Motorola is offering the full seven-year software update treatment that Samsung and Google do.

#10318. Building Email Integrations: APIs, Webhooks, Automation, and Deliverability

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Email remains an important communication channel for web applications. From account verification and password resets to product announcements and customer notifications, many applications depend on email to keep users informed.

For developers, however, implementing email functionality involves more than connecting a service and sending a message. A reliable email system needs to handle authentication, dynamic content, delivery failures, user preferences, event tracking, and integrations with other application components.

Using an email service provider (ESP) can simplify this process. Most modern providers offer REST APIs, SMTP relays, templates, automation features, and reporting tools that developers can integrate into existing applications.

This guide explores the technical considerations involved in building email integrations, including API-based sending, webhook handling, automation workflows, and deliverability.

There are two common ways to connect an application to an email delivery service: SMTP and REST APIs.

SMTP (Simple Mail Transfer Protocol) is a standard protocol used to transfer email messages between servers. Developers can connect an application to an SMTP server using credentials and configuration settings.

REST APIs provide another approach. Instead of communicating through an email server protocol, an application sends HTTP requests to an endpoint. The provider processes the request and returns a response.

Both methods can support transactional and application-generated emails, but their implementation differs.

An application already supports SMTP configuration.

Developers want a relatively straightforward integration.

Existing frameworks or libraries provide built-in SMTP support.

An application needs programmatic control over email operations.

Developers want structured responses and error handling.

Email functionality needs to integrate with other application services.

The system requires event tracking or additional API capabilities.

The right approach depends on the application's architecture, expected email volume, and integration requirements.

An API integration allows an application to trigger emails in response to specific events.

For example, an ecommerce application might send an order confirmation after a successful payment. A SaaS application could send an account verification message after registration.

A typical integration follows this process:

The backend prepares the recipient and message data.

The backend authenticates with the email provider.

The application records the response and handles any errors.

Consider a Node.js application that needs to trigger an email campaign through an API.

Some platforms, including Mailmodo, provide REST API functionality for triggering campaigns and integrating external applications with email workflows.

The following example demonstrates the general structure of an HTTP request using a campaign-triggering endpoint:

This example uses the documented Mailmodo trigger endpoint and request structure. The campaign ID and API key must be replaced with the values from the relevant account.

Notice that the API key is loaded from an environment variable rather than written directly into the source code.

This is an important security practice. Credentials should never be exposed in frontend JavaScript, public repositories, or client-side application bundles.

Not every email provider offers the same integration capabilities. Developers should evaluate providers based on their API documentation, authentication methods, supported endpoints, event notifications, and integration flexibility.

For example, Elastic Email provides a REST API that developers can use to send emails and manage different email operations from an application.

Its API uses HTTPS requests and API-key authentication. Developers can use the available endpoints to send messages, manage campaigns, retrieve information, and configure webhook notifications.

When evaluating an email API, consider these technical requirements:

Authentication: Check how API keys are generated, stored, restricted, and rotated.

Documentation: Look for clear endpoint descriptions, request examples, response formats, and error codes.

SDK availability: Official libraries can reduce the amount of integration code required.

Permission management: Separate credentials for sending emails and accessing account information can reduce unnecessary exposure.

API limitations: Review connection limits, request timeouts, rate limits, and account-level restrictions before deploying an integration.

A provider with extensive features is not necessarily the best option for every project. The important consideration is whether its API supports the application's actual requirements.

Sending an email is only one part of the communication process. Applications may also need to know what happens after a message is submitted.

A webhook allows an external service to send an HTTP notification to an application when a particular event occurs.

Depending on the provider, events may include:

For example, an application could receive a delivery-failure notification and update the corresponding email record in its database.

A basic Express.js webhook endpoint might look like this:

This is a simplified example rather than a complete provider-specific webhook implementation. A production endpoint should validate the provider's signature or other authentication mechanism and follow its documented payload structure.

It should also handle duplicate events safely. Webhook providers may retry notifications when an application does not respond successfully.

An idempotent event handler prevents the same notification from creating duplicate database updates or triggering repeated actions.

Email automation connects application events with predefined communication sequences.

Instead of manually sending every message, developers can create workflows that respond to user activity.

Consider a SaaS application with the following registration process:

If the user does not complete onboarding, a follow-up message may be triggered.

A simplified workflow can be represented as:

In a production application, email delivery should generally be handled through a background job queue rather than blocking the registration request.

A queue also makes it easier to retry temporary failures, manage sending volume, and prevent email delays from affecting the main application.

Developers should consider tools such as Redis-backed queues or framework-specific job processors when building larger systems.

Automation platforms can also help manage more complex journeys. For instance, a developer can connect application events to an external email workflow instead of implementing every communication sequence independently.

The key is to keep business logic in the application while using the email service to manage message delivery and relevant campaign operations.

A successful API response does not necessarily mean that an email has reached the recipient's inbox.

Email deliverability depends on several technical factors, including domain authentication, sender reputation, message quality, and recipient engagement.

Developers should pay attention to the following configurations.

Sender Policy Framework identifies the mail servers authorized to send messages on behalf of a domain.

A correctly configured SPF record helps receiving servers evaluate whether an email originates from an authorized source.

DomainKeys Identified Mail adds a cryptographic signature to outgoing messages. Receiving servers can use the corresponding public key in DNS to verify the signature.

Domain-based Message Authentication, Reporting, and Conformance builds on SPF and DKIM. It allows domain owners to publish policies for handling messages that fail authentication checks and receive reports about authentication activity.

These three mechanisms should be configured carefully, especially when an application sends emails through multiple providers.

Email systems generate useful operational data. However, developers should avoid treating every available metric as an accurate measure of user engagement.

More reliable application-level signals can include:

These events can be connected with email campaign data to understand how communication affects application activity.

Developers should also maintain a clear separation between email delivery records and user account records. This makes it easier to investigate delivery issues without unnecessarily modifying customer data.

Before deploying an email integration, developers should review the following areas:

API security: Store credentials in environment variables or a dedicated secrets manager.

Domain authentication: Configure SPF, DKIM, and DMARC.

Error handling: Account for failed requests, invalid recipients, and temporary provider errors.

Background processing: Use queues for asynchronous email delivery.

Webhook validation: Verify incoming notifications and handle duplicate events.

Monitoring: Track delivery failures, bounce rates, and application-level outcomes.

Testing: Test email templates across different clients and devices before production deployment.

These practices help create an email system that is easier to maintain, troubleshoot, and scale.

Email integration is an important part of modern application development, but a reliable implementation requires more than connecting an SMTP server or calling an API endpoint.

Developers need to consider authentication, asynchronous processing, webhook security, automation logic, domain configuration, and event monitoring.

REST APIs are useful for applications that need programmatic control over email operations, while SMTP remains a practical option for systems that already support standard mail-server connections. Webhooks add another layer by allowing applications to respond to delivery events and update their internal records.

By choosing an integration method that fits the application architecture and following sound security and deliverability practices, developers can build email functionality that supports both immediate communication needs and long-term application growth.

#10317. Multimodal Embedding & Reranker Models with Sentence Transformers

Sentence Transformers is a Python library for using and training embedding and reranker models for applications like retrieval augmented generation, semantic search, and more. With the v5.4 update, you can now encode and compare texts, images, audio, and videos using the same familiar API. In this blogpost, I'll show you how to use these new multimodal capabilities for both embedding and reranking.

Multimodal embedding models map inputs from different modalities into a shared embedding space, while multimodal reranker models score the relevance of mixed-modality pairs. This opens up use cases like visual document retrieval, cross-modal search, and multimodal RAG pipelines.

If you want to train your own multimodal models, check out the companion blogpost: Training and Finetuning Multimodal Embedding & Reranker Models with Sentence Transformers.

Traditional embedding models convert text into fixed-size vectors. Multimodal embedding models extend this by mapping inputs from different modalities (text, images, audio, or video) into a shared embedding space. This means you can compare a text query against image documents (or vice versa) using the same similarity functions you're already familiar with.

Similarly, traditional reranker (Cross Encoder) models compute relevance scores between pairs of texts. Multimodal rerankers can score pairs where one or both elements are images, combined text-image documents, or other modalities.

For example, you can compare a text query against image documents, find video clips matching a description, or build RAG pipelines that work across modalities.

Multimodal models require some extra dependencies. Install the extras for the modalities you need (see Installation for more details):

VLM-based models like Qwen3-VL-2B require a GPU with at least ~8 GB of VRAM. For the 8B variants, expect ~20 GB. If you don't have a local GPU, consider using a cloud GPU service or Google Colab. On CPU, these models will be extremely slow; text-only or CLIP models are better suited for CPU inference.

Loading a multimodal embedding model works exactly like loading a text-only model:

Some models might require a revision argument for now if the integration pull requests for the model is still pending. Once they're merged, you'll be able to load them without specifying a revision, like above.

The model automatically detects which modalities it supports, so there's nothing extra to configure. See Processor and Model kwargs if you want to control things like image resolution or model precision.

With a multimodal model loaded, model.encode() accepts images alongside text. Images can be provided as URLs, local file paths, or PIL Image objects (see Supported Input Types for all accepted formats):

You can compute similarities between text embeddings and image embeddings, since the model maps both into the same space:

As expected, "A green car parked in front of a yellow building" is most similar to the car image (0.51), and "A bee on a pink flower" is most similar to the bee image (0.67). The hard negatives ("A red car driving on a highway", "A wasp on a wooden table") correctly receive lower scores.

You might notice that even the best matching scores (0.51, 0.67) aren't very close to 1.0. This is due to the modality gap: embeddings from different modalities tend to cluster in separate regions of the space. Cross-modal similarities are typically lower than within-modal ones (e.g., text-to-text), but the relative ordering is preserved, so retrieval still works well.

For retrieval tasks, encode_query() and encode_document() are the recommended methods. Many retrieval models prepend different instruction prompts depending on whether the input is a query or a document, similar to how chat models might apply different system prompts depending on the goal. Model authors can specify their prompts in the model config, and encode_query() / encode_document() automatically load and apply the correct one:

Under the hood, both are thin wrappers around encode(), they just handle prompt selection for you. Here's what cross-modal retrieval looks like:

These methods accept the same input types as encode() (images, URLs, multimodal dicts, etc.) and pass through the same parameters. For models without specialized query/document prompts, they behave identically to encode().

Multimodal reranker (CrossEncoder) models score the relevance between pairs of inputs, where each element can be text, an image, audio, video, or a combination. They tend to outperform embedding models in terms of quality, but are slower since they process each pair individually. The currently available pretrained multimodal rerankers focus on text and image inputs, but the architecture supports any modality that the underlying model can handle.

The rank() method scores and ranks a list of documents against a query, supporting mixed modalities:

The reranker correctly identifies the car image (document 0) as the most relevant result, followed by the combined text+image document about a car in a European city (document 3). The bee image (document 1) scores lowest. Keep in mind that the modality gap can influence absolute scores: text-image pair scores may occupy a different range than text-text or image-image pair scores.

You can also check which modalities a reranker supports using modalities and supports(), just like with embedding models:

You can also use predict() to get raw relevance scores for specific pairs of inputs:

A common pattern is to use an embedding model for fast initial retrieval, then refine the top results with a reranker:

Since the corpus embeddings are pre-computed, the initial retrieval is fast even over millions of documents. The reranker then provides more accurate scoring over the smaller candidate set.

Multimodal models accept a variety of input formats. Here's a summary of what you can pass to model.encode():

You can check which modalities a model supports using the modalities property and supports() method:

The "message" modality indicates that the model accepts chat-style message inputs with interleaved content. In practice, you rarely need to use this directly. When you pass strings, URLs, or multimodal dicts, the model converts them to the appropriate message format internally. Sentence Transformers supports two message formats:

The format is auto-detected from the model's chat template.

Since all inputs get converted into the same message format internally, you can mix input types in a single encode() call:

If a model doesn't follow either format and you need full control, you can pass raw message dicts with role and content keys directly:

This bypasses the automatic format conversion and passes the messages directly to the processor's apply_chat_template().

You may want to control image resolution bounds or model precision. Use processor_kwargs and model_kwargs when loading the model:

See the SentenceTransformer API Reference documentation for more details on these kwargs.

In Sentence Transformers v5.4, tokenizer_kwargs has been renamed to processor_kwargs to reflect that multimodal models use processors rather than just tokenizers. The old name is still accepted but deprecated.

Here are the multimodal models supported in v5.4, also available in the v5.4 integrations collection:

The older CLIP models continue to be supported:

These simple CLIP models still work well on lower-resource hardware.

To learn how to finetune these multimodal models on your own data, see the companion blogpost: Training and Finetuning Multimodal Embedding & Reranker Models with Sentence Transformers.

Google Maps is rolling out an update on Android Auto that provides better navigation routes specifically for motorcycles.

That makes sense, as Android Auto has been working to better accommodate motorcycles for a while, and some motorcycles even now have Android Auto support built-in.
