#10300. Is Kling 4.0 the Right AI Video Generator for Your Project?

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

A short clip can help a project in different ways. It can show an idea you have not filmed, put an existing design in motion, or give an announcement something to look at. The same approach will not work if the clip needs to demonstrate a real feature or show exactly what happened. Before choosing a generator, decide what the viewer needs to learn from the shot.

This article uses Kling 4.0 as a worked example, but the decision process applies to any AI video generator. It covers how these tools turn prompts and images into video, how Kling 4.0 and a few alternatives differ, how to choose a starting mode, how to add exact text and branding outside the generated clip with a short ffmpeg script, and when real footage is the better choice. Feature details come from each vendor’s own pages at the time of writing and change often, so confirm current terms before you plan a production.

● Generated video is best for imagined shots. It suits concepts, backgrounds and early explorations, not instructions or faithful records.

● Your starting material decides the mode. A written idea, a reference image or a pair of opening and closing frames each call for a different input.

● Keep exact wording out of the generated clip. Titles, dates and logos belong on separate layers in an editor.

● Tools differ on control, cost and licensing. Compare inputs, length, resolution, credits and terms before you commit.

● Always review. Watch the whole clip at its final size and check it against the real product or design.

Most current systems extend diffusion models across time. A model learns to turn noise into a coherent set of frames guided by a prompt, and sometimes by an image or a clip. The research paper Video Diffusion Models describes this extension from images to video. The practical consequences are easy to observe.

● The prompt describes change over time. One visible change and one camera instruction usually work better than a long list of actions.

● Reference material steers but does not lock. A picture can suggest shape and colour without guaranteeing an exact match.

● Longer clips give more room for drift. Faces, logos and fine text are the first things to change between frames.

● Cost grows with length and resolution. Most hosted tools charge credits per second, so short previews are cheaper than full shots.

If you only have an idea, start with text. For a short announcement, you might ask for a band of light to move across a wall of coloured tiles. No one needs to recognise a particular wall, so the model can decide how it looks. Give it one visible change and a clear view of the subject. A prompt such as Soft morning light travels slowly across a wall of blue ceramic tiles. Fixed camera, no lettering is enough to see whether the idea works.

If you already have an illustration or a photo, reference mode gives you another starting point. Suppose you want a short concept clip for a desk accessory that only exists as a drawing. The picture can show the general shape and colour while the prompt describes the view you want. A video reference can help when it is the motion that is hard to explain, such as a slow camera slide. Say what each asset is meant to guide, and do not add a clip just because you have one.

Use keyframes when a particular view matters at a particular moment. Start with an opening image. If a short reveal also needs to end with the object facing forward, add an ending image to show that view. That is different from a reference image that mainly shows what the object looks like. Neither method guarantees an exact match, so check the result rather than assuming the uploaded picture has locked the design.

No single tool fits every project. The table summarizes what each option’s own page states, and “not stated” means the page did not say, not that the feature is absent.

Reading the table: hosted studios such as the one on JXP are the quickest way to test an idea and need no setup, but you pay per second and work within their supported inputs. Kling’s own site is the place to check announcements and API options directly, since its page says little about durations or resolution. Runway positions its models for motion quality and prompt following, while Google’s Gemini API video documentation suits teams building generation into their own products. The Diffusers video guide covers open-source pipelines for developers who want local control and are ready to manage GPUs and licences.

Trying an idea before making it. An illustrator might want to see how an imagined landscape feels when the light changes. A quick clip gives the team something to discuss: is the change visible, and does it happen at the right pace? It does not need to be the final animation to answer those questions.

Showing a product concept. A rotating view or a slow camera move can help people discuss how a design might be presented. It is useful early, when the shape and lighting are still being explored. Once the clip represents a product someone can buy, the standard changes. If a port moves or a button appears that the real product does not have, it is the wrong clip for that job.

Making a short visual for a post. A few seconds of moving colour can give an event announcement or a project update a distinctive opening. Put the name, date and other exact wording in your editor so they are readable and easy to change. The background only needs to support the message. If it competes with the text, use less movement or keep the background still.

Generated video is unreliable at lettering, so add titles in an editor or with a script. The command below overlays a title on a generated background and then checks the file properties. It assumes you already have a clip named background.mp4 and ffmpeg installed.

-vf "drawtext=text='Launch Night | 12 March':fontcolor=white:fontsize=64:x=(w-text_w)/2:y=(h-text_h)/2:box=1:boxcolor=black@0.35:boxborderw=24" \

-c:v libx264 -pix_fmt yuv420p -an announcement.mp4

-show_entries stream=width,height,r_frame_rate,duration \

-of default=noprint_wrappers=1 announcement.mp4

Because the text lives in the command, you can reuse the same background for three events by changing one string. The font may need to be set with a fontfile option on some systems. This is the practical version of keeping the moving background in one file and the editable details in another.

If people will follow the clip as instructions, use real footage or a screen recording for the steps. A convincing shot of an app is not proof that a button is in the right place. A generated close-up of a product is not a reliable way to show how its parts fit. You can still use an imagined opening, but make the switch to the real demonstration clear.

Think about revisions, too. If your team expects to adjust the same title, logo or date every week, put those elements on separate layers in an editor. And if the only movement you need is a slow zoom on an approved picture, apply that zoom directly. There is no reason to risk changing the picture when a simple edit will do.

This matters when someone else will maintain the video. A reusable announcement template is easier to hand over if the moving background is one file and the event details are editable. If the team likes the movement but needs three versions with different dates, they can reuse the same clip. If every change calls for a new generation, the time you saved on the first version may disappear on the second.

The Kling 4.0 video generator on JXP currently offers 720p and 1080p settings and clip lengths from 3 to 30 seconds. According to its page, reference mode accepts up to 10 images and 5 videos, keyframe mode takes a first frame, middle frames and an optional last frame, and credits are charged per second with a higher rate at 1080p. For a first attempt, choose the frame shape you plan to use and make the clip only as long as it needs to be. Check the displayed credit cost before generating, because a short preview can tell you whether the direction works before you spend on a longer shot.

Decide what a good result looks like before you generate it. For the tile background, you need to see the light move without distracting from the words you will add. For a product concept, check whether the shape stays recognisable as the viewpoint changes. Watch the whole clip at the size the audience will see it. If the shot misses the point, revise one thing at a time: the motion, the framing or the source image.

● Read the licence. JXP’s page lists a commercial use license on each plan and says outputs are for creative and lawful use, with the user responsible for reviewing them. Other tools have different terms.

● Use inputs you have the right to use. Do not upload other people’s copyrighted work or photos of people without permission.

● Do not misrepresent products or events. A generated clip should not suggest features or footage that do not exist.

● Consider provenance. C2PA is an open standard for Content Credentials that records where content came from and how it was edited, and some tools support it.

● Disclose where required. Follow platform and advertising rules on labelling AI-generated or altered content.

● Fine text, logos, hands and fast motion can drift or flicker between frames.

● Reference images and keyframes steer the result but do not guarantee an exact match.

● Vendor specifications, such as resolution and length, can differ between a model announcement and a particular platform.

● Credit costs and plan terms change, so check them on the day you generate.

● Long or exact sequences are often cheaper and safer to film than to generate.

Short imagined shots, concept clips and moving backgrounds, where some details can be left open and the clip is reviewed before use.

Use text when you only have an idea, reference mode when you have a picture or clip to guide the look, and keyframes when specific views matter at specific moments.

Not reliably. Use real footage or a screen recording for instructions and demonstrations.

No. Hosted studios, vendor sites, developer APIs and open-source pipelines all exist. Compare supported inputs, length, resolution, cost and licensing against your project.

Kling 4.0 is a good candidate when the missing piece is an imagined shot and you can describe what it needs to do. Pick one such shot, try it, and put it next to the material you already have, and compare at least one alternative before you commit. If the project needs exact instructions or a faithful record, use the real thing. A useful first result is one that does its job in the edit, not simply one that looks impressive on its own.

#10299. The PR you would have opened yourself

Making transformers models available in mlx-lm using a Skill and test harness

We provide a Skill and a test harness to help port language models from transformers to mlx-lm, so they become (almost) instantly available the moment they are added to transformers. The Skill is designed to support contributors and reviewers as an aide, not an automation. We explain why we did it, how, and comment about how to meaningfully contribute to open source in the age of agents.

In 2026, code agents started to actually work. What used to be auto-completion at the side of your editor turned into a system that one-shots reasonable solutions from brief specifications. The generated code usually works out of the box, covers what you asked for, and makes reasonable assumptions about details you didn't specify. This is great. As Jensen Huang puts it, we've instantly gone from 30 million to one billion coders in the world. Creative minds are unleashed.

Take the transformers library as an example. It has hundreds of contributors, is used in thousands of projects, has been downloaded over a billion times. Suddenly, anyone with an agent can instruct it to find some open issue, fix it, and submit a PR. And that's exactly what's happening. Those people feel happy because they are contributing to a great library, but the sad reality is that, most of the time, they don't realize they are not.

Why not? There are two assumptions that agent-generated PRs usually miss.

Codebases like transformers care deeply about the code. It's cool to build projects where it doesn't matter what the code looks like, but transformers is not one of them. Being used by thousands of people, transformers is primarily built as a human-to-human communication method, through code. Model files read top to bottom, because we want practitioners to understand them without jumping through complex abstractions. This permeates throughout the library design and is the reason why, for example, we favor flat hierarchies.

Agents don't have that context. Because design decisions are not explicit, agents suggest refactors to "improve" the codebase by following "best practices", without realizing they are breaking implicit contracts between the library and its users. They are verbose, generalize too early, don't notice when a change affects other areas, introduce subtle bugs, break performance. They are also sycophantic, and accept any idea as good and follow it through diligently, including ones a maintainer would have pushed back early on with a terse comment.

A small number of maintainers still has to read every PR, understand it, decide if the design direction is right, identify side effects, and write feedback. PR volume has gone up tenfold, but the amount of maintainers has not (and cannot, because team coordination does not scale).

Transformers is one of the first projects to feel this pressure because of sheer volume, but the same dynamic is happening everywhere. As an example from a different domain, App Store reviewers are swamped because anyone can now build and submit an app, so many do.

The same logic applies to MLX: their maintainers care deeply about the code and read every PR carefully. We wanted to see whether agents could help contributors land high-quality model ports fast, and at the same time support reviewers in their work. Not only do we aspire to produce PRs that could have come from a careful human submission, but we also provide additional artifacts to increase the signal: generation examples, numerical comparisons, and a separate non-agentic test harness for reproducibility.

Another connection between transformers and MLX is that, most times, mlx-lm models are ported from transformers implementations. Because transformers focuses on clarity and readability, it has become the source of truth for model definitions. Downstream contributors wait until the transformers implementations are ready before they port to other frameworks. As a side effect, this is an excellent environment for an agent because it naturally limits the scope: rather than creating an implementation from scratch, the agent relies on transformers code as the source of truth.

This approach supports our goal: when a model lands in transformers, it should be available on MLX shortly after.

We built a Skill that mlx-lm contributors can use to port a model from transformers to MLX. Given a prompt like "convert the olmo_hybrid architecture to MLX", the Skill sets up a virtual environment to work on, discovers and downloads the relevant models from the Hub, reads the transformers modeling code, writes the MLX implementation, and runs a battery of tests. If results don't look right, it debugs and iterates, and does not declare success until it's satisfied.

We designed it to be useful to reviewers as much as contributors.

For the contributor, the Skill of course handles all the scaffolding: finding model variants on the Hub, diffing their configs to spot parameters that vary across model variants, downloading checkpoints, setting up editable installs of both mlx-lm and transformers. But it also handles the more difficult modeling tasks. It pays attention to salient architecture details and verifies sensitive areas, like RoPE configurations, that may result in hard-to-find bugs. It detects when the config doesn't declare a dtype and infers it from the safetensors metadata header. It runs per-layer comparisons between transformers and MLX to pinpoint exactly where divergence occurs. These are the kinds of checks that only someone with porting experience would think to run.

For the reviewer, the Skill produces a PR that is upfront about being agent-assisted, but does look like a careful human submission. Reviewers will see that the code follows mlx-lm conventions: idiomatic solutions, no unnecessary comments, no speculative abstractions, no modifications to shared utilities without explicit approval. Given that the code is agent-assisted, we try to include more data than the median PR, to provide as much signal as possible. The PR body includes a report with a summary of the variants and their architectural differences, generation examples, numerical comparisons, dtype verification, per-layer comparisons against the transformers baseline. The PR always discloses that it was agent-assisted, and the Skill will not open it until the contributor has accepted the results.

For verification, the Skill generates a test manifest for a separate, non-agentic test harness that is, by design, easily reproducible and not subject to LLM hallucinations or complacency (more on this below).

Skills are recipes for agents: simple text files with guidelines that steer the model through a complex task. They are not magic; you can achieve the same results via prompting and iteration. But they provide consistency (every run follows the same process, whereas different people would prompt differently), minimize ambiguity and serve as documentation: anyone can read the Skill to understand what it does, identify missing cases and suggest improvements.

We bootstrapped the Skill by porting a model ourselves, in conversation with Claude. I asked it to port GLM 4.7 from transformers to mlx-lm, giving instructions as I would during a normal session. One trick: I pointed Claude at a checkout of mlx-lm from which I had deleted the already-existing implementation, so I could compare the output against the ground truth. After a few iterations I had a working implementation, a conversation that revealed how Claude approached the problem, and the first draft of the Skill, which Claude created as a summary of the process. I edited it heavily, and incorporated the learnings from @gabegoodhart, who kindly shared their own porting conversation for a different model 🙌.

We repeated this loop several times and the Skill grew. On the technical side, we covered stuff such as RoPE bugs that may produce plausible output that degrades with long sequences, float32 precision contamination that silently kills inference speed (you'd be surprised how frequently these things happen!), config fields that vary across model variants in ways the implementation must handle, distributed inference for super large models that don't fit on a single machine. We taught it how to invoke the hf CLI to discover and download models. Most importantly, we instructed it to run the tests that experienced porters would, and to not declare success until they pass.

On the cultural side, we covered softer characteristics and explained the conventions that make a PR easy to review: don't use comments to explain code (the reviewer has to parse the comment and the code 🤦‍♂️), never propose refactors, don't touch shared utilities without asking. These rules cost the agent nothing but save the reviewer lots of time.

The end result: the contributor types a prompt, and the Skill produces a PR like this one, plus a test manifest for the external test harness.

The Skill shares a comprehensive results report as part of the PR. All these come from tests the agent runs during conversion, but we didn't want the reviewer to take a leap of faith to accept them. To go a step forward, we created a separate, non-agentic test harness that runs systematic tests on the converted code. This brings a couple of benefits:

The test harness is not a CI gate. Some checks are straightforward (is the output dtype correct?), but most are qualitative. Is it normal that a pre-trained model repeats itself in long sequences? Is a 4% relative logits difference against the transformers baseline acceptable? These are judgement calls based on experience with similar architectures. The harness provides useful signal, but it's the reviewer and contributor who still have to make the call.

The Skill is designed for the people who are already opening mlx-lm model PRs, or who would do it manually on their own. It's not meant for mass consumption, because PRs to mlx-lm are rarely accepted on sight. The typical cycle is: contributor opens a PR, reviewers point out improvements, both sides iterate until the quality bar is met. If this is true for expert submissions, it will remain true for agent-assisted ones.

If you're not prepared to engage in that cycle, you probably shouldn't be opening a PR. The reviewers will make an effort to understand your code (even knowing it was agent-assisted), so you should do the same. Own the code, and be ready to incorporate their feedback. In particular, don't hand reviewer comments back to an agent and post whatever it produces. LLMs double down on their decisions, go on tangents, and don't push back effectively. Once you engage with the reviewer, this becomes a person-to-person conversation, so it's your turn to discuss and be respectful of the time they put in.

You can also use the Skill to learn; you don't need to submit anything until your confidence and experience build. Read the Skill to identify problem areas you weren't aware of: it contains nearly 15 thousand words among the skill file, reference docs and utility scripts. Point it to your own fork of mlx-lm, try a conversion, and compare your output against the accepted implementation once it lands in the official repo. If you do this a few times, you'll learn a lot about transformers, MLX, and language model architectures.

We developed and tested the Skill using Claude Code. The same approach would work with Codex or other coding agents, but we haven't tested them. If you try the Skill in a different environment, please let us know how it goes!

The Skill works well for LLMs in mlx-lm, but there's plenty of room to grow.

The bottleneck in open source is not typing speed: it's understaning the codebase to change it without breaking the implicit and explicit contracts with users. Agents can help in this process, if we teach them what matters. We explored what this looks like in the context of mlx-lm, and hope it's useful for contributors and reviewers to land high-quality model conversions faster!

Thanks a lot to Ben, Shaun, Aritra for reading previous versions of this post and making it so much better 🙌

We are incredibly indebted to Apple for making MLX an open-source project, and to the community for instantly recognizing its value and contributing enthusiastically 🙏

#10295. How Consumer AI Companions Handle Context Windows, Persistent Memory, and Voice Latency

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

AI companions are the most demanding consumer use of large language models right now. A coding assistant can forget your last message and still be useful. A companion that forgets your name, your running story, or the plan you made last Tuesday has failed at its one job. On top of that, users now expect voice calls that feel like a phone conversation, not a walkie-talkie exchange with a five-second pause.

Three engineering problems decide whether a companion app works: how much of the conversation fits in the model's context window, what the app remembers once the window fills up, and how fast the voice pipeline answers. Here is how consumer companions handle each one, with real tier and pricing examples, and what developers can take from their designs for their own products.

Most LLM products are judged on single answers. Companions are judged on continuity. That creates pressure in three places at once:

Every consumer companion is a different set of trade-offs across those three constraints, and the trade-offs are increasingly how the apps are priced.

The context window is the total number of tokens the model can see when it writes the next reply. In a companion app, that budget is spent before the user says anything:

When the chat log outgrows what is left, the oldest messages fall out. The user experiences this as the companion "forgetting" mid-conversation. This is why context size is now a headline spec in the category, and a paid feature. SpicyChat AI, for example, gives free accounts a 4K context window, then scales memory to 8K on its $19.95/mo tier and 32K on its $29.95/mo tier. Janitor AI runs about 9K of context on its own JanitorLLM. Independent uncensored AI chat benchmarks record these context sizes alongside refusal behavior and pricing, because context length predicts how long a roleplay stays coherent better than any marketing claim.

Some apps sell memory in messages rather than tokens. Fantasy GF's pricing page lists a 60-message base "smart memory" and 5x that, 300 messages, on its Ultra plan. Others sell it as a memory multiplier on higher subscription tiers. The pattern is consistent across the category: memory depth is the upgrade lever, not the model itself.

No consumer app keeps an entire relationship in the prompt. Persistent memory is a separate system that writes to storage and reads back into the context window on each turn. In practice it has three layers:

The differences users notice are usually retention policies, not algorithms. Crushon AI's own subscription docs say free-plan chat history is deleted after 7 days of inactivity, while paid plans keep it for the membership period. Paid tiers across the category commonly promise that memories never expire. There is also a security angle worth stating plainly: companion chat logs are among the most sensitive data a consumer product can hold. A 2024 breach at Muah.ai, first reported by 404 Media, exposed roughly 1.9 million users' email addresses together with their private prompts. Any app that builds persistent memory is also building a liability, and developers copying the pattern should treat the memory store as the most protected part of the system.

A voice call in a companion app is three models chained together: speech-to-text, the LLM, and text-to-speech. Run them strictly in sequence and a single reply can take several seconds, which reads as dead air. The apps that feel fast attack each stage the same way:

With every stage streaming, time-to-first-audio can land close to a second on a good connection, which is roughly the threshold where a conversation stops feeling laggy. Voice is also expensive to run - three model calls instead of one, plus audio bandwidth - which is why it is metered harder than text. Fantasy GF charges 8 tokens per minute for voice calls (4 on Ultra), which turns the 100 monthly tokens on its entry plan into about 12 minutes of call time. SpicyChat, for its part, only adds text-to-speech at its top tier. Latency engineering and unit economics are the same problem here: faster pipelines cost less per call, and cheaper calls are what make voice viable below the top plan.

Tier details below come from each app's own pricing or documentation pages, checked November 16, 2026, and cross-checked against il.ly's AI companion testing guide, which hands-tests 15 companion apps across memory, media, and voice.

Two takeaways from the table. First, nobody sells a bigger base model - they sell a bigger window into the same one. Second, the free tiers are deliberately memory-poor: limited context and short retention are the upgrade prompt.

Even if you never build a companion, these apps are a useful reference architecture for any stateful LLM product:

Consumer AI companions have turned three hard infrastructure problems - bounded context, durable memory, and real-time voice - into their pricing pages. Context size, memory depth, and voice access are the tiers. If you are building anything stateful on an LLM, this category is worth watching closely: it is solving continuity and latency problems at consumer scale, in public, one subscription tier at a time.

It is the total amount of text, measured in tokens, that the model can consider when writing its next reply. The character definition, stored memories, recent chat, and the new message all share that budget. When the conversation exceeds it, the oldest content drops out and the companion appears to forget.

Yes, through a memory system separate from the context window. Apps summarize older chats, extract stable facts about you into a profile, and retrieve relevant past moments into the prompt. Retention varies: some free tiers delete chat history after as little as 7 days of inactivity, while paid plans typically keep memory for the membership period.

A voice turn runs three models - speech-to-text, the LLM, and text-to-speech - instead of one, plus audio transfer. Providers pass that cost on through per-minute token charges or by locking voice behind higher tiers.

For casual chat, 4K to 9K tokens works. For long-running roleplay or a companion expected to hold plot threads for weeks, 32K and up, or a well-built memory layer on top of a smaller window, makes the visible difference.

#10294. Ecom-RLVE: Adaptive Verifiable Environments for E-Commerce Conversational Agents

TL;DR — We extend the RLVE framework from single-turn reasoning puzzles to multi-turn, tool-augmented e-commerce conversations. EcomRLVE-GYM provides 8 verifiable environments — product discovery, substitution, cart building, returns, order tracking, policy QA, bundle planning, and multi-intent journeys — each with procedural problem generation, a 12-axis difficulty curriculum, and algorithmically verifiable rewards. We train a Qwen 3 8B model with DAPO over 300 steps and present early results demonstrating that environment scaling and adaptive difficulty transfer to agentic, real-world task completion.

This project originated in the Pytorch OpenEnv Hackathon and is still evolving, follow us for updates 🔥

Large language models can hold fluent conversations, yet deploying them as shopping assistants reveals a persistent gap: fluency ≠ task completion. A customer who asks "find me a USB-C charger under $25 that ships in two days" needs an agent that invokes the right catalog search, filters on three hard constraints, avoids hallucinating product IDs it never retrieved, and handles follow-ups when the top result goes out of stock.

Supervised fine-tuning can teach surface-level tool use from demonstrations, but it cannot scale to the combinatorial space of constraint configurations, partial-information dialogues, and multi-step transactional workflows that real e-commerce demands.

Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) offers an alternative: the agent optimises for outcomes — did the products satisfy the constraints? Was the cart correct? Was the return initiated for the right order line? The challenge is constructing reward functions that are both verifiable (no LLM-as-a-judge subjectivity) and adaptive (difficulty that grows with the policy's capability).

RLVE-Gym provides 400 environments for sorting, multiplication, Sudoku, and other algorithmic-reasoning tasks; however, those are all single-turn, text-in / text-out puzzles — extending to agentic domains was left as future work.

EcomRLVE-GYM fills that gap: we stay in the verifiable regime (e-commerce outcomes can be checked algorithmically) while extending to multi-turn, tool-augmented, agentic conversations — environments where the agent must act (call tools, modify world state) rather than merely reason (produce a text answer) and compensates for the deficiency of the search system.

EcomRLVE-GYM transforms customer-service outcomes structurally verifiable:

Every signal above can be evaluated by a program with access to the hidden ground-truth goal. No human annotation or LLM-as-a-judge is needed.

Before we explain the framework, here is what a single EcomRLVE episode looks like at difficulty d = 4. The environment generates a hidden goal, a simulated user opens the chat, and the agent must use tools to satisfy the request. Every action is verified algorithmically — no LLM judge required.

The reward is fully computed by code: F1 over (product, variant, qty) tuples, an efficiency bonus for finishing in fewer turns, and a hallucination check that every recommended product ID was actually retrieved. If the agent had picked the Lightning variant instead of USB-C, the simulated user would have corrected it mid-dialogue — and the F1 would have dropped.

Each environment covers a distinct real-world shopping scenario. The agent must complete the task using tools (catalog search, cart operations, order lookups, policy queries) and is scored by a program — not a human or another LLM.

Every environment uses the same three-part reward signal:

Invalid outputs (malformed JSON, illegal tool calls) trigger an immediate failure score, creating a strong incentive for well-formed responses from step one.

A single difficulty number d controls 12 independent aspects of a task simultaneously. This is important because e-commerce conversations are hard in many different ways at once — not just along one dimension.

Here are four representative difficulty axes:

The other eight axes cover turn budget, input noise (typos, slang), context switches, retrieval depth, order-history size, policy complexity, and tool budget. The full breakdown is in the technical report.

Adaptive scheduling. Each environment tracks the agent's success rate independently and only advances to harder problems once the agent is passing the current level reliably. This keeps every environment training at the agent's capability frontier — avoiding both "too easy to learn from" and "too hard to make progress on".

Cart building is a good showcase because it requires the full search → inspect → clarify → act loop, has a binary ground truth, and introduces a challenge absent from most recommendation benchmarks: variant selection.

To succeed, the agent must develop five distinct skills:

The agent uses six tools to accomplish this:

The generator samples 1–5 target products (scaling in difficulty with d), each potentially requiring a specific variant (USB-C vs Lightning, Matte vs Glossy) and a quantity > 1. The agent must:

Real product catalogs have sparse variant data — many products have none, and those that do typically vary only by colour or size. To create a richer discrimination task, we synthesize variants at episode initialization:

At d = 0 the agent adds a single product with no variant complexity — learning the basic catalog.search → cart.add workflow. At d = 6 it juggles 3 items, nearly all requiring a specific variant, with half needing qty > 1.

The cart must be exactly right — correct product, correct variant, correct quantity. Partial credit is given for partially correct carts, but a perfect score requires every item to match. If the agent adds the wrong variant, the simulated user corrects it mid-dialogue ("that's the Lightning version, but I need USB-C"), giving the agent a chance to self-correct before the episode ends.

Two real E_CART episodes from a Qwen 3 8B agent. Same environment, same agent — difficulty alone changes the game.

At d=1 the agent solves the task in 3 clean turns. At d=8 it spirals — picking Bamboo instead of Charcoal, XL instead of XS, never fixing the air fryer despite two user corrections, then hallucinating that the variant doesn't exist. This is exactly the kind of multi-step error cascade that the difficulty curriculum surfaces, and that adaptive training should teach the agent to recover from.

A verifiable environment needs a user simulator that behaves realistically. We use Qwen3.5 (9.7B) to generate natural, varied user messages rather than canned templates — covering everything from typo-filled requests to mid-conversation topic switches.

Two design choices matter for training quality:

Preferences match stated constraints. Each simulated user has a hidden set of preferences (price sensitivity, brand loyalty, shipping speed, etc.). These are deliberately biased toward whatever constraints the user communicated — so if the user said "under $25", the reward function actually cares about price. Without this, an agent could be penalised for correctly following the user's instructions.

Strategic omission. The LLM deliberately withholds some constraints from the opening message to force the agent to ask clarifying questions. The system tracks exactly what was and wasn't mentioned, so the agent is never penalised for information it was never given.

Following RLVE's methodology, we define nested environment collections:

We hypothesise — consistent with RLVE's findings — that C8 agents outperform single-environment specialists, even on the specialist's own task.

We trained Qwen 3 8B with DAPO on C1 (Cart Building) for 300 steps as an initial viability study.

We saw progressive growth in difficulty reached, confirming that adaptive scheduling produces a steady learning signal rather than the saturation (static-low) or starvation (static-high) patterns predicted by the RLVE paper.

Yu, Q., Zhang, Z., Zhu, R., et al. (2025). DAPO: An Open-Source LLM Reinforcement Learning System at Scale. arXiv:2503.14476

Shao, Z., Wang, P., Zhu, Q., et al. (2024). DeepSeekMath: Pushing the Limits of Mathematical Reasoning in Open Language Models. arXiv:2402.03300

DeepSeek-AI. (2025). DeepSeek-R1: Incentivizing Reasoning in LLMs through Reinforcement Learning. Nature.

#10291. AI and the Future of Cybersecurity: Why Openness Matters

Following the announcement of Mythos and Project Glasswing, institutions throughout the world are grappling with the potential dawn of a new era of cybersecurity. In this post, we break down the current situation, discuss the role of openness, and situate the future of cybersecurity within the larger AI ecosystem.

Mythos is a “frontier AI model”, a large language model (LLM) that can be used to process software code (among many other things). This follows a general trend in LLM development, where LLM performance on code-related tasks has recently skyrocketed. What’s particularly significant about Mythos is the system it’s embedded within: It's the system, not the model alone, that has enabled Mythos to rapidly find and patch software vulnerabilities. Understanding this distinction is key to understanding the current landscape of AI cybersecurity.

What Mythos demonstrates is that the following system recipe is powerful:

Together, these ingredients can uncover software vulnerabilities, find exploits, and build patches. It’s in this recipe — not in any one model — that both the benefits and the risks come in.

This matters because others can build comparable systems. Smaller models embedded in systems built with deep security expertise could potentially produce similar outcomes more cheaply, which is particularly promising for defense. AI cybersecurity capability is jagged: It doesn’t scale smoothly with model size or general benchmark performance. The system the model is embedded within matters a lot.

So what Mythos has demonstrated is that it’s possible to build an AI system that finds and addresses software vulnerabilities. We already knew this was possible and there has been increasing work on this, but we’re just beginning to explore what it means in the context of agentic AI: Systems that can rapidly and autonomously take action.

As autonomous systems that identify software vulnerabilities proliferate (and they will), open code and tooling can help level the playing field. Software security has become a speed race across four stages: detection, verification, coordination, and patch propagation. Open ecosystems distribute these across a community, where more closed-source projects centralize knowledge and action across all four stages inside a single vendor, representing a single point of failure where only one organization can see and fix the code. The distributed nature of open development is robust to such constraints, and can be especially powerful in communities with dedicated security professionals, like the Linux kernel security team, the Open Source Security Foundation, and the team at Hugging Face working on model and supply-chain security.

A common argument for more closed systems is proprietary obscurity, where the code underlying a system is inaccessible. Unfortunately, this provides less protection than it used to. AI systems are increasingly able to assist with reverse engineering of stripped binaries, which matters because most legacy firmware and embedded code is closed, binary-only, and no longer maintained. That code represents a huge attack surface, and it’s becoming more legible and accessible as AI tools improve.

There’s also a risk created by how AI is being used inside closed codebases. When companies adopt AI coding tools under the wrong incentives (for instance, evaluating engineers by the volume of features shipped rather than code quality) AI-accelerated development can introduce more vulnerabilities into proprietary code than traditional development would. Those vulnerabilities then sit inside a closed codebase where only one organization can find and fix them, while AI-enabled attackers are increasingly capable of discovering them from the outside. The combination of more vulnerabilities produced more quickly, behind a single-organization firewall, is exactly the kind of imbalance that open ecosystems are positioned to avoid.

Underlying all of this is capability asymmetry between attackers and defenders. Open models and open tooling narrow that gap by giving defenders access to the same class of capabilities attackers can reach for — capabilities that would otherwise be concentrated within a small number of well-resourced entities.

Cybersecurity defense is where open source and AI agents can play a key role together. Based on the System Card, it appears that Mythos is capable of operating with close to full autonomy, something we’ve advised against due to the potential loss of control. AI agents that are instead semi-autonomous, where the types of actions they can take are prespecified and certain steps require human approval, hit a sweet spot of benefit and risk. In semi-autonomous systems, people remain in control, and the AI agent is responsible for specific subtasks. This is possible to do with open code that organizations can run privately within their own institutions, specifying allowable tools, skills, and system access privileges. With this setup, AI agents can be deployed defensively, finding vulnerabilities and assisting with patching under an organization’s own controls.

The semi-autonomous approach depends on humans being able to actually understand what an AI agent did and why. That’s much more possible when the system is built on open components, such as open agent scaffolding, open rule engines, and auditable decision logs and traces, than when it’s a black box. The “human in the loop” is only meaningful if the human can see into the loop.

Companies don’t have to build these capabilities entirely from scratch. There’s a rich open-source ecosystem of security tooling, including vulnerability scanners, intrusion detection systems, log analyzers, and fuzzing frameworks, that AI agents can be integrated with.

For high-stakes organizations, starting from open, auditable foundations means security teams can actually inspect how their monitoring works, rather than trusting a single vendor’s claims. This is particularly important where sensitive data and processes are involved, and where sensitive material should generally not be flowing through external AI providers. Open systems can be rigorously analyzed by in-house security professionals, fine-tuned on an organizations’s own secure data, modified to produce organization-specific oversight mechanisms, and run entirely within an organization’s own infrastructure, keeping everything behind appropriate firewalls.

Attackers will develop models that take advantage of vulnerabilities. A significant part of the answer is leaning into transparent practices: open security reviews, published threat models, shared vulnerability databases, and open tooling that any team can adopt. The alternative of each organization trying to secure itself in isolation with proprietary tools doesn’t scale against attackers who are coordinating and sharing techniques in their own communities.

The future of AI cybersecurity will be shaped less by any single model and more by the ecosystems that surround them. Openness provides defenders with the visibility, the control, the community, and the shared infrastructure to stay ahead.

#10290. Android Auto update improves support for wide displays, but not everyone will see it [Gallery]

Google has rolled out a new update for Android Auto that improves support for wider display formats, but there’s a good chance you won’t be able to see it.

Android Auto has to scale to a lot of different display shapes and sizes, and its functionality varies depending on what you’re using as the platform adapts to what your display can handle. This can sometimes mean you are locked out of a specific feature or need to access it another way. A couple of infamous examples of this include the “Report” option in Google Maps being hidden on smaller displays, as well as the weather card only being on larger, taller displays.

That said, Google is now making an effort to improve how apps on Android Auto adapters to wider formats.

In the latest app update (v18.2), Android Auto is tweaking apps to switch from a top-bar layout to a sidebar for navigation. So, in Spotify, this means the “Home,” “Recents,” “Browse,” and “Library” shortcuts move to a sidebar rather than being up top.

It’s a good use of space, as it allows more content to be visible on wide but short displays. Android Authority spotted the change across Spotify, YouTube Music, and Phone, implying this is probably a platform-level change rather than being tied to individual app updates.

It’s a great change, but one you might not be able to see.

As mentioned, Android Auto adjusts to take advantage of whatever display space it has available, and that often includes putting Google Maps off to the side of other apps. While you can easily set Maps to take up the full display, other apps are less likely to be able to do that, with Maps semi-permanently off to the opposite side. In a car with a wide display we tested for this new format, Maps prevented any other apps from going wide enough to show the new layout, so your results may vary. In many cases, this new layout may simply not be visible. In a way, though, that’s a good thing – it shows that Google is addressing even the most niche aspects of Android Auto, and that’s a win for everyone.

#10289. Serving a Local LLM to Several Users: Ollama, LM Studio, llama.cpp and vLLM Benchmarked

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

When one person chats with a local model, it barely matters which server you run. On one RTX 3090 with the same model file, Ollama, LM Studio and llama.cpp wrote text within about 10 percent of each other, because all three run llama.cpp underneath. That changes when your app sends several requests at once. With four requests, the best setup produced more than three times as much text as the worst, and the cause was a default setting, not the engine. With 32 requests, vLLM produced 2.5 times as much text as the best llama.cpp setup I tested.

This article puts those numbers side by side and shows which setting to change for your app.

I ran every test on one machine. The full write-ups, with every command and the raw results, are on homebrewserver.club.

Ollama, LM Studio and llama.cpp loaded the exact same GGUF files, checked by SHA-256. vLLM cannot run GGUF files well, so it loaded a 4-bit AWQ file of the same model (9.1 GB). Answer quality was not compared.

The tests ran between 8 and 16 November 2026, and speeds on this machine varied by a few percent from one day to the next. Treat a gap under about 5% as a tie. All of this is one consumer GPU and one model family, so read the numbers as a guide to how the servers behave, not as a ranking for your hardware.

This is the short prompt with a 512-token answer.

Ollama and LM Studio both start llama.cpp's llama-server program for each model they load. Ollama has done this since version 0.30, and a comment in its source code says so. On Linux, LM Studio's CUDA runtime is a folder with llama.cpp libraries and a llama-server binary.

Ollama logs the command it starts when you set OLLAMA_DEBUG=1. When llama.cpp was started by hand with that exact command, in a run next to Ollama, its speed matched Ollama's within 1%. So Ollama adds no speed cost of its own. LM Studio was 5 to 10% slower in this test. The test did not separate whether that came from its llama.cpp build or its other start options.

For one user, the gap between Ollama and LM Studio was about 0.4 s on a 512-token answer from the 9B model. You would notice it in long answers, and hardly in a chat window.

A web app rarely sends one request at a time. A chat page, a background summary job and an agent can all call the same model at the same moment. The next test sent four requests at once, each asking for 256 tokens, and measured the total output per second.

A slot is one request that the server works on at the same time as others. llama-server sets the number of slots with -np (short for --parallel), and Ollama and LM Studio pass their own setting through to it.

With one slot, the server answers the four requests one after another, so the total stays at the speed of a single request. That is Ollama's default. With four slots, the server puts the four requests through the model together, and the total rose to more than twice that of one slot. That is the default in LM Studio and llama.cpp. vLLM was the fastest at four requests, but it was tested only with the 9B model. Its lead grows with more requests, as the section after next shows.

For your app, this means that the fourth user of a default Ollama server waits for the first three answers to finish before their own answer starts.

The obvious fix is OLLAMA_NUM_PARALLEL=4. It worked for the 9B model, though in one of three rounds Ollama still answered at the speed of a single request. With the 27B model, it made Ollama slower than its default.

The cause is how each server sizes the context, the memory that holds each request's prompt and answer. Ollama picks the context from the GPU's memory: 32,768 tokens on a 24 GB card, according to its docs. With four slots, it gives each slot its own 32,768 tokens, so it started llama-server with a 131,072-token context. The Ollama FAQ says the memory needed grows with the number of parallel requests multiplied by the context length.

That context did not fit next to the 27B model in 24 GB. ollama ps showed 16% of the model on the CPU, and the total speed fell to 33.1 tokens per second.

LM Studio and llama.cpp handle it differently. Their four slots share one pool of context:

The price of LM Studio's default is a short context. Four requests sharing 8,192 tokens leave little room for long documents or a long chat history. If your app sends long prompts, load the model with a larger context.

In Ollama, setting a smaller context with OLLAMA_CONTEXT_LENGTH next to OLLAMA_NUM_PARALLEL should avoid the spill to the CPU. The test did not try this, so measure it on your own card.

The last test went further, from 1 to 32 requests at once, with the 9B model. It compared vLLM, a server built to serve one model to many users, with llama.cpp at its defaults and with more slots. Ollama and LM Studio were tested only up to four requests, so they are not in this table.

With its defaults, llama-server chose four slots by itself, so it worked on four requests and queued the rest. Its total stayed near 330 tokens per second from 4 requests to 32. Setting -np 16 or -np 32 roughly doubled the total at 16 requests.

vLLM's lead came from each request running faster inside a large batch. At 32 requests, each vLLM request generated about 61 tokens per second, against about 27 on llama.cpp with 32 slots. vLLM's README names the two techniques behind this: PagedAttention, which stores each request's working memory in small blocks, and continuous batching, which adds new requests to the batch the GPU is already working on.

Total output tells you how much work the server does. The wait for the first word tells you how the app feels to the user behind the last request:

For a web app, that is 22.5 seconds of spinner before any text appears. Long prompts make every wait longer, on both servers. With eight requests of about 4,120 tokens each, the last request waited 7.9 s on vLLM and 8.8 s on llama.cpp with 32 slots.

If you set the slots yourself, the llama-server README lists three options that work together:

If you run an older llama.cpp, update first. Four requests at once ran 14 to 22% faster on v1.0.0 than on the build from five days earlier, while one request stayed the same. The most likely reason is a new CUDA kernel in v1.0 for steps of 2 to 24 tokens on RTX 30-series and newer cards.

vLLM's throughput comes with two costs that matter on a shared machine.

It reserves most of the GPU. By default, vLLM takes 92% of the card's memory before it loads anything, and fills what the model does not need with cache. With a desktop and a browser holding about 2 GiB, vLLM refused to start:

Setting --gpu-memory-utilization 0.6 alone was not enough with this model, because the default limit of 256 sequences needed more cache than fit. Adding --max-num-seqs 32 fixed it. With both settings, vLLM held 12.7 GiB and kept the same speeds. llama.cpp works the other way: it sizes its cache from -c and -np and never asked for more than 15.1 GiB in this test.

It starts slowly. llama-server answered requests 2 to 5 s after its container started. vLLM compiles the model before it serves anything. That took 72 s with its compile cache already on disk, and 173 s on the first start without it. Changing a vLLM argument triggered a fresh compile.

It also needs a different model file. vLLM loads Hugging Face safetensors, so a 4-bit model is a separate AWQ or GPTQ upload. The AWQ file here was 9.1 GB against 5.7 GB for the GGUF, because its recipe leaves some layers unquantized. Check the file size, not only "4-bit", when you size a model for your card.

All four servers have an OpenAI-compatible API under /v1, so the same client code works with each one. You change the base URL and the model name. These are the ports used in the tests:

In Node.js with the openai package, that looks like the sketch below. The measurements came from a Python test client, and this snippet was not part of them:

Qwen3.5 thinks before it answers unless you turn it off. The tests sent "chat_template_kwargs": {"enable_thinking": false} in the request body to vLLM and llama.cpp.

None of the servers asked for a password in these tests. llama-server also warned at start-up that its CORS rule allowed all origins. Bind the port to 127.0.0.1, as in the table, and set --api-key on llama.cpp or vLLM if anything else on your network can reach it.

Before you choose, count how many requests your app really sends at the same moment. Log the timestamps for a day, or count the parallel calls your agent makes per user action. If that number is one, any of these servers will do. If it is four or more, the slot setting will change your users' wait more than the choice of engine.

Not for one request with the same settings. Ollama runs llama.cpp's own server, and the two were within 1% when started with the same command. llama.cpp was faster with four requests at once, because it starts four slots by default and Ollama starts one.

Ollama gives each parallel request its own full context. With four slots on a 24 GB card, that was 131,072 tokens, which pushed 16% of a 27B model onto the CPU. A smaller context may avoid that, but this test did not measure it.

When many requests arrive together. At 32 requests, vLLM produced 2.5 times the output of llama.cpp with 32 slots and kept every first-word wait under a second. For one request at a time, llama.cpp was 5% faster and started in seconds instead of more than a minute.

Usually not. All four serve OpenAI-compatible endpoints under /v1, so you change the base URL and the model name.

#10288. On-Device Speech Recognition and Text-to-Speech in Google AI Edge Gallery

Today, we are introducing on-device Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) and Text-to-Speech (TTS) capabilities in Google AI Edge Gallery. Voice is often the most natural way to interact with AI on phones and wearables. Recent advances in compact speech architectures now make it possible to run accurate, multilingual ASR and expressive TTS models entirely on device, all within a small memory footprint, with low latency, and completely offline. By pairing these lightweight speech models with on-device small language models (SLMs) like Gemini Nano and Gemma 4, developers can build apps that stream live transcriptions as the user speaks and synthesize natural spoken replies locally.

This release brings together major advancements across both Google’s system speech models and the open-weight ecosystem:

Below, we’ll explore how this local voice pipeline powers the new XR (Extended Reality) Language Teacher showcase, upgrades AI Chat in Google AI Edge Gallery, and how you can build with these APIs and models today.

Learning a language while traveling happens in the real world, often in underground stations, busy markets, or abroad where Wi-Fi and roaming data may not be available. To show how vision, language, and speech models can work together 100% locally on your phone with no network connection needed, we built the XR Language Teacher showcase in Google AI Edge Gallery. Simply point your camera at an unfamiliar object or menu, ask "What is that, and how do I ask for one?", and immediately hear an explanation in your language alongside authentic pronunciation in the local language.

Link to Youtube Video (visible only when JS is disabled)

With inference running locally on a paired phone, the same experience works standalone on a phone and extends naturally to hands-free smart glasses. To see how we adapted Language Teacher for intelligent glasses check out our recent talk at Android Dev Summit: Building Audio-First Experiences for Intelligent Eyewear with Gemini Nano.

Beyond the XR Language Teacher showcase, we also built ASR and TTS directly into Google AI Edge Gallery’s main AI Chat feature, giving on-device SLMs like Gemini Nano and Gemma 4 a natural, offline voice interface while on the go.

Link to Youtube Video (visible only when JS is disabled)

While multimodal models like Gemma 4 can process audio inputs directly, we provide a modular solution for cascading language models with separate, lightweight voice models for latency optimization and flexibility. Depending on your target devices and model requirements, our open-source code on GitHub shows you the optimized and recommended solution for Android using ML Kit, as well as MediaPipe Tasks and LiteRT for cross-platform coverage and open model support.

For developers building for Android devices, ML Kit’s GenAI Speech Recognition and Text-to-Speech APIs provide a standardized, platform-integrated path out of the box. With the underlying speech models managed through AICore and Google’s on-device speech services, developers get production-grade quality without having to manage model downloads or worry about APK size bloat. Your app also benefits automatically from hardware acceleration across NPU and TPU backends (when available) and seamless background model updates.

Integrating ASR and TTS into cross-platform applications usually requires handling low-level audio framing, Voice Activity Detection (VAD), and complex decoding pipelines. MediaPipe Task simplifies this by providing unified, turnkey ASR and TTS APIs across iOS, macOS, Windows, Linux, and Web that abstract away manual pre-processing, audio stream routing, and platform-specific audio management into simple, high-level interfaces:

Under the hood, ML Kit and MediaPipe Tasks are powered by LiteRT, Google’s high-performance on-device AI inference infrastructure. Cross-platform applications requiring even more fine-grained control over speech processing or custom model architectures can also build on it directly.

Speech models often rely on multiple subgraphs and auxiliary assets, such as encoder/decoder subgraphs and tokenizers for ASR, or phonemizer dictionaries, voice embeddings, and vocoders for TTS. All required components for each model are packaged into a single .litertlm file for easy deployment. The app ships with ready-to-use .litertlm models, including Parakeet-TDT-0.6B-v3 (multilingual ASR), PocketTTS 100M (multilingual TTS), Phonon 31M (ultra-lightweight English TTS), and Kokoro-82M (multilingual TTS). Beyond these, the vibrant Hugging Face LiteRT Community with over 10K+ followers offers a growing catalog of open-weight models, like Whisper, Qwen3-ASR and Moonshine for ASR, or Qwen3-TTS and Matcha for TTS. For developers seeking custom implementations or support for additional open-weight voice models, LiteRT provides a rich set of multimodal model examples to help you get started, with more on the way.

Adding a local voice pipeline takes on-device SLMs beyond typing-based chat interfaces, enabling natural, voice-first interactions that work anywhere, completely offline. All the building blocks to try these experiences or integrate them into your own apps are available today:

#10286. WhatsApp officially adds scheduled messages, and the rollout is scheduled too

It’s about time. WhatsApp announced today that it is finally adding support for scheduled messages in its app.

A staple of many other messaging apps, WhatsApp is adding scheduled messages to its app. This gives users the ability to write a message but schedule sending it to another user or group chat at a later time.

Scheduled messages on WhatsApp can be sent up to 14 days after you draft them in both 1:1 chats and group chats. You can schedule through a long-press on the send button, with a menu popping up to let you pick the future time when the message will be sent. You can also see scheduled messages before they’re sent to cancel sending or edit the message.

WhatsApp notes that these messages are sent even if your phone’s battery is dead or if the device is off, and everything is still end-to-end encrypted. It works with text, photos, and videos, but apparently not with voice notes.

That said, the rollout is also scheduled out. WhatsApp says the feature will start showing up for users “over the coming weeks” globally, so you might be waiting a bit longer for this long overdue release.

#10285. QIMMA قِمّة ⛰: A Quality-First Arabic LLM Leaderboard

QIMMA validates benchmarks before evaluating models, ensuring reported scores reflect genuine Arabic language capability in LLMs.

If you've been tracking Arabic LLM evaluation, you've probably noticed a growing tension: the number of benchmarks and leaderboards is expanding rapidly, but are we actually measuring what we think we're measuring?

We built QIMMA قمّة (Arabic for "summit"), to answer that question systematically. Instead of aggregating existing Arabic benchmarks as-is and running models on them, we applied a rigorous quality validation pipeline before any evaluation took place. What we found was sobering: even widely-used, well-regarded Arabic benchmarks contain systematic quality issues that can quietly corrupt evaluation results.

This post walks through what QIMMA is, how we built it, what problems we found, and what the model rankings look like once you clean things up.

Arabic is spoken by over 400 million people across diverse dialects and cultural contexts, yet the Arabic NLP evaluation landscape remains fragmented. A few key pain points have motivated this work:

Translation issues. Many Arabic benchmarks are translations from English. This introduces distributional shifts. Questions that feel natural in English become awkward or culturally misaligned in Arabic, making benchmark data less representative of how Arabic is naturally used.

Absent quality validation. Even native Arabic benchmarks are often released without rigorous quality checks. Annotation inconsistencies, incorrect gold answers, encoding errors, and cultural bias in ground-truth labels have all been documented in established resources.

Reproducibility gaps. Evaluation scripts and per-sample outputs are rarely released publicly, making it hard to audit results or build on prior work.

Coverage fragmentation. Existing leaderboards cover isolated tasks and narrow domains, making holistic model assessment difficult.

To illustrate where QIMMA sits relative to existing platforms:

QIMMA is the only platform combining all five properties: open source, predominantly native Arabic content, systematic quality validation, code evaluation, and public per-sample inference outputs.

QIMMA consolidates 109 subsets from 14 source benchmarks into a unified evaluation suite of over 52,000 samples, spanning 7 domains:

A few things stand out about this design:

This is the methodological heart of QIMMA. Before running a single model, we applied a multi-stage validation pipeline to every sample in every benchmark.

Each sample was independently evaluated by two state-of-the-art LLMs:

We chose two models with strong Arabic capability but different training data compositions, so that their combined judgment is more robust than either alone.

Each model scores a sample against a 10-point rubric, with binary scores (0 or 1) per criterion:

A sample is eliminated if either model scores it below 7/10. Samples where both models agree on elimination are dropped immediately. However, where only one model flags a sample, it proceeds to human review in Stage 2.

Flagged samples are reviewed by native Arabic speakers with cultural and dialectal familiarity. Human annotators make final calls on:

For culturally sensitive content, multiple perspectives are considered, since "correctness" can genuinely vary across Arab regions.

The pipeline revealed recurring quality issues across benchmarks; not isolated errors, but systematic patterns reflecting gaps in how benchmarks were originally constructed.

False or mismatched gold indices, factually wrong answers, missing or raw text answers.

Corrupt or illegible text, spelling and grammar errors, and duplicate samples.

Stereotype reinforcement and monolithic generalizations about diverse communities.

Misalignment of gold answers with evaluation protocols.

Code benchmarks required a different intervention. Rather than discarding samples, we refined the Arabic problem statements in 3LM's Arabic adaptations of HumanEval+ and MBPP+, leaving task identifiers, reference solutions, and test suites completely unchanged.

QIMMA uses LightEval, EvalPlus and FannOrFlop as its evaluation framework, chosen for consistency, multilingual community adoption, and reproducibility.

QIMMA standardizes prompting by question format, with six template types:

All prompts are in Arabic. For MizanQA and ArabCulture, benchmark-specific system prompts from the original papers are preserved.

Results as of April 2026; covering top 10 evaluated models. Visit the live leaderboard for current rankings.

#10282. 5 Things Most Developers Get Wrong When Turning Images into HTML

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Turning a design image into a working webpage can look simple.

You have a picture (a mockup, a screenshot, a Figma export), and your job is to turn it into working HTML in a browser.

But here is the catch. A design image is static, while a webpage is dynamic and responsive across different screen sizes and devices. A webpage needs to load quickly, adapt perfectly to different screen sizes, and allow touch interactions on mobile devices.

Most mistakes in this process happen when the conversion is treated as copying a picture instead of rebuilding it.

This section walks you through the mistakes developers often make, and more importantly, how to fix each of them.

Whether you are slicing a client mockup or converting a screenshot into code, avoiding these mistakes can save you from hours of rework. Let’s get into the details.

A screenshot reflects how a page appears at a particular display. But it doesn’t show how the layout will behave when the content changes or the screen gets smaller.

Developers sometimes try to copy the exact positions and dimensions of every element. To match the screenshot, they may use fixed widths, large margins, and absolute positioning.

This can work at one screen size, but the layout may break on smaller screens or when a heading wraps onto an extra line.

The better approach is identifying the layout rules behind the design. CSS Grid can arrange the cards in columns. Flexbox can help align elements within each card. And media queries can adjust the layout for smaller screens.

Pixel-level comparison can be useful in some cases, but it should not come at the cost of a flexible layout.

When developers recreate a design, it’s easier for them to focus on shapes and spacing rather than the purpose of each element. So, they may use generic elements for headings, buttons, navigation areas, and content sections instead of choosing elements that reflect each element's purpose.

This may produce the right appearance, but it often makes the code harder to maintain and understand. And when developers fail to use the right HTML elements, it can also create accessibility problems later.

So don’t put everything inside several unnamed containers. Instead, use a clear structure with appropriate headings, meaningful alt text for informative images, and real buttons for actions.

Semantic elements (e.g., header, nav, main, section, and footer) can also help organize a large page when they match the content’s purpose.

A design image may have headings, descriptions, prices, labels, or button text.

Reusing the entire image to reproduce the original design feels quick. But it can create problems when that text has to work as part of a responsive web page.

For example, there’s a promotional banner that contains a heading, a short description, and a CTA button. If you use the entire banner as one image, you can’t easily change the heading, translate the text, or make the button work as a real element.

So, don’t treat the image like that. Instead, use the original image where appropriate and recreate the text and button in HTML. CSS can control their position, size, color, and spacing.

Make sure you distinguish between visual elements that should remain images and text that should be recreated as HTML.

Not every part of turning images into HTML needs to be done manually.

Developers sometimes spend too much time on recreating basic elements when there are free online conversion tools available. These tools can help them get an initial version much faster.

An online conversion tool may be helpful when you need to extract text or generate a rough starting layout from a design image.

For example, you can upload a design image into an online image to html converter to get a starting point (rather than starting from a blank file). Review the tool’s output. Identify the parts you can reuse (as they are) and tweak the parts that need adjustments.

Keep in mind that the first result generated by the tool isn’t the final code. You may need to reorganize the HTML, refine the CSS, and adjust the layout to make it responsive.

Use automation where it saves time and your own judgement where it matters.

A screenshot shows just one view of a page. It doesn’t show how the layout may change on a phone or how people using a keyboard/screen reader can interact with it.

So, developers who focus only on the desktop design may end up with:

content that becomes too small on mobile devices

There’s also a chance of accessibility problems when images lack suitable alt text/interactive elements.

Let’s say a page has three cards in a row. On the desktop, this arrangement may work well. But on a phone, you may need to stack the cards vertically so their content remains readable.

That’s why accessibility should be considered during the same process. Use meaningful headings and provide appropriate alt text for images. Also, maintain sufficient text contrast and make sure interactive elements can be operated with a keyboard.

Lastly, don’t forget to test the page on both desktop and mobile screen sizes before finalizing it.

HTML and CSS handle the structure and appearance of a webpage, but JavaScript makes it possible to add interactive features.

For example, a design image may contain a navigation menu with a button. When recreating this design, developers should make sure the button performs an actual action rather than simply looking like a clickable element.

You can use JavaScript's event listeners to handle these interactions.

Now, add JavaScript to make the menu functional:

In this example, clicking the button opens or closes the navigation menu. The aria-expanded attribute also communicates the menu's current state to assistive technologies.

This is a simple example of why converting a design image into HTML involves more than matching its appearance. Developers also need to recreate the behavior of interactive elements using appropriate HTML, CSS, and JavaScript.

The process of turning an image into HTML feels easy when you treat it the right way.

Start by identifying the main sections, text, images, and interactive elements. Then create meaningful HTML and build the layout with CSS. Make the necessary adjustments to ensure it works across different screen sizes.

Use a conversion tool when it can really save time. But don’t forget to review the generated output of the tool thoroughly before using it.

A screenshot is a visual reference, not a complete set of development instructions. And the best result for you isn’t simply a page that looks like the image.

It is a page that also works well, adapts well, and stays easy to maintain.
