#10267. 9to5Google’s Best of 2026

We reviewed dozens of products in 2026, and the one through line across all of them was cost. Because of RAMageddon, everything was more expensive, and it became somewhat easier to separate the products that were good because they were cheap from the ones that were good at any price.

This year was a lot of things, but it was primarily a reminder that the best products are created through careful iteration. Only one product on this list, the XREAL Aura, represents an emerging class. The rest, from the Fitbit Air to the Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8, showcase years of work in optimizing for design, weight, battery life, and performance. Some take more risks than others, but to us they all represent the very best of their respective categories.

Price: $99.99/$129.99 (special editions)Black Friday deal: Save $30 on the Google Fitbit Air Champagne Gold & Obsidian Bundle. Ends 12/02.Release date: May 26, 2026

A screenless Google device outside of a smart speaker wasn’t something I thought I needed. Yet the Fitbit Air has become one of my favorite products to come out of Mountain View in years. Fitness tracking is something I want happening quietly in the background, not another reason to check a screen.

That’s what the Air gets right. It isn’t trying to reinvent fitness tracking; it packages it in a comfortable, lightweight band that stays out of the way. Health tracking data isn’t locked behind a paywall, and there’s no display demanding attention throughout the day.

Smart rings and full-featured watches have their place, but this slim wearable strikes a particularly appealing balance. It gives me useful information when I want it without becoming another device to manage. It’s comfortable, inexpensive, and easy to live with—and sometimes that’s exactly what makes a product great.

— Damien Wilde, Daniel Bader & Andrew Romero

Price: $2,499Black Friday price: $1,899Release date: November 1, 2026

I’m primarily a TV person, especially when it comes to gaming. But after spending time with XGIMI’s Horizon 30 Pro, I’ve been enjoying a very different setup. I loved the older Horizon Pro 4K and used it until this arrived; the 30 Pro feels like a substantial leap forward.

VRR support has made it possible to play my Steam Machine on a roughly 200-inch image in the bedroom, while the built-in speakers do an impressive job of filling the room. Going from Forza Horizon 5 at 120fps to Blue Planet on BBC iPlayer is effortless thanks to Google TV.

The swiveling base is more useful than it might sound. I can position the projector in the corner of the room and let XGIMI’s keystone correction handle the rest. It’s an expensive upgrade, but for a home cinema setup that doubles as a giant gaming display, it’s a beast.

I still wish the Steam Controller cost less. Beyond that, though, I have very little to complain about: this is the best controller I’ve used in years. It’s comfortable, gives Windows users a way to control their PC, and brings together some of the best ideas from my beloved Steam Deck.

Steam Input is the real selling point. The depth of customization makes this controller feel at home on a PC in a way few alternatives do. I haven’t connected with a new controller this quickly in a long time.

That doesn’t mean everyone needs one. Most people would be well served by an 8BitDo controller—or even a Stadia controller converted to Bluetooth. But if you play on PC and want the premium option, this is my pick.

Price: $1,899.99Black Friday price: $1,549.99Release date: August 7, 2026

The Galaxy Z Fold 8 is my favorite foldable of 2026. I’ve been enthralled with its design since reviewing it in July, and it won’t be leaving my daily rotation anytime soon.

The short, compact outer screen is refreshing to use, but it’s the inner display that changed the way I think about foldables. Its proportions feel more flexible than the square-shaped displays that have become so common across the category. Samsung’s motivations for adopting this form factor may be obvious, but the result works—and that’s what matters when I’m using it every day.

— Ben Schoon, Daniel Bader & Andrew Romero

Price: Ear (3): $179 / Ear (3a): $99Black Friday price: Ear (3): $94 / Ear (3a): $69Release date: Ear (3): Sept 18, 2025 / Ear (3a): July 7, 2026

Ear (3a) earns the nod here, but this is really a celebration of Nothing’s entire audio lineup. Its clean sound profiles, thoughtful designs, and compatibility with Android and the other devices I use have kept me listening all year.

Ear (3) remains my primary pair of earbuds, while Ear (3a) gets plenty of use when pocket space is at a premium. Ear (open) and Nothing Headphone (1) Pro round out the rest of my listening needs.

I still stand by calling Ear (3a) simply ‘the best earbuds.’ More broadly, Nothing has built an audio lineup worth paying attention to, especially when end-of-year discounts make it easier to try.

Price: ~$1,999Release date: April 21, 2026 (China) / Nov 2026 (Global)

If there’s one phone from 2026 I wish I could return to, it’s the Oppo Find X9 Ultra. ColorOS has quietly become one of the best Android experiences by getting the small details right, and the Ultra’s camera hardware and shooting experience remain standouts—even next to Oppo’s newer Find X10 Pro Max.

This is one of those increasingly rare smartphones that feels unwilling to compromise. I’ll be thinking about it until there’s a proper successor, and the prospect of not getting one in 2027 is disappointing.

I wish Oppo had sold this phone officially in the US. Importing comes with real complications, but the Find X9 Ultra is one of the few phones good enough to make me consider it.

Price: ~$1,720Release date: March 13, 2026

It’s been a remarkable year for foldables, but the Honor Magic V6 is my favorite of the bunch. Its combination of durability, battery life, and camera quality finally made me stop thinking about going back to a conventional slab phone.

The cameras are a big part of that. I used to rely entirely on my Panasonic GH5 for work photos; now I often reach for the Magic V6 instead. Its large 1/2-inch telephoto sensor helps it deliver the kind of dependable results I want when I need to capture something quickly.

It’s also held up to far more punishment than I’d normally put a foldable through. After a mud torture test and a trip through the dishwasher, I’m still using it months later. Battery life has been another major strength.

Honor’s software still has rough edges, but the improvements are substantial, and the seven-year update promise matters. The remaining problem is availability: I’d love to see Honor make its phones officially accessible across North America.

Android XR has had an awkward start, but the XREAL Aura feels like the kind of product the platform needed from the beginning. It puts a fresh idea into a form factor that’s easier to imagine wearing than a bulky headset.

Think of it as smart glasses that behave more like a VR headset. Open the app drawer with a pinch—or use the tethered compute puck—and your chosen app appears as a floating window you can move around. It’s like having a tablet suspended wherever you need it.

That makes remote work and entertainment feel surprisingly natural, especially when the glasses weigh less than a fifth of many VR headsets. There are compromises: hand gestures can be finicky, and while Bluetooth game controllers work, there isn’t a Meta Quest-style motion controller available for immersive gaming.

Even so, Aura makes a compelling case for Android XR. It’s an appealing option for people interested in immersive entertainment who don’t want the weight and bulk of a conventional VR headset.

DroidDeck has changed the way I think about gaming on Android. It isn’t the first project to bring PC games to a phone, but it feels like one of the most capable. The pitch is straightforward, even if the technology isn’t: run Steam on your Android device.

Rather than emulating an entire PC in the traditional sense, DroidDeck brings together translation layers using projects such as FEX and Proton. The technical details are complicated, but the practical result is that your phone can run games it wasn’t originally designed to understand.

Performance across my devices has been impressive—good enough that I’ve seen games run better than on my Steam Deck. The project is also free, community-driven, and highly customizable. The trade-off is that support for brand-new hardware can take time.

If you’ve been on the fence about mobile gaming, pairing DroidDeck with a controller such as my favorite, the GameSir G8 Galileo, is a great way to see how far it’s come.

Price: $179.99 / $219.99 (special editions)Release date: October 27, 2026

The Fitbit Air is a good fitness tracker and, to my eye, an attractive bracelet. But years of wearing watches have trained me to expect the time on my wrist. Even toward the end of my time with the Air, I kept glancing down for a clock that wasn’t there.

The Fitbit Edge fixes that central complaint. Its always-on display reduces battery life to roughly two or three days, but that’s a trade-off I’m happy to make. The software’s Pixel Watch-inspired look also helps it feel like part of a more cohesive lineup. For me, a small screen makes a meaningful difference.

Price: $29.99Release date: November 11, 2026

We waited so long for a first-party Google tracker that the Find My Device network had time to become Find Hub. The Pixel Tag makes the wait worthwhile with a more integrated experience: everything is managed in the Find Hub app, rather than spread across separate software.

‘Notify when left behind’ was overdue, and ‘Ring this phone’ has worked well for me. These are practical features, but they’re also reminders of how much first-party hardware can do to improve the software around it.

I also like the pill-shaped design. Google didn’t simply copy the AirTag; it made something that feels at home in the Pixel family. It’s a small thing, but it’s pleasant to hold—and surprisingly satisfying to fidget with.

Price: $349.99Black Friday price: $314.99Release date: July 6, 2026

A dock needs to do more than look good, but Keychron’s Thunderbolt 5 dock makes a strong first impression on a desk. Its machined aluminum case fits neatly into my setup, and the usefulness goes well beyond the finish.

I switched between devices more often this year. Moving my work from a Windows PC to the Mac mini M6 left the PC on gaming duty, while the Googlebook launch gave me another computer to plug into the same monitors and workstation.

The Keychron dock makes those changes simple: I connect the USB-C input cable and let it handle the display and data connections. Its own power supply, four USB-A ports, three USB-C ports, SD card reader, and wired Ethernet connection give me the flexibility I need. It might be the most useful addition I’ve made to my desk all year.

I don’t think I’ll stop talking about the Boox Picco anytime soon. It’s a wonderfully simple little e-reader with a straightforward operating system and battery life that stretches across days or weeks, depending on use.

You can attach it magnetically to the back of your phone or slip it into almost any pocket. But the bigger benefit is how easy it makes picking up a book, whether I’m out of the house or just moving from one room to another.

At around $100, it’s an appealingly focused device. In a year when so much attention has gone to retro gadgets and handhelds, the Picco captures a similar pleasure: a small piece of technology that does one thing well.

Price: $499.99Black Friday price: $399.99Release date: October 14, 2026

If one gadget came out of nowhere to steal the show for me in 2026, it was the Alexa Tablet 12 Pro. Amazon rebooted its tablet lineup, dropped the Fire branding, and embraced a much more familiar version of Android. Install a third-party launcher to remove the permanent Alexa search bar, and it feels like a regular mid-range Android tablet—with full Play Store support, no sideloading required.

The hardware is where it really wins me over. The base configuration pairs 8GB of RAM with 128GB of storage, which is more than enough for browsing, movies, YouTube, and casual games. But the display is the standout: this is a much better LCD than I expect from a tablet under $1,000, and the nanomatte finish looks and feels fantastic.

I’m as surprised as anyone that Amazon finally figured out its tablet lineup. A little help from the person behind Microsoft’s Surface line seems to have gone a long way. At this price—and especially on sale—I struggle to recommend anything else, including Apple’s base iPad. It’s that good.

Price: $99Black Friday price: $84Release date: July 21, 2026

I have always been a reader, but in my effort to spend less time on my phone this year, I did my utmost to return to e-paper displays for most long-form reading.

The XTEINK X4 Pro is a tiny 4-inch touch-capable e-paper display with a backlight and plenty of battery life. Its magnets help the device stick to the back of most phones (though it’s a bit tall for some smaller devices like the Pixel 11 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro), and it supports custom firmware through the Crosspoint project.

While it occasionally feels cramped to read on, the sheer number of formatting and font options makes it easy to adjust the reading experience to suit your tastes. And because it supports KOReader, reading progress syncs with most other devices, including Kobo e-readers and supported phone apps.

What were your favorite products of 2026? Let us know in the comments.

#10266. Sizing GPU Memory for a RAG Service: KV Cache, Context and Concurrency

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

A retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) app is usually drawn as a language model plus a vector database. When it goes live, the part that fails first is rarely the retrieval. It is GPU memory on the generation model, because a model that loads fine for one request can run out of memory when several users send long questions at once.

This article shows how to estimate that limit before you deploy, with a short script you can run, and then covers what else in the pipeline can slow responses down.

Serving a model takes more than its weights. The GPU also holds:

the key-value (KV) cache, which grows with the length of every active request

memory used by the inference runtime itself

SitePoint's guide to running a local LLM on 10GB of VRAM makes the same point for a single desktop GPU: the usable budget is the total VRAM minus overhead, and the KV cache grows with the context window, so the real model budget is smaller than the number on the box.

For a RAG service, the KV cache matters even more. Retrieved passages are pasted into the prompt, so every request carries a long context, and every concurrent request holds its own cache.

The cache size per token depends on the model's architecture: two tensors (keys and values) for every layer, for every KV head. This script turns those numbers into a rough limit on concurrent requests:

def kv_bytes_per_token(layers, kv_heads, head_dim, dtype_bytes=2):

# Keys and values, for every layer, for one token.

return 2 *layers *kv_heads *head_dim *dtype_bytes

def max_concurrent(vram_gb, weights_gb, ctx_tokens, per_token, reserve_gb=2.0):

budget = (vram_gb - weights_gb - reserve_gb) * GIB

return int(budget // (ctx_tokens * per_token))

per_token = kv_bytes_per_token(32, 8, 128)

print(per_token // 1024, "KiB per token")

n = max_concurrent(24, 16, ctx, per_token)

print(ctx, "tokens ->", n, "concurrent requests")

For a 24 GB GPU holding about 16 GB of fp16 weights with 2 GB kept in reserve, it prints:

The numbers are estimates. Real runtimes add their own overhead, and the architecture values come from the model's configuration file, so read them from the model you actually use. The pattern is what matters: doubling the context length halves the number of requests that fit. A RAG prompt that stuffs in ten retrieved chunks costs real capacity.

Serving runtimes do not simply crash when the cache is full. The vLLM documentation on optimization and tuning explains that when KV cache space is insufficient for all batched requests, the engine preempts some of them and recomputes them later, which can hurt end-to-end latency. Its suggested remedies include giving the cache more memory, reducing the number of concurrent sequences or batched tokens, or sharding the model across GPUs.

So the symptom of undersizing is often not an error. It is slow, uneven responses under load. Test with realistic prompt lengths and several simultaneous users, not a single request.

Embedding and ingestion have a different profile from generation. Embedding is often lighter than serving a large language model, and some teams run it on CPU. Document parsing, chunking and tokenization also run on CPU, so a fast GPU cannot make up for a slow CPU upstream. SitePoint's tutorial on a local RAG system for private documents walks through chunking, embeddings, vector storage and reranking, and is a good map of which stages run where.

RAM: vector indexes, document loaders and caches all live in system memory, so large collections need more of it.

Storage: model files, indexes, logs and backups add up. Fast storage shortens model loading and re-indexing.

Network: if the vector database, application server and model server sit in different places, latency adds to every request.

Two layouts are common. A single instance runs everything and is simplest for prototypes and internal tools. Separated services put ingestion and retrieval on smaller machines and keep the GPU for generation, which scales better as traffic grows.

Memory estimates only hold if the GPU memory is really yours. On a shared or time-sliced GPU, other workloads can take memory and compute away from your service, which makes capacity hard to plan. Hosting providers describe this in different terms, such as passthrough, vGPU, MIG and time-slicing. For a view of how one GPU hosting provider explains those allocation methods, GPU Mart's GPU virtualization guide compares them. It is a hosting company's page, so confirm any provider's claims about isolation and performance with your own load test.

Whatever provider you choose, ask these questions:

Is the physical GPU assigned to you exclusively, or partitioned or time-sliced?

Do you have root access to install your own drivers, CUDA libraries and containers?

Which minimum commitments, regions and support terms apply?

A small stack can run as a handful of containers: an API service for request handling and prompt assembly, an ingestion worker, a vector database and a model server. Keeping them separate lets you monitor each one's memory and CPU use and move the heavy one to bigger hardware without rewriting the rest.

For a service that stays up all month, a fixed monthly term is easier to forecast than hourly capacity. Hourly capacity suits testing quantization settings or processing a one-off document batch.

Is GPU memory always the bottleneck for RAG?

Not always. Generation usually hits memory first, but slow parsing, a small CPU or a distant vector database can dominate response time.

Does quantization solve the memory problem?

It shrinks the weights, but the KV cache still grows with context length and concurrency. Test with your real prompt sizes.

It depends on volume. Small workloads can run on CPU, while a large ingestion job may benefit from a GPU for a limited time.

Size a RAG service for the worst realistic moment, not the single-request demo. Estimate the KV cache from the model's architecture, remember that long retrieved contexts reduce how many requests fit, watch for preemption under load, keep CPU, RAM, storage and network in the plan, and find out whether the GPU is exclusive or shared. The script above is small, but it turns a vague worry about memory into numbers you can check.

#10264. DeepInfra on Hugging Face Inference Providers 🔥

We're thrilled to share that DeepInfra is now a supported Inference Provider on the Hugging Face Hub!

DeepInfra joins our growing ecosystem, enhancing the breadth and capabilities of serverless inference directly on the Hub's model pages. Inference Providers are also seamlessly integrated into our client SDKs (for both JS and Python), making it super easy to use a wide variety of models with your preferred providers.

DeepInfra is a serverless AI inference platform offering one of the most cost-effective pricing per token in the industry. With a catalog of over 100 models, DeepInfra makes it easy for developers to integrate a wide range of AI capabilities into their applications with minimal setup.

DeepInfra supports a broad spectrum of model types - from LLMs to text-to-image, text-to-video, embeddings, and more. As part of this initial integration, DeepInfra is launching support for conversational and text-generation tasks on Hugging Face, enabling access to popular open-weight LLMs such as DeepSeek V4, Kimi-K2.6, GLM-5.1, and many more. Support for additional tasks (text-to-image, text-to-video, embeddings, and more) will roll out soon!

Read more about how to use DeepInfra as an Inference Provider in its dedicated documentation page.

See the full list of models supported by DeepInfra here.

Follow DeepInfra on Hugging Face: https://huggingface.co/DeepInfra.

DeepInfra is available through the Hugging Face SDKs - huggingface_hub (>= 1.11.2) for Python and @huggingface/inference for JavaScript.

The following examples show how to use DeepSeek V4 Pro through DeepInfra. Use a Hugging Face token to authenticate - the request will be routed to DeepInfra automatically.

Hugging Face Inference Providers are integrated in most Agent Harnesses - including Pi, OpenCode, Hermes Agents, OpenClaw, and more. This means you can plug DeepInfra-hosted models straight into your favorite tools without any extra glue code. Browse the full list of integrations here.

For direct requests, i.e. when you use the key from an inference provider, you are billed by the corresponding provider. For instance, if you use a DeepInfra API key you're billed on your DeepInfra account.

For routed requests, i.e. when you authenticate via the Hugging Face Hub, you'll only pay the standard provider API rates. There's no additional markup from us; we just pass through the provider costs directly. (In the future, we may establish revenue-sharing agreements with our provider partners.)

Important Note ‼️ PRO users get $2 worth of Inference credits every month. You can use them across providers. 🔥

We also provide free inference with a small quota for our signed-in free users, but please upgrade to PRO if you can!

#10262. Motorola Signature 27 hands-on: Pure elegance on display

It’s hard to believe we finally got a proper premium phone from Motorola again, and it feels a bit like the return of the Moto X.

Motorola’s slow regeneration in North America from a mostly budget device-minded company to one offering the most expensive non-folding flagship phone might become the thing of legend. That’s not to say the company hasn’t shown true greatness in the past — the Moto X, Moto Z, and Razr lines are proof of that — but it’s always shied away from pulling out all the stops until the Motorola Signature 27 arrived.

Freshly unboxed and sitting in my hands, the textile-clad Capulet Olive Motorola Signature 27 colorway has impressed me in every way, shape, and form over the past 24 hours. It’s a much longer period of time than I usually get with hands-on opportunities and, yet, the newness of the experience has yet to wear off.

Part and parcel to that experience is the design. For whatever reason, this is the year Motorola seems to have truly figured out what makes a phone nice to hold. The textile back, ribbed metal frame, rounded corners, and curved edges on the front and back of the phone are purely blissful to hold. It’s a reminder that a phone can be as good looking as it feels instead of being a flat, boring, off-balance slab like too many phones are now.

The weight also surprised me. On paper this sits right in the middle of all the Ultra/Pro Max-named phones, yet it feels lighter for some intangible reason. The camera hump makes it slightly top-heavy, and it’s almost as wobble-free as a Pixel (there’s just one off-center camera hump).

The new 120Hz LTPO tandem OLED display is as top-notch as you’re going to get. I had all of maybe 2 hours of direct sunlight yesterday to test it with, and boy does it ever get bright. The rest of the time, I’ve been either inside or out in overcast weather, all of which it looked brilliant in. And it uses a combination of DC dimming above 20% brightness, and 2160Hz PWM dimming below 20% brightness, making it super comfortable for me.

Motorola’s software has evolved again with this release, and the verdict is still out on whether or not this is actually better than the company’s Android 16 designs. The build of Android 17 that ships with this phone utilizes some major design changes we’ve only seen on a few random low-end Motorola phones, and I’m not sure I care for the gentle gradients on the quick toggle icons and some other system UI elements. It feels like a weirdly cheap effect that clashes with Material Design’s flatter motif.

Despite that, this is the most Pixelly (is that a word?) a Motorola phone has ever felt. Features like Rambler, Sign to Text, and Create My Widget are here and work impeccably well. Gemini Intelligence is also on the way, and while there’s no specific ETA for that at the moment, it’s exciting to know that the most advanced Android features — which are currently only available on a very small number of devices — are coming to this phone.

With the additional $200 bonus, that leaves the cost at a whopping $1060

This may also be the fastest phone I’ve used to date. Everything is unbelievably snappy. Tap an icon and the thing opens instantly. Animations are zippy, and the new lock screen and customization options feel cohesive. Plus, all the favorite Moto actions and gestures are still here, which I greatly appreciate.

I’ve got some lofty expectations for this camera hardware, too, and it’s because Motorola is talking up such a big game. DXOMark’s camera review rated it the 2nd-best smartphone camera in the world, just under the Huawei Pura 80 Ultra and above the iPhone 18 Pro. Some people don’t take much stock in DXOMark, but it’s still worth noting that they’ve praised the heck out of the camera and Motorola is also pushing this as a winner in a way they’ve never done before.

The hype for the Motorola Signature 27 certainly seems to be realized, and now only time will truly tell if it can live up to the lofty expectations Motorola’s $1,599 price has set for it. If nothing, it’s certainly off to a good start and has made an excellent first impression.

#10261. How Agent Anomaly Detection scores on benchmarks we didn't write

AI agents now read email, book travel and move money for the people who use them. Every tool call also pulls in text that someone else wrote, and whoever controls that text can try to steer the agent. OWASP calls this agent goal hijack and ranks it first in its Top 10 for Agentic Applications (2026).

In September we announced Agent Anomaly Detection in Private Preview on Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform. It reads your agents' traces and logs asynchronously, without adding latency, and flags sessions where an agent acts outside its intended boundaries. We tested this feature against benchmarks for this top risk of agent goal hijack.

Security tools tend to look good on tests their own team wrote, so we ran five non-Google-written, public agent-security benchmarks through Agent Anomaly Detection without changing anything. In four of them, the harmful instruction hides in data that a tool returns. In the fifth, the user asks for harm directly.

The model itself didn't follow about half of the harmful instructions it read. It refused three in four direct requests for harm, and ignored or failed at about 30% of the instructions hidden in tool output. Of the ones that were executed, Agent Anomaly Detection flagged 87% for post-execution review. It raised false alarms on 2% to 16% of benign sessions, depending on the tools the agent uses. Poisoned memory is the clear gap: when instructions planted in the agent’s long-term memory made it act, Agent Anomaly Detection caught 4 of 18.

We ran each benchmark case through an agent built with the Agent Development Kit (ADK) using gemini-2.5-flash, on the benchmark's simulated apps. The agent sent its traces and logs to Agent Anomaly Detection, as a customer's agent would. Then the benchmark's own Python check read the final state of the apps, such as whether money left the account, and labeled the session. Deterministic code decides the label, not a model, so an injected instruction can't mislead the grader, and Agent Anomaly Detection cannot cheat the benchmark. Each agent first ran at least 300 benign sessions, because Agent Anomaly Detection learns how each agent usually behaves.

We also recorded whether a tool returned the harmful instruction to the agent. In many cases, the agent never opens the email or file that holds it. So each harmful session ends one of three ways:

In AgentHarm, the user sends the request, so the agent always reads it.

The five benchmarks are AgentDojo (NeurIPS 2024), InjecAgent (ACL 2024 Findings), Agent Security Bench (ASB, ICLR 2025), AgentDyn (2026) and AgentHarm (ICLR 2025). ASB plants the instruction in the agent's long-term memory. In all, Agent Anomaly Detection scored 1,774 sessions.

Agent Anomaly Detection flagged 87% of the harmful instructions that the agent carried out, and raised a few false alarms on ordinary office work. It's strongest on goal hijack and tool misuse, and weakest on poisoned memory.

Each finding carries a threat category, and four of Agent Anomaly Detection’s five categories align with the OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications. We graded each OWASP category on what this study showed, not on what Agent Anomaly Detection is designed to catch.

Public benchmarks concentrate on goal hijack and tool misuse, so our evidence is strongest there. We did not find public benchmarks with labeled agent traces for cascading failures or for identity and privilege abuse. Shared benchmarks for those categories would help the whole field.

By benchmark, Agent Anomaly Detection flagged 85% of the carried-out harmful instructions on AgentDojo, 87% on InjecAgent, 99% on AgentDyn and 81% on AgentHarm. Over all harmful sessions, including the ones that the agent never read or resisted, it flagged 45% to 62%. In the 141 sessions where the agent never read the instruction, nothing happened, and it flagged just 1.

Results held across the apps. In 8 of the 11 apps, Agent Anomaly Detection flagged at least 95% of the carried-out harmful instructions. The lowest rate was in AgentDojo's Slack app, at 63%. Many of those instructions ask for one small action, such as a page visit, which looks like normal browsing.

Agent Anomaly Detection also flags many requests that the agent refuses. In AgentHarm, the agent refused most requests and carried out 108 of 412, and Agent Anomaly Detection still flagged 55% of the refused sessions, because the request sits in the user's own message, which it reads. When the agent didn't follow an instruction hidden in tool output, it flagged only 11% to 25%, because the instruction sits deep inside a tool result.

False alarms were rare on ordinary office work: on the three injection benchmarks, whose benign sessions are office tasks, Agent Anomaly Detection flagged 2% to 4% of benign sessions. On AgentHarm it flagged 16%. Those benign tasks are twins of the harmful ones, so they post to social media, run terminal commands and download files. High-impact tools in normal use look more like misuse.

Agent Anomaly Detection did less well in five areas. It flagged only 11% to 25% of the instructions that the agent resisted, because a resisted instruction changes little in how the agent behaves. It missed more small actions, like single page visits, because they look like normal work. And it raised more false alarms for agents whose everyday work uses high-impact tools. If your agent is one of them, expect more findings at first, and triage them by severity and threat category.

The other two areas are new agents and poisoned memory. Some Agent Anomaly Detection methods need a few hundred sessions of history: on AgentDyn, it flagged 33% of carried-out harmful instructions when each agent had about 220 benign sessions, and 99% with 360. And it caught only 4 of the 18 sessions where poisoned memory made the agent act.

Protect your agents with defense in depth. Use controls that stop harmful actions before they run, and Agent Anomaly Detection to find what gets through.

We used one agent model and simulated apps, and the benchmarks' benign tasks are likely simpler than your production traffic, so your false-alarm rate can differ. Agent Anomaly Detection returned no result for about 6% of the sessions we sent; counting those as misses lowers the overall rates by 1 to 2 points.

Agent Anomaly Detection is in Private Preview. To request access, read the Agent Anomaly Detection overview.

#10259. From Script to Screen: A Developer's Workflow for Long-Form AI Video

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Generating a single AI video clip is easy now. You send a prompt and get a few seconds of footage back. The trouble starts when the goal is three, five, or ten minutes of video where the same character looks the same in every scene, the style does not drift, and the captions line up with the picture.

Most guides stop at the clip. This one covers the part after it, treating a video as a small build pipeline: a storyboard that is data, prompts generated from that data, clips normalised and stitched with ffmpeg, and captions derived from the same source. If you want to wire a generation model into your own application first, SitePoint's guide to integrating generative video APIs into web applications covers the request and webhook side. If the finished video is headed to a YouTube channel, how to get a YouTube API key and use the Data API is a good starting point for the publishing side. Everything between those two is below.

Long-form AI video fails at the seams between clips, not inside them. Plan for continuity before you generate anything.

A storyboard stored as JSON can be validated, versioned, diffed, and turned into prompts by code, which a pile of loose prompts cannot.

Repeat the full character description in every prompt. Models do not remember the previous clip.

Clips from different generations rarely share resolution, frame rate, or codec settings. Normalise them before joining.

Captions are cheapest when generated from the script and measured clip durations, not transcribed afterwards.

Current video models generate short clips, commonly a handful of seconds each. A longer video is therefore many clips, and every clip is an independent generation. The model has no memory of what the character wore in the previous one.

That produces three kinds of failure. The character drifts, so hair, clothing, or proportions change between scenes. The style drifts, so lighting and colour grade shift from cut to cut. And the technical specs drift, so one clip is 24 frames per second at one resolution and the next is something else. Each of these is fixable, but only if the project is organised so the fixes can be applied consistently.

Start with a structured storyboard instead of a document full of prompts. One file holds the style, a "character bible", and an ordered list of scenes.

"style": "soft watercolor picture book illustration, warm evening light, 16:9",

"mira": "a nine year old girl with short curly black hair, a yellow raincoat and red rubber boots",

"lantern": "a small round paper lantern with a gentle orange glow and a tiny smiling face"

"setting": "a narrow cobblestone street in light rain",

"action": "walks slowly past closed shops, looking up at the sky",

"camera": "slow push in from a medium shot",

"narration": "It had rained all afternoon, and the street was quiet."

"action": "finds the lantern glowing on a wooden crate and kneels beside it",

"narration": "Then she noticed something glowing under the awning."

Because it is data, a script can check it before you spend any generation credits. Two checks pay for themselves quickly: every character named in a scene must exist in the bible, and no scene may be longer than the clip limit of the model you use.

const known = new Set(Object.keys(board.characters));

errors.push${scene.id}: unknown character "${name}");

${scene.id}: ${scene.duration}s is over the ${MAX_CLIP_SECONDS}s clip limit, split it into shots

Treat MAX_CLIP_SECONDS as a setting. Limits differ between models and change over time, so check the one you are using rather than trusting the number in this example.

Never write the per-scene prompt by hand. Generate it, so the style line and the character descriptions are identical every time.

The character description appears word for word in every scene that includes that character. This is the single most effective consistency tactic that needs no special tooling. Changing a detail, say the colour of the boots, becomes one edit in the bible instead of a search through twenty prompts, and the diff shows exactly what changed between versions.

Put the style line first and keep it identical across all scenes.

Describe one action per clip. Two sequential actions in one prompt often produce a blend of both.

Keep camera directions simple. A single move per clip is more reliable than a combination.

Avoid naming real people, brands, or existing characters in prompts. Beyond the rights issue, it makes results harder to reproduce.

Clips from separate generations often disagree on resolution, frame rate, pixel format, or codec parameters. Joining them directly can produce stutters, green frames, or an outright error. Convert every clip to one agreed format first.

-vf "scale=1280:720:force_original_aspect_ratio=decrease,pad=1280:720:(ow-iw)/2:(oh-ih)/2,fps=24,format=yuv420p" \

-an -c:v libx264 -crf 18 "norm/$(basename "$f")"

The filter scales each clip to fit a 1280 by 720 frame, adds padding if the aspect ratio differs, sets 24 frames per second, and forces a widely compatible pixel format. The -an flag drops any audio the model generated, since narration will be added as one track later. Name clips with zero padded numbers such as s01.mp4 and s02.mp4, so a shell glob sorts them in story order.

Once every file shares the same parameters, the concat demuxer can join them without re-encoding:

for f in norm/*.mp4; do echo "file '$PWD/$f'"; done > list.txt

ffmpeg -y -f concat -safe 0 -i list.txt -c copy stitched.mp4

Hard cuts are the safe default. Crossfades are possible with ffmpeg's xfade filter, but they require careful offset arithmetic and a re-encode, so add them only when a cut genuinely looks wrong.

Captions are easiest when they come from the script, not from a speech recognition pass over the finished video. The storyboard already holds the narration text and each scene's length, so an SRT file is a few lines of code. Use measured durations rather than planned ones, because a generated clip is often a little shorter or longer than requested.

const { execFileSync } = require('node:child_process');

const ms = Math.round(totalSeconds * 1000);

const h = String(Math.floor(ms / 3600000)).padStart(2, '0');

const m = String(Math.floor((ms % 3600000) / 60000)).padStart(2, '0');

const s = String(Math.floor((ms % 60000) / 1000)).padStart(2, '0');

const rest = String(ms % 1000).padStart(3, '0');

const end = cursor + scene.duration; // set from measureSeconds() after generation

${blocks.length + 1}\n${toTimestamp(start)} --> ${toTimestamp(end)}\n${scene.narration}\n

Update each scene's duration from measureSeconds on the normalised clip before calling buildSrt. If a narration line is long, split it across two caption blocks so it stays readable. Then combine picture, voiceover, and captions in one final step:

ffmpeg -y -i stitched.mp4 -i narration.mp3 -i captions.srt \

-c:v copy -c:a aac -c:s mov_text -shortest final.mp4

Soft captions like these can be switched off by the viewer and read by assistive technology, which is better than burning text into the picture. Keep the .srt file as well, since most platforms accept it as a separate upload.

Everything above is a good fit when you need repeatability: many videos from templates, versioned storyboards, automated publishing, or tight control over the model. The price is that you own the glue code, the ffmpeg settings, and the failures.

For one off projects, or when the people making the video are not developers, a managed platform is often the more sensible choice. Tools such as magiclight.ai bundle story to video generation, character handling, voice, and an editor in one interface, and advertise videos of up to 50 minutes. Check the specifics yourself, because claims like that are marketing, and results depend on your content. One point matters for developers in particular: if you need to automate generation from your own code, confirm that the platform you pick offers an API or export route before you build a workflow around it. A tool with a good editor and no programmatic access suits a different job than the pipeline in this article.

A short manual pass catches what automation does not. Watch the whole video once at normal speed, looking only at continuity. Read the captions against the audio. Check that no real person's likeness, brand mark, or protected character slipped into the footage. Finally, check the disclosure rules of the platform you publish on, since many now ask creators to label realistic synthetic media, and the rules change.

The model is only one component of a long-form AI video. The reliability comes from the structure around it: a validated storyboard, prompts generated from it, clips forced into one format, and captions derived from measured data. Each of those is ordinary software engineering, and none of it depends on which generation model you choose, so the pipeline survives when the model changes.

Start with a two minute video and four or five scenes. Fix the seams there before scaling up, because every continuity problem you find at that size is one you will not have to hunt for in a ten minute project.

#10258. Granite 4.1 LLMs: How They’re Built

An in-depth technical walkthrough of data engineering, pre-training, supervised fine-tuning, and reinforcement learning behind the Granite 4.1 LLMs.

TL;DR — Granite 4.1 is a family of dense, decoder‑only LLMs (3B, 8B, and 30B) trained on ~15T tokens using a multi‑stage pre‑training pipeline, including long‑context extension of up to 512K tokens. The models are further refined with supervised fine‑tuning on ~4.1M high‑quality curated samples and reinforcement learning via on‑policy GRPO with DAPO loss (Yu et al., 2025). Notably, the 8B instruct model matches or surpasses the previous Granite 4.0‑H‑Small (32B‑A9B MoE) despite using a simpler dense architecture with fewer parameters. All Granite 4.1 models are released under the Apache 2.0 license.

Building high‑quality small language models goes beyond simply scaling compute—it requires rigorous data curation throughout training. For Granite 4.1, we prioritized data quality over quantity, progressively refining the data mixture across five pre‑training stages. We further curated supervised fine‑tuning data using an LLM‑as‑Judge framework and applied a multi‑stage reinforcement learning pipeline to systematically strengthen performance in math, coding, instruction following, and general chat.

Granite 4.1 models use a decoder-only dense transformer architecture. The core design choices include Grouped Query Attention (GQA), Rotary Position Embeddings (RoPE), SwiGLU activations, RMSNorm, and shared input/output embeddings.

All three model sizes share the same training pipeline and data strategy, differing only in architecture dimensions.

Granite 4.1 is trained from scratch on approximately 15 trillion tokens using a five‑phase training strategy. Phases 1–2 focus on foundational pre‑training, phases 3–4 perform mid‑training with progressively higher‑quality data annealing, and phase 5 introduces long‑context training, extending the context window to 512K tokens. Each phase employs a distinct data mixture and learning‑rate schedule, gradually shifting from broad web‑scale data to more curated, domain‑specific content.

Figure 2: The five-phase pre-training pipeline. Phases 1–2 are pre-training, Phases 3–4 are mid-training (high-quality data annealing), and Phase 5 is long context training (LCE).

The first phase establishes broad language understanding using a general mixture of training data with a power learning rate schedule and warmup.

Phase 2 sharply increases the proportion of code and mathematical data, pivoting toward stronger reasoning capabilities while still maintaining general language coverage.

Phase 3 transitions into mid-training with a more balanced, high-quality mixture and an exponential decay learning rate schedule. This is where we start blending in chain-of-thought and synthetic instruction data.

The fourth phase continues mid-training with a linear learning rate decay to zero, focusing the model on the highest-quality data available.

Figure 3: How the data mix evolves across the pre-training phases. Notice the progressive shift from web-heavy (Phase 1) to quality-heavy with instruction and reasoning data (Phases 3–4).

The fifth and final phase also part of of mid-training extends the context window from 4K to 512K through a staged long-context extension process:

The LCE phase uses an exponential learning rate schedule starting at 1e-4 and decaying to 0. To ensure the model natively handles long sequences without degrading short-context performance, we do a model merge after each LCE stage. RULER benchmark of base models:

Supervised fine‑tuning (SFT) is what turns the base model into a reliable instruction‑following assistant, making data quality critically important—since even a small number of incorrect or hallucinated samples can instill undesirable behaviors. To address this, we apply a rigorous LLM‑as‑Judge framework alongside rule‑based filtering to curate high-quality samples. Together, the pipeline automatically assess each sample against structural, semantic, and behavioral criteria, fixing issues when possible and filtering out samples that fail to meet our quality standards.

Figure 4: The SFT data quality pipeline. Raw conversation data passes through an LLM-as-Judge with a multi-dimensional rubric, producing accept/borderline/reject verdicts. Hard-reject defects (hallucination, false premise, incorrect computation) trigger automatic rejection regardless of score.

Our rigorous LLM‑as‑Judge framework evaluates only assistant responses, treating system prompts, user inputs, retrieved documents, and tool outputs strictly as contextual information. This ensures that the judge assesses what the model says, rather than what it was asked to do. In RAG settings, responses that are not grounded in the retrieved context are flagged as hallucinations, while tool‑use outputs are validated against the set of allowed tools and their parameter schemas.

We employ specialized judge prompts tailored to different SFT data types, including multi‑turn dialogue, RAG‑augmented responses, tool‑calling interactions, and multilingual conversations. Each response is scored across six weighted dimensions—instruction following, correctness, completeness, conciseness, naturalness, and calibration (with optional critical‑thinking checks). Samples are accepted, flagged as borderline, or rejected based on deterministic score thresholds, with hard‑reject rules overriding scores for severe defects such as hallucinations, false premises, or incorrect computations.

To complement semantic evaluation, we apply a deterministic rule‑based pipeline that enforces structural integrity through text normalization, truncation and length filtering, schema validation, and leakage detection. A final global deduplication step ensures dataset‑wide uniqueness. All filtering and correction actions are fully auditable.

After passing through the LLM-as-Judge, rule-based filtering, and global deduplication pipeline, we fine-tune base models on these approximately 4.1 million high-quality samples. The following details apply to all three model variants:

After SFT, we apply a multi-stage reinforcement learning pipeline to further improve the model's capabilities across specific domains. Rather than a single RL pass, we run multiple targeted RL stages, each optimizing for different capabilities.

We use On-policy GRPO (Group Relative Policy Optimization) (Shao et al., 2024) with DAPO (Decoupled Clip and Dynamic sAmpling Policy Optimization) loss (Yu et al., 2025) which provides more stable training signals compared to standard GRPO. However, due to computationally intensive nature of dynamic sampling, we switch it off during our training runs.

Figure 10 depicts our Reinforcement Learning pipeline for training Granite 4.1 models. Through extensive experimentation with a variety of reinforcement learning recipes, we found that this sequence of steps minimizes catastrophic forgetting while simultaneously maximizing performance across multiple domains.

Figure 10: The Granite 4.1 reinforcement learning pipeline consisting of four sequential stages: Multi-domain RL, RLHF, Identity and Knowledge-calibration RL, and Math RL.

In this stage, the model is trained jointly on a unified mixture of data drawn from multiple domains. Every gradient update therefore reflects the full diversity of tasks, which prevents catastrophic forgetting, boosts overall benchmark performance, and minimizes regressions on any individual task.

The different domains covered in this stage include:

During this stage, we trained the models on 45,504 unique prompts (averaged across all Granite 4.1 models) and found that a learning rate of 5e‑7 with a KL‑loss coefficient ($\beta$) of 0.05 performed best for multi‑domain reinforcement learning.

To further improve the model's helpfulness and chat ability, we train our model on generic-chat prompts using a multilingual scalar reward model. With this stage, we observed an average improvement of ~18.9 points (averaged across the three Granite 4.1 models) in Alpaca-Eval compared to the SFT checkpoints.

To mitigate policy drift from its previously learned knowledge, we use a conservative learning rate of 3e-7 and higher KL-loss coeff $\beta$ of 0.09 in this stage. We use an average of 17,920 unique prompts in this RLHF stage.

In this stage, we train the model for a few steps (~40 training steps) on identity and knowledge calibration prompts. We observed that this small training stage significantly improves the model's self-identification capabilities.

Similar to the RLHF stage, we used a learning rate of 3e-7 and KL-loss coeff $\beta$ of 0.09, and we use 1728 unique prompts in this stage.

During our RL training, we found that the RLHF stage causes a drop in math benchmark scores (e.g., in GSM8K, DeepMind-Math). The Math RL stage enables the model to recover from this drop and surpasses the original SFT performance on math benchmarks: ~3.8 points on average for GSM8K, and ~23.48 points on average for DeepMind-Math. We use an average of 13,504 unique prompts in this stage and similar to the multi-domain RL stage, we used a learning rate of 5e-7 and KL-loss coeff $\beta$ of 0.05.

Supported languages: English, German, Spanish, French, Japanese, Portuguese, Arabic, Czech, Italian, Korean, Dutch, and Chinese.

Granite 4.1 delivers competitive instruction‑following and tool‑calling capabilities without relying on long chains of thought. By avoiding extended reasoning traces, it provides predictable latency, stable token usage, and lower operational cost. This makes Granite 4.1 a production‑ready, open‑source choice for enterprise workloads where efficiency, reliability, and cost control are critical.

A striking result: the Granite 4.1-8B dense model consistently matches or outperforms the previous-generation Granite 4.0-H-Small, a 32B-parameter Mixture-of-Experts model with 9B active parameters.

Figure 13: Granite 4.1-8B (dark blue) vs. Granite 4.0-H-Small 32B-A9B (light blue) across benchmarks. The 8B dense model matches or exceeds the larger MoE model on IFEval, AlpacaEval, MMLU-Pro, BBH, GSM8K, DeepMind-Math, Evalplus, ArenaHard, BFCL V3 and MBPP(+).

Figure 14: Comparison across the Granite 4.1 family — 30B, 8B, and 3B models. Scores scale predictably with model size, with the 30B model leading across all benchmarks.

We also released fp8 quantized variants of the Granite 4.1 models, optimized for inference with vLLM. The precision is reduced from 16‑bit to 8‑bit, resulting in approximately a 50% reduction in both disk footprint and GPU memory usage. Quantization is applied only to the weights and activations of linear operators within the transformer blocks using LLM Compressor, while all other layers are preserved at their original precision.

We trained the Granite 4.1 Language Models on an NVIDIA GB200 NVL72 cluster hosted on CoreWeave:

This infrastructure provides the scalable, high-bandwidth interconnect needed for efficient distributed training at the token volumes required (15T+ tokens across pre-training alone).

Granite 4.1 models are available under the Apache 2.0 license. Here's how to get started with the 30B instruct model wiht tool calling example:

Granite 4.1 marks a significant step forward for high‑quality, open‑source language models. By prioritizing data quality and rigor at every stage—from pre‑training curation to supervised fine‑tuning and multi‑stage reinforcement learning—we deliver a substantially improved post‑training pipeline. The result is stronger instruction following, tool use, and conversational performance, showing that carefully trained dense 8B models can rival much larger MoE architectures. We’re excited to see how the community adopts and builds on these models.

#10255. Adding Benchmaxxer Repellant to the Open ASR Leaderboard

"When a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure." (Goodhart’s Law)

TLDR: Appen Inc. and DataoceanAI have provided high-quality English ASR datasets covering scripted and conversational speech over multiple accents. To prevent potential risks of benchmaxxing or test-set contamination, we will keep these datasets private for a high-quality measure of performance on multiple tasks.

We’re not updating the average WER at this time: by default, the leaderboard’s Average WER remains computed on public datasets only. You can optionally include the private datasets using the toggle to see their impact 👀

Since its launch in September 2023, the Open ASR Leaderboard has been visited over 710K times. We’re blown away by the community’s interest and motivation to keep pushing speech recognition 🗣️

Two words sum up the objectives (but also challenges) in maintaining a benchmark like the Open ASR Leaderboard:

Standardization: models can have different conventions for their usage and outputs, e.g. with/without punctuation and casing. Datasets have the same challenges and can be structured differently. To this end, all test sets have been gathered into a single dataset on the Hub for easy access and previewing. Moreover, to standardize model outputs and dataset transcripts, we use a normalizer that (among other things) removes punctuation and casing, and maps to American spelling. It is based on the normalizer of Whisper.

Openness: the UI code and evaluation scripts are open-sourced. This has helped not only to incorporate new models, but also to improve the quality of the evaluation procedure through community feedback and contributions.

Standardization and openness are essential for meaningful benchmarking, but they also make benchmarks more susceptible to benchmark-specific optimization ("benchmaxxing"), where models improve leaderboard performance without corresponding gains in real-world robustness. As models and use cases evolve, the Open ASR Leaderboard will continue incorporating high-quality datasets and new evaluation settings to better reflect real-world performance and improve robustness against benchmark-specific optimization.

As discussed in our report, there is no single "catch-all" ASR model: some perform better on American English, others on diverse accents and multilingual settings, while others are optimized for speed or conversational audio. Different applications also prioritize different capabilities, so a model that performs less well on one dimension is not necessarily a worse model overall. The goal of the Open ASR Leaderboard is to capture these nuances and provide a more holistic view of ASR performance.

To this end, we have worked with Appen Inc. and DataoceanAI to curate high-quality datasets for ASR benchmarking. Below is some information on the various splits.

Below are sample audio showing the variety of content (scripted, conversational, acronyms, disfluencies, proper nouns).

While private datasets may sound contrary to the spirit of openness, we believe that incorporating such datasets will increase the trustworthiness of the Open ASR Leaderboard, as they are less likely to be exploited for benchmaxxing, whether by model developers who explicitly use the public test sets or who try to find training data that closely resembles a particular dataset to boost their score in the macroaverage.

With these datasets, we can also provide targeted metrics to highlight gaps and biases between controlled and often saturated settings (scripted, American accent) and more nuanced conditions (conversational and non-American accents). Below is a screenshot of the new "Private data" tab.

We intentionally do not provide a score on each split, to avoid model developers from boosting their score with a specific data provider or accent.

Get your model on the Open ASR Leaderboard, and we'll run the evaluation! As before, the process for adding a model to the leaderboard takes place on the Open ASR Leaderboard GitHub:

While you wait for your model to be added to the Open ASR Leaderboard, you can self-report your metrics on the public sets by adding a YAML file like this to your model card. Your model will then appear on an (unverified) leaderboard that appears on the dataset page (see screenshot below). More on this approach to decentralized evaluation can be read here.

They could. We’ve asked Appen and DataoceanAI to not provide this data to their clients. But even if they do not provide this exact data, data from a similar distribution could still help the model on the corresponding evaluation set (similar to benchmaxxing by optimizing for a challenging task from the public sets). To this end, having multiple data providers balances out the advantage a model may get from having used data from one of the providers. And we are open to more data providers and eval sets for the "Private data" tab!

Moreover, to ensure that the private sets do not affect the model ranking, we’ve defaulted the Average WER to not include the Private sets in its macroaverage.

In the screenshot below, you can see that "Private data" is toggled off. This means that the macroaverage across datasets does not include it.

Simply toggle on "Private data" splits to include them in the macroaverage.

The "Rank Δ" column shows how the ordering changes relative to the default macroaverage configuration. Including or excluding public datasets also changes the macroaverage, allowing users to tailor the evaluation to the use cases and data distributions most relevant to their application.

We’re excited to hear the community’s feedback on how the new track and dataset toggling features help users identify the model(s) that best fit their application(s). We’re also looking into evaluations that better reflect real-world noisy conditions, and you can expect some news on that 😉

While preparing the private evaluation sets, we took extra care to ensure consistent audio and transcript quality across datasets, including developing tooling to identify challenging cases such as low signal-to-noise conditions or transcript mismatches, since these factors can meaningfully affect WER. More on that in a future post!

Explore ASR model performance across languages

Just a quick observation on how we evaluate our models: The two data vendors mentioned earlier are offering datasets directly to ASR service providers for training. With that in mind, it feels like we should be extra prudent about mixing private data into our evaluations.

At the same time, we're missing out on a lot of high-quality, open-source speech datasets simply because their creators don't have sales teams advocating for them. It would be a huge step forward to open a channel where the research community can recommend these datasets to the leaderboard directly.

P.S. I found myself relating a lot to King George in the movie Hoppers recently. That beaver king just believes the best about everyone. I want to bring that same optimism here—hoping that everyone continues to follow the leaderboard rules, avoids training on open-source test sets, and actively cleans their training data of any contamination.

The two data vendors mentioned earlier are offering datasets directly to ASR service providers for training. With that in mind, it feels like we should be extra prudent about mixing private data into our evaluations.

Completely agree, that is why we don't include these new datasets in the default average WER computation. We hope that users have this nuanced view of the data sources. But also on the types of content, which is why we added splits on scripted/conversational and American/non-American accents.

It would be a huge step forward to open a channel where the research community can recommend these datasets to the leaderboard directly.
