#10218. Shipping a Trillion Parameters With a Hub Bucket: Delta Weight Sync in TRL

TL;DR, because you have models to train and we respect that:

Async RL just got a lot cheaper. Read on.

If you read our previous post on the landscape of async RL training, you already know the punchline. Every async RL library, regardless of how it spells "actor model" or which color its NCCL backend is painted, eventually trips over the same root: weight synchronization.

The inference engine speaks the policy of step N. The trainer just finished step N+1. The fresh weights have to get from one side to the other before the inference engine starts drifting hopelessly off-policy. This sits on the critical path whether you are running sync or async: a blocking transfer is wasted idle compute of GPUs not generating tokens. With a sparse delta path you collapse that idle time into seconds, and the trainer does not even have to wait for the inference engine to be ready: it just publishes "weights ready" and uploads the weights to the shared bucket the moment its optimizer step finishes, while the inference engine fetches on its own time.

Fireworks put a very memorable number on this in their post Frontier RL Is Cheaper Than You Think: for a frontier 1T-parameter checkpoint at fp8 (their setting), a full snapshot is 1024 GiB, and that is what conventional wisdom says you have to ship every time you update your rollout fleet. That is the kind of number that gets people to start drawing diagrams with mega-clusters, RDMA fabrics, and dedicated cross-region links. Their measured average delta between adjacent checkpoints lands at 20.3 GiB, or 1.98% of the full model, and "more than 98% of weights in bf16 format remain bit-equivalent between consecutive checkpoints".

Cursor's Composer 2 report tells a parallel story. They run training and inference in different regions and stitch them together with a shared S3 bucket (their exact words), into which the trainer uploads compressed weight diffs every training step. Each cluster independently downloads and reconstructs from the shared delta chain, "requiring no direct connectivity to the training cluster". The two sides never speak to each other about parameters directly. The bucket is the wire.

Both papers agree on three things, and we want to repeat them slowly, because the rest of this post is essentially a faithful open source translation:

The only thing missing was a version of this story that you can pip install. So we wrote one.

Before we wire anything up, it is worth understanding why this whole game is even winnable. The "98% of weights do not change" claim sounds suspiciously like one of those numbers that works in the demo and falls apart in the wild. It is not. It falls out of how bf16 arithmetic works at the learning rates RL uses.

A bf16 number has 7 mantissa bits. Between two consecutive powers of two, there are exactly 27=1282^7 = 12827=128 representable values, so the spacing between adjacent bf16 numbers around ∣w∣|w|∣w∣ is roughly ∣w∣⋅2−7|w| \cdot 2^{-7}∣w∣⋅2−7. An update gets absorbed by the bf16 cast whenever it sits below half of that spacing, i.e., when ∣Δw∣<∣w∣/256|\Delta w| < |w|/256∣Δw∣<∣w∣/256. This is the "bf16 visibility threshold" PULSE plots in their Figure 3.

Now look at what Adam does. At an RL learning rate of, say, 3×10−63 \times 10^{-6}3×10−6, the update to a single weight is: Δw=−η⋅m^v^+ϵ\Delta w = -\eta \cdot \frac{\hat{m}}{\sqrt{\hat{v}} + \epsilon}Δw=−η⋅v^​+ϵm^​

The normalized step m^/(v^+ϵ)\hat{m}/(\sqrt{\hat{v}}+\epsilon)m^/(v^​+ϵ) is roughly order one, so ∣Δw∣≈η≈3×10−6|\Delta w| \approx \eta \approx 3 \times 10^{-6}∣Δw∣≈η≈3×10−6. For most weights, ∣w∣|w|∣w∣ sits somewhere around 10−210^{-2}10−2 to 10−110^{-1}10−1 (PULSE reports a median of 0.019 for representative LLM weights). The threshold ∣w∣/256|w|/256∣w∣/256 at that magnitude is around 4×10−54 \times 10^{-5}4×10−5 to 4×10−44 \times 10^{-4}4×10−4, which is bigger than the update.

In other words: the optimizer is whispering, and bf16 cannot hear it. The update gets absorbed by rounding, the byte representation of www does not change, and from the inference engine's perspective, this weight did not move. Multiply that by a few hundred million parameters, and you get the >99% sparsity number, for free, with zero approximation.

This is exactly the argument made formal in the PULSE paper (Mihai & Belilovsky, 2026). They define two thresholds. The absorption bound 10η10\eta10η is the conservative worst case for an Adam update, and the effective bound η\etaη is the regime you actually live in. The bf16 visibility threshold is ∣w∣/256|w|/256∣w∣/256. Whenever the update sits below the visibility threshold, it gets absorbed, and the bf16 byte does not change. Their Figure 3 plots both bounds against a cloud of representative LLM weights, and the conclusion is unambiguous: at η=3×10−6\eta = 3 \times 10^{-6}η=3×10−6, the absorption bound itself already sits below the visibility threshold for almost every weight in the model. They measure this empirically across Qwen2.5 (0.5B/1.5B/7B), Llama-3.2-3B, and Gemma-3-4B, and consistently find a mean per-step sparsity of ~99%, with a standard deviation of 0.2 to 0.4% over 400 training steps. The worst-case step stays above 98%. So <1% changed is not a lucky measurement; it is what the arithmetic guarantees.

We do not have to predict this analytically (and indeed, we tried predicting the change mask from Adam's mmm and vvv statistics, but recall was a sad 30%, more on that later). We just need to observe which bytes flipped. That is a tiny boolean tensor per parameter, computed right around the optimizer step.

Here is where the second piece of the story comes in, and where this post stops being a translation of Fireworks/Cursor and starts being a Hugging Face thing.

A Bucket is a repo type on the Hub designed for high-frequency object storage. No commit ceremony, no PR workflow, no LFS quirks. You add files, you list files, you download files. The Python interface is two functions:

That is it. Two function calls and your weights are in flight.

Under the hood, buckets are backed by Xet, the Hub's content-defined chunking storage layer. Xet looks at every file you upload, slices it into chunks based on its actual content (not fixed offsets), and deduplicates against everything already in the bucket. The practical upshot, which is delightful in this context, is that even if we were too lazy to write the sparse encoding and just uploaded full anchors every step, Xet would still only transfer the changed chunks. Sparse encoding + Xet stack: we pay for what moved, and we pay for it once.

This is the open source equivalent of the "shared S3 bucket" both Fireworks and Cursor reach for, except the storage layer already knows about content hashing, your existing HF token already has permission, and it composes natively with the rest of the stack (Spaces, datasets, models).

The full architecture has exactly three boxes and one shared substrate:

The property to internalize, the one Cursor's paper sells hard and that holds verbatim here: the trainer and the rollout server never talk to each other about weights. They exchange a tiny POST containing {"repo_id": ..., "filename": ...}, and that is the entire control plane. The actual byte transfer happens between each side and the bucket, in parallel, with no shared network fabric.

The trainer writes. Replicas read. The Hub does the plumbing.

Now we can open the hood. The protocol has four parts: a wire format, a bucket layout, a 30 line vLLM extension, and a trainer side change detector. It is honestly less code than it sounds.

We picked safetensors for the on-disk and on-wire format. It is already the canonical checkpoint format on the Hub, every reasonable framework can read it, and the header carries arbitrary string metadata. That metadata field is where we hide the protocol.

There are two kinds of files in the bucket.

Anchors look like a normal checkpoint: one tensor per parameter, full bf16 weights, written every NNN syncs (we default to N=10N=10N=10).

Deltas are the interesting bit. For each parameter that actually changed, we store two entries: a flat int32 tensor of element indices, and a bf16 tensor of values at those indices.

The cadence is straightforward: anchor every Nth step, delta in between. Both end up in the same bucket under anchors/ and deltas/ prefixes. Each new inference replica only needs to grab the most recent anchor and then replay the deltas since.

The trainer needs to know which bf16 elements actually flipped. We do this with a tiny BF16ChangeDetector that registers a pre-step and post-step hook on the optimizer:

The actual code in the PR has a bit more plumbing (matching optimizer param objects to model params via data_ptr(), because Accelerate wraps them as different Python objects), but the idea fits on a napkin: snapshot, step, diff.

This is ground truth. We tried the more elegant path of predicting the mask from Adam's mmm and vvv statistics, using the bf16 ULP threshold directly. It works in principle. In practice, recall was around 30%, which means we would have shipped a delta missing two thirds of the actual updates. Adam's normalization is messy enough that the analytical threshold is not tight. So we just compare bytes. It costs one bf16 CPU snapshot of the model on the trainer side, which we are willing to pay.

The four phases of the new _sync_weight flow are:

The line that matters is the parenthesis. Inference was paused for 1.1 seconds. The remaining 9.4 seconds were spent uploading, which occurred while the rollout server was still generating tokens. With NCCL, we were paying the full sync time as pause time. Here we are paying for it as background time.

vLLM has a clean abstraction for this called WeightTransferEngine. We implement a DeltaWeightTransferEngine whose receive_weights method is, in spirit:

We register it via vLLM's --worker-extension-cls flag, which means no fork of vLLM is required. You install TRL into the same image as vLLM, point the CLI at our class, and you are done.

Worth mentioning: vLLM itself has an in-flight effort to land sparse weight transfer natively, vllm-project/vllm#40096. It adds receive_sparse_weights() and trainer_send_sparse_weights() directly on the WeightTransferEngine base class, with patches encoded as (indices, values) and applied in place via index_copy_(), removing the GPU/CPU validation roundtrip entirely. The PR reports a transfer of 0.16 MB in 0.40 ms for a sparse patch on Qwen3-1.7B versus 942 MB in 192 ms for a full dense send.

One honest caveat in our implementation on the inference side: we keep a CPU bf16 snapshot of the model so we can reconstruct full tensors from sparse (indices, values) patches, because load_weights in vLLM today expects full tensors. Once #40096 (or its successor) lands and exposes an in-place sparse load_weights path, we can apply the indices directly on the GPU and drop the snapshot!

This is the part we are smug about. Everything we have described so far works on your laptop, but the point of routing weights through a Hub bucket is that the trainer and the rollout server do not have to live anywhere near each other. So we ran a fully disaggregated training with three machines, none of which share a network:

Setting this up is genuinely a few hf CLI calls. The vLLM Space's Dockerfile is essentially the upstream vLLM image plus pip install trl@... plus the entrypoint:

And kick off training from anywhere on the planet that can talk HTTPS:

The trainer never opens a port. The Space never sees the trainer's IP. The Wordle environment does not know either of them exists. They all talk to the Hub. Training converged on the immediate-EOS sanity check, then on real Wordle rollouts: reward went up, delta payloads stayed in the 20 to 35 MB band, and the inference-paused window per sync stayed around a second. The full run logs are linked in the companion PR.

Async RL training without a cluster. If you have one GPU and a Hugging Face account, you can now do real disaggregated training. Your trainer is on the GPU; your rollout fleet lives in Spaces; your environment lives in another Space; weights move through a bucket. This used to require either a colocated setup (with all the throughput compromises that brings) or a real cluster with shared networking. It does not anymore.

Multi-replica inference, for free. Stand up two vLLM Spaces, or ten. They all pull from the same bucket. Xet content-addresses storage so consecutive anchors share chunks at rest (which keeps your bucket from blowing up), and the Hub's edge cache makes repeated downloads of the same file cheap to serve. Want a globally distributed rollout fleet? That is now a small DevOps exercise, not a research project.

A wire format you can debug with your existing tools. A delta is a safetensors file. You can safe_open it from a notebook, list its keys, inspect the indices, compute the sparsity yourself. We have spent enough hours in tcpdump on opaque NCCL streams to appreciate this.

A path to frontier scale. The 20 to 35 MB number is for Qwen3-0.6B. The interesting question is what the curve looks like once you turn the dial up. Let us do the napkin math.

Take Llama-3.1-405B. In bf16 that is 810 GB on disk. PULSE measures ~99% mean per-step sparsity at RL learning rates, so the actual delta sits around 1% of the parameters. Their deployment-measured encoding hits 108 MB on a 7B model, which is the ~130× reduction PULSE reports. Scaled linearly to 405B, the delta lands at roughly 6 GB per step.

What does that buy you in wall-clock? NCCL is fast inside a cluster, sure. Assume a generous 100 GB/s aggregate broadcast bandwidth (multi-node, RDMA, the works). A full sync is 810 GB / 100 GB/s ≈ 8 seconds of inference pause, every step. With the delta path, the trainer streams 6 GB to a bucket in the background while generation keeps running, and the rollout server's actual paused window is just the apply step, which on this scale lands at a couple of seconds. So even before we leave the cluster, delta cuts the visible pause by 4× and the bytes on the wire by ~130×.

Now leave the cluster. NCCL straight up does not work across clouds. Once you want a rollout fleet in us-east, another in eu-west, maybe one in a Hugging Face Space, the bucket-based path is the only path. At 1 GB/s of usable internet bandwidth, a single full broadcast would take 13 minutes; the delta does it in 6 seconds.

For a 1 TB-class model in the Fireworks framing, their own measured numbers show 20.3 GiB deltas vs the 1024 GiB full snapshot, a ~50× reduction. PULSE's tighter, sparse encoding would push that further (extrapolating ~15 GB per delta, closer to ~65×). Either way, you are in a regime where shipping weights through commodity object storage stops being a hack and starts being the only sensible architecture.

We are not pretending this is finished. Here is the honest list.

Product teams keep asking engineers for the same feature: “Can users fix the reaction in this clip without reshooting it?” It lands on the backlog as “add expression editing,” and it hides a lot of decisions.

This guide compares the realistic integration options in 2026, sketches a pipeline architecture, models costs, includes a small runnable job helper, and covers the consent and audit logging you need before changing a real person’s face. Vendor details change quickly, so check each vendor’s documentation before you build against it.

Information about features, pricing, APIs and policies in this article was checked on November 10, 2026 and may change. Check each vendor’s documentation before you build against it.

Performance transfer is great for animation, but someone has to record a new take for every change. If your promise is “fix the reaction in the footage you already have,” direct editing fits better.

DRAMA is an AI facial changer from SyncMonster. In the web app, users upload a video or image (MP4, MOV, JPG, PNG), pick a face, choose an emotion, and set intensity on a slider from subtle to strong. The app offers four core emotions (Happy, Sad, Angry, Excited) plus presets such as Surprised, Serious, Evil and Intimidating, with the extra presets on paid plans. It supports emotion blending and editing one face in a group shot without touching the others. SyncMonster states that edits keep the original resolution, lighting and details such as glasses and beards, which is a vendor claim you should test on your own footage.

For developers, SyncMonster publishes public API documentation for DRAMA. Here is what those docs state, as checked on November 10, 2026:

A few things to note honestly. The same generate endpoint also serves other SyncMonster features behind their own flags, so read the parameter table carefully. In the version we checked, the parameter table marks an audio input as required on generate, and the drama-only example includes one, so plan for that in your request builder. The emotion values exposed in the API are the four core emotions, and the extra app presets did not appear in the API docs. The docs describe polling only, with no webhooks mentioned, and they do not publish rate limits, an SDK, or a numeric maximum video duration (an error code exists for exceeding a duration limit).

Runway exposes Act-Two through its developer API as the character_performance endpoint. You send a character (image or video) and a driving performance video, and Act-Two transfers facial expression, and optionally body and hand motion, onto the character. Output is 24fps.

Runway’s API pricing guide lists Act-Two at 5 credits per second of output, with credits priced at $0.01 each, so $0.05 per second. Earlier documentation mentioned a 15-credit minimum per generation, and the current pricing page does not list one, so check for minimums before you budget short clips. The documentation also exposes an expression intensity setting to control how strongly the performance is applied.

The catch is the input requirement: every edit needs someone to act the new reaction. That suits character animation, but it is a heavy ask for a user who wants a slightly warmer smile in an interview clip. It also drives one character per generation.

LivePortrait is an open-source portrait animation framework from Kuaishou’s KwaiVGI group. It animates a source image or video using a driving video or a saved motion template, supports video-to-video portrait editing, and offers retargeting controls for eyes and lips.

The README sets up a Python 3.10 conda environment and expects Git and FFmpeg, with an NVIDIA GPU recommended. It also notes that Apple Silicon runs roughly 20x slower than an RTX 4090, and that Humans mode needs PYTORCH_ENABLE_MPS_FALLBACK=1 on a Mac. That matters if you were hoping to prototype on a MacBook and ship the same setup. A basic run adapted from the README looks like this:

Here -s is the source portrait (an image or video) and -d is the driving clip. Retargeting is exposed through additional options and the Gradio interface, so check the README for current names because they change between releases. Also read the repository’s license file before you plan any commercial use.

The Hugging Face Spaces demo is handy for experiments, but production means owning GPU provisioning, queueing, model updates and quality review. You still steer with a driving input rather than a “happier by 30%” control.

Rule of thumb: if expression editing is a feature rather than your product, buy. If you need on-prem processing or model-level changes, build on LivePortrait and budget for ops.

Whatever the backend, the pipeline has five stages.

Here is the shape of the worker loop. This is illustrative pseudocode only, not any vendor’s SDK or real endpoints:

The idempotency and backoff tips below are easy to get wrong, so here is a small vendor-neutral module. The key function hashes the input file together with the parameters, so a retry with the same input maps to the same job. The poller backs off exponentially up to a ceiling and gives up after a maximum wait. It uses only the Python standard library.

A short test confirms the behavior: the same input gives the same key regardless of parameter order, different parameters give a different key, and the poller returns once the state becomes done.

Credits are not a shared currency across vendors, so compare units first and money second.

For prototyping, the DRAMA web app has a free plan (60 credits, 1080p, up to 2 minutes of processing, 2 projects, watermarked output), which is enough to judge quality on your own sample footage before writing integration code. The docs we checked list API billing in credits but do not state a dollar price per API credit, so confirm that with SyncMonster before you finalize a pricing model. Do not assume web-app plan credits convert at the same rate as API credits.

Plan details are as listed by the vendor on November 10, 2026 and can change.

Changing a real person’s expression can change what viewers believe they felt, so treat this as a product requirement.

For a product feature that edits reactions in existing footage, the DRAMA API is the most direct hosted option among those compared here: face detection with thumbnails for selection, per-face edits, and emotion values you set in code, with no driving performance. Go in knowing its current limits: four emotion parameters in the API, polling instead of webhooks, and no published rate limits or SDK. Starting with the free plan on your own clips is a low-risk way to judge quality. Product details and API access for this AI expression changer are on SyncMonster’s site.

Choose the Runway API if your users want to animate characters from an acted performance. Choose LivePortrait if you need on-prem processing or model-level control and have the GPU and ops capacity. Leave Flawless DeepEditor to studio editorial teams, and Photoshop to still-image workflows.

Yes. DRAMA by SyncMonster has a hosted REST API for editing expressions in existing video using emotion values, and Runway offers Act-Two through its API for performance transfer. LivePortrait is open source and can be wrapped in your own service.

Yes, with a direct editing tool. The DRAMA API takes emotion values from 0 to 1 for happy, sad, excited and angry on a selected face. Runway Act-Two and LivePortrait both expect a driving performance or motion template.

Run face detection first, let the user pick a face, then send that face’s ID with the edit request. The DRAMA API returns a face ID and a thumbnail for each detected face for this purpose.

Per vendor docs as of November 10, 2026: the DRAMA API bills 0.5 credit per second for face detection and 1 credit per second for drama generation, while Runway’s Act-Two API bills 5 credits per second at $0.01 per credit. LivePortrait costs whatever your GPU time costs.

Yes, but its README notes Apple Silicon can be about 20x slower than an RTX 4090. An NVIDIA GPU is recommended for anything beyond experiments.

Not a public one. DeepEditor is an Avid Media Composer extension with access by application, aimed at film and TV editorial teams.

Log the requester, consent record, selected face, emotion and intensity, backend used, input and output hashes, credits used, and a timestamp, and keep the original file.

#10214. Agents are sessions, not requests: size GKE node pools for AI agent sessions

Sorry, your browser doesn't support playback for this video

Your company wants to move its coding agents from developer laptops to a shared GKE cluster, for persistence, scale, and governance. Each of those agent sessions stays open all day but works only part of it, and how you run them decides how much of your node bill pays for waiting.

By the end of this article, you will know why an agent session needs a different runtime than a web request, how Agent Substrate and AX run sessions on GKE, and how to identify cost optimization opportunities in your GKE node pools. This article assumes you know Kubernetes Pods and node pools. If not, check out the GKE overview.

A web request lasts milliseconds. The server answers it, keeps nothing, and serves the next one, so Kubernetes scales a web app by its traffic: more requests, more Pods.

An agent session works another way. A coding agent's workspace can stay open for the developer's whole workday: it keeps its memory and its files between prompts, and it works only after a prompt arrives.

How much of that day does the agent really work? Much less than it waits. In a July 2026 study of agent traces, Banruo Liu and colleagues found that in a typical session with several prompts, the agent waits for the user about 80% of the time. A turn, one prompt and the agent's whole response to it, takes about 6.5 minutes of agent work on average

Put those numbers on one developer's day. With 2 prompts an hour over an 8 hour workday, which is our assumption, the agent works 22% of the day and waits for nearly 78% of it. If each session holds a machine, you pay for that waiting time

Teams usually pick one of two answers, and both work well for web apps.

The first is to give each session its own Pod. The session keeps its state, but its Pod holds 1 vCPU and 1 GiB all day. For example, a c3-standard-4 node fits 3 such Pods after GKE's reservations, so in our cost model 100 coding agents need 34 nodes and about USD 1,288 a month, for agents that work 22% of the time.

The second is to scale the Pod to zero between prompts. The node's capacity is released, and files on a persistent volume survive, but the process and its memory do not, so the next prompt starts a new agent process.

Based on that, you want a third option: keep the session, and free the machine while the session waits.

Agent Substrate and AX are built for that: the developer's session stays open, and the sandbox that serves it gives its machine back while the session waits. Together they cover the parts of an agentic platform that are the same for most teams: the control plane, the runtime, and the sandbox. Agent Substrate answers where and how an agent runs. AX answers what the agent is.

Following the CNCF donation of gVisor, Agent Substrate, and OpenRL in November 2026, you can run Agent Substrate on GKE or on other Kubernetes clusters. Agent Substrate 1.0 is generally available on GKE.

One distinction helps from here on. The session is the multi turn interaction between the developer and the agent, with its conversation history. The compute that serves it is an isolated sandbox: an actor in Agent Substrate, or a Task in AX. Parking acts on the sandbox, and the session stays open.

Agent Substrate answers where and how an agent runs. It separates the stateful agent from the compute it runs on. An actor is the sandbox for one agent, and it holds the agent's running processes, files, and identity. A worker is a reusable sandbox drawn from a warm pool of Kubernetes Pods, and one worker hosts several actors.

An agent runs code that a model wrote, so anything in its environment can leak through a prompt injection or a bad command, API keys included. Gateways control the actor's inbound and outbound traffic and add credentials on the way out, based on the actor's identity, so credentials stay out of the agent's environment.

SuspendActor snapshots an idle actor to object storage and frees its worker, and the next request restores the actor on a warm worker with room for it. Agent Substrate snapshots memory by default and falls back to files when it cannot capture memory. Many parked sessions share a small warm pool, so in our cost model the same 100 agents need 16 nodes instead of 34.

AX answers what the agent is and what it knows. You declare a Task, which says what runs (image, command, and limits), and a Workspace, which says what the agent knows (repositories and files). AX runs each Task as an actor. ax suspend parks the task and keeps its /workspace. Today AX asks for a volume snapshot, so the files come back on resume and the agent's processes start fresh (runner guide).

AX passes suspend, resume, and delete to Agent Substrate. The AX roadmap plans to add budgets, policies, and gateways, which limit what an agent may do, and a record of what each task did.

Two details decide the bill before you size anything.

First, you decide when a sandbox parks. Agent Substrate does not suspend an idle actor by itself (#424), so your agent harness, or the service in front of it, calls the suspend API after an idle timeout. Until then, an idle actor keeps its worker. When idle actors hold every worker, a request for another actor waits up to 5 seconds by default, then fails with HTTP 503 (Agent Substrate docs).

Second, you decide how much CPU each sandbox is promised. An actor is sized by its CPU and memory limits, and each worker books those limits against the capacity you declare for its pool (API guide). Our cost model sets that capacity to what the node really has, so every actor keeps its full limit. You can declare more capacity than the node has, and then you overcommit CPU at the pool instead of in each Pod.

Our cost model prices parking for the same 100 coding agents, at Google Cloud on-demand list prices, as of November 2026, in us-central1.

With a 2 minute idle timeout, each session holds a worker nearly 29% of its open time. A warm pool sized for bursts (the 99th percentile of sessions holding a worker at once, if sessions act independently, plus 15% headroom) needs 15 nodes. Add one node that runs around the clock for the Agent Substrate control plane and its PostgreSQL database, and a job that scales the pool to zero after hours:

Parking saves nearly 40% of the node bill. The pool is full about once in 3,000 turns, so a prompt rarely meets that 503. In an hour at 2.5 prompts instead of 2, the same 15 nodes are full for 3% of turns, so size the pool for your busiest hour.

Keep in mind that parking pays most when your agents wait the most. At 2 prompts an hour, the saving is nearly 40%. At 4 prompts an hour, the agent works 44% of the hour, the pool grows to 27 nodes, and the saving is 4%. Above about 4 prompts an hour, one Pod per session becomes the cheaper option, so measure your prompt rate first.

Also, the pool size is yours to set. The autoscaling option in the GKE install guide follows worker Pods, not suspended actors, so scale the pool to zero after hours with a scheduled job: a pool that runs all 730 hours of the month costs nearly twice the one Pod per session bill.

Finally, the fleet size matters. The Agent Substrate control plane costs the same for 10 sessions or 1,000, so parking pays from about 37 coding sessions, or 13 for an assumed chat assistant that works about a minute an hour.

Overcommit changes the comparison. If your Pods request less CPU than their limit, Kubernetes places them by their requests. A Pod that requests 0.25 vCPU with a 1 vCPU limit packs 12 to a node (its 1 GiB of memory caps it there), so the same 100 coding agents fit on 9 nodes, fewer than our parked pool. Agent Substrate can overcommit too, through the capacity you declare on the worker pool, and our cost model does not price that case.

Overcommit has the same cost on both sides: agents share CPU and slow down when their neighbors are busy, during builds and tests. Compare like with like before you decide to park: Pods and actors with the same CPU guarantee.

Back to the shared cluster. Agents are sessions, not requests: size the warm pool for the sessions that hold a worker, not the sessions that are open.

We would park long lived sessions that wait most of the hour, and keep one Pod per session when developers prompt more than about 4 times an hour. Size the warm pool for working time plus a short idle timeout at your busiest hour, and compare with your current Pods at the same CPU guarantee before you park.

Thanks for reading! If you run agent sessions on Kubernetes today, how many prompts an hour do your users send? The prompt rate is the input we are least sure of. You can reach Ivan on LinkedIn or X with your numbers, questions, and corrections.

#10213. Android app developers will have to publicly post address, phone number in 2027

Following new regulations, Google Play will require Android app developers to publicly post a business address starting in 2027 and, while there are workarounds, it’s not going to be the easiest thing.

New Digital Services Act regulations in the EU and UK will require developers to share a phone number and address publicly. While this is only required in those regions, this information will be visible worldwide. Google does not allow PO boxes to be used for this requirement, meaning that many smaller developers will be left with limited options beyond posting their own personal address.

Exceptions to the rule include apps that are not published in the UK or Europe, or developers that qualify as “non-traders” which is essentially those making no money off of their apps.

Here’s how Google defines a “trader” in the context of Android apps:

The Verge notes that a “registered agent service” can be used as a business address for those who don’t have a physical office, and that Apple is allowing iOS developers to use a PO box if they prove the box is linked to a physical address.

Google will require Android app developers to confirm their trader status and their address by February 1, 2027. Account-wide status can be found in the Google Play Console via Manage account > Account details > About you, while status on a per-app basis can be handled via Monitor and improve > Policy and programs > App content.

#10212. Reachy Mini goes fully local

After building your Reachy Mini, you'll install the conversation app and start talking to it. Until now, you had to send your audio to a server. But not anymore. Today we'll walk you through running the whole stack locally.

This stack is powered by speech-to-speech, our cascaded VAD → STT → LLM → TTS pipeline that exposes a Realtime API-compatible /v1/realtime WebSocket. Once you launch the backend, point the robot at it from the UI.

Cascades are the most flexible option in the open-source landscape today, and with the right pieces they're also the fastest. We'll recommend the components we like best, but the whole point of a cascade is that you can swap them. New models drop every week.

This blog walks you through running conversations with Reachy Mini fully locally. No cloud, no API keys, no data leaving your machine. Here's a video showing this live:

To serve the LLM, we'll use Hugging Face's llama.cpp. If you need to install it, the simplest way is brew install llama.cpp or winget install llama.cpp, for more help, check the docs. First, we'll run:

And done! The first time it will download the model, subsequent launches are fast.

We'll begin by simply installing the library

Then, while we are serving the LLM in another terminal, we can simply run:

And you can start talking to the model through your terminal! The first time it will need to download Parakeet-TDT 0.6B v3 and Qwen3TTS, but subsequent launches are fast.

Here's a video showing the local conversation mode:

Now, after you've tried it in --mode local, you can run again the command without that option to serve speech-to-speech to the robot.

Once you have llama.cpp and speech-to-speech running, you can start the robot with the desktop app and launch the conversation app. In the UI from the conversation app, you need to choose the local mode by clicking on "edit connection" in the HF backend. Here's a video showing how to do it:

And you're done. You can start talking to your robot. Every stage of the pipeline is a trade-off: there are faster TTS models with lower quality, slower STT models with higher quality. We optimized for multilingual, you might want to optimize for a single language. The rest of the blog covers how to customize.

Hosted realtime backends are convenient, but running your own engine unlocks three things:

The speech-to-speech repo gives you all of that in a single CLI. It boots a WebSocket server at /v1/realtime that speaks the same protocol Reachy Mini already knows how to talk to.

A cascaded voice pipeline has four stages: VAD, STT, LLM, and TTS. For three of them, we pick solid defaults so you can focus on the LLM:

We are opinionated about these choices, feel free to swap them out for your own if you have a preference.

The LLM is the layer with the most impact on latency and overall performance of the system. We support two options: run a model locally (llama.cpp, MLX, Transformers, vLLM), or use a server with a Responses API (OpenAI, Gemini, HF Inference Endpoints, llama.cpp, vLLM, etc).

The main bottleneck in the system is LLM inference latency. To address that, we support external inference engines exposed through the Responses API protocol.

The speech-to-speech engine therefore supports a second mode where the LLM lives in a separate process as long as it speaks the Responses API protocol. You launch your model server in one terminal, you launch the voice loop in another terminal, and the two talk over HTTP.

Requires vLLM ≥ 0.21.0. Full support for the Responses API protocol, including tool-call streaming used by the speech-to-speech backend, landed in vLLM 0.21.0. Older versions will boot but trip up as soon as the assistant tries to call a tool.

When serving a model through vLLM for this pipeline, three flags are effectively required:

Terminal 1: vLLM inference server (Qwen/Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507):

The --speculative-config line enables Multi-Token Prediction (MTP). It is optional, but it has a great impact on end-to-end latency. Leave it on whenever the model supports it.

Same protocol, but the model runs on a managed GPU on Hugging Face. Deploy any chat model as an Inference Endpoint, then point the voice loop at the endpoint URL:

If you don't want to manage your own endpoint, use an Inference Provider. Hugging Face routes your request to a third-party backend (e.g. Together, Fireworks, Replicate) with a single URL:

When you want to test against a frontier model with zero infra, point the same flag at OpenAI:

The --responses_api_* flags work the same for any provider that implements the protocol (OpenRouter, Together, Fireworks, …). Swap the base URL and the API key, keep the rest of the pipeline identical.

If you are on a Mac, MLX is the lowest-friction way to run a real model with sane latency. We recommend Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507, which is small enough to feel instant on M-series chips and capable enough to hold a conversation.

The server listens on ws://127.0.0.1:8765/v1/realtime by default. Leave it running, connect the conversation app to the local backend, and you are talking to your robot.

Same idea, but using vanilla transformers. Use this if you are on a CUDA box, on Linux, or if you want to swap models freely without re-converting weights for MLX.

Tip. Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 is another good option for LLM because it gives a good speed/quality balance on a single consumer GPU. You can point --model_name at any HF model the backend supports — for example a larger Gemma, Qwen, or a Mistral.

If you are running the voice engine on your laptop and the conversation app on a Reachy Mini Wireless, the only thing that changes is the URL. Make sure the engine binds to a LAN address (not just 127.0.0.1) and use the laptop's IP from the robot when you select the IP in the UI.

If you don't know your IP, here's how to find it:

Look for "IPv4 Address" under your active adapter.

You want the 192.168.x.x or 10.x.x.x one. If you see 169.254.x.x, you're not actually on the network.

#10210. Your Pose Model Gives You Coordinates, Not Meaning

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Pose detection in the browser is a solved problem. You can load a model, point it at a webcam, and get a skeleton tracking a human body in real time, on a laptop, with no server involved.

And then you have a skeleton that follows someone around the screen, which is a toy.

The gap between that toy and a feature someone would pay for is smaller than most developers expect, and it isn't made of machine learning. It's made of trigonometry you already know. This article builds a working bicep-curl rep counter to show exactly where that line falls — and more importantly, which side of it your bugs live on.

I'm using MediaPipe Pose Landmarker from Google AI Edge, which is Apache-2.0 licensed and runs entirely in the tab. Here's the whole setup:

Point that at a

Thirty-three points. Each one is a normalised coordinate — x and y run 0 to 1 across the frame, z is a relative depth estimate — plus a visibility score saying how confident the model is that it can actually see that joint.

That's the entire output. Coordinates and confidences.

The model has no concept of exercise. It doesn't know what an arm is for. It has never heard of a bicep curl. It reports where it thinks your joints are, thirty-odd times a second, and stops.

Everything that turns that into a product is yours, and it's ordinary code.

A bicep curl is a change in the angle at the elbow. The elbow angle is defined by three of those 33 points: shoulder, elbow, wrist. In MediaPipe's pose topology those are indices 11, 13 and 15 on the left side, 12, 14 and 16 on the right.

Getting the angle is two vectors and a dot product:

This is the same maths you'd use to point a game character in a direction. Nothing about it is machine learning, and that matters for a reason I'll come back to.

One thing to notice: I'm ignoring z entirely. The depth estimate is relative, not metric — it's good enough for working out which parts of a body are nearer the camera, and not good enough to measure anything. For a 2D elbow angle, using it adds noise and buys nothing.

Here's where almost everyone's first attempt breaks.

The naive version looks at the angle and counts whenever the arm is up:

Run that at 30 frames a second and one slow curl gives you about twenty reps. You haven't counted repetitions. You've counted frames in which the arm happened to be bent.

A rep isn't a state. It's a transition between states:

Fifteen lines, and that's the feature. The counter increments exactly once per cycle, on the edge, because the guard on phase makes every other frame in that cycle a no-op.

If you used a single threshold — say, 100 degrees — you'd get a counter that fires repeatedly whenever someone holds their arm near 100 degrees and the estimate jitters by a degree either side. Every tiny fluctuation across the line is a transition, and every transition is a rep.

Two widely separated thresholds give you hysteresis. Once the arm is "up," it has to travel all the way past 150 degrees before the counter will consider another rep. Noise of a few degrees can't produce a count because no amount of jitter near 55 crosses 150.

This is the same trick a thermostat uses to avoid switching the heating on and off every few seconds, and it's the single most useful pattern in this whole category of work. Any time you turn a continuous signal into discrete events, you want two thresholds, not one.

visibility is the field people skip, and skipping it is how you get phantom reps.

When a joint goes out of frame or gets occluded, the model still returns a coordinate for it. It is obliged to return 33 points. What it does is return a guess, with a low visibility score attached — and a guessed wrist position can swing wildly between frames, which looks exactly like a very fast curl.

Returning null and having update bail out means an occluded frame holds the current state rather than corrupting it. The arm stays "up" until the model can actually see it come down.

If you want to be stricter, smooth the angle over the last three or four frames with a rolling median before it reaches the state machine. A median rejects single-frame outliers in a way a mean doesn't.

Once you've written one of these, you start recognising the shape everywhere:

None of those require a different model. They're the same 33 coordinates with different geometry sitting on top, and the geometry is a few dozen lines each.

Here's why I keep insisting on the distinction between coordinates and meaning.

When my rep counter miscounts, I don't retrain anything. I don't collect a dataset, I don't label examples, I don't spin up a training job. I look at two things: my thresholds, and my state machine. One of them is wrong.

That's a normal bug in normal code, and you already know how to find it. You can log the angle. You can set a breakpoint on the transition. You can write a unit test that feeds a synthetic sequence of angles through update and asserts the count — no camera, no model, no fixtures:

The hard part of this problem — turning pixels into joint positions — was solved by a research team and shipped to you as a file you can download. The part that's left is the part you're already good at.

You are not blocked on machine learning knowledge. You were blocked on nobody telling you this was available.

I set delegate: 'GPU' above without comment, and it deserves one. MediaPipe Tasks lets you choose between a CPU path and a GPU path, and availability of the GPU path varies by browser, platform and graphics driver.

The practical consequence is that you have to test the CPU path, because for some meaningful share of your users it isn't a fallback — it's the only path they will ever take. If you develop on a machine where the GPU delegate works and never exercise the CPU one, you have shipped something you've never run.

That, and the question of how often you should run the model at all, is a bigger subject than this article. It's the next one.

#10209. Google Docs can now do more with Microsoft Word documents without converting the file

Google Docs is getting an update in how it handles Microsoft Word documents, adding the ability to compare revisions without converting the file.

You can already upload a Microsoft Word document (.docx) to Google Drive and use it within Docs without converting the file, but there are some limits. One of those was comparing documents, which Google is now fixing with an update.

Rolling out now, Google Docs can now directly compare two documents, even if one is in a Microsoft Word format. #10208. Profiling in PyTorch (Part 1): A Beginner's Guide to torch.profiler

What you cannot profile, you cannot optimize.

Whether you are trying to squeeze more tokens per second out of a Large Language Model (LLM), shave milliseconds off inference, or just understand why your training loop runs slower than the spec sheet promises, the path eventually runs through profiling.

The catch is that profiling has a steep on-ramp. The traces are dense walls of colored rectangles. The events carry intimidating names. Most tutorials assume you can already read them. So even when we know we should be profiling, opening a trace can feel like a chore best left for later (or for someone else). This post, and the series it kicks off, is our attempt to lower that on-ramp.

This is the opening post of Profiling in PyTorch, a series where we slowly build the skill of reading profiler traces and use it to drive optimization:

We document the journey from a beginner's point of view. No prerequisites apart from basic PyTorch. Treat this as a leisurely read with some "Aha!" moments. The structure of the post is intentionally question-led: we open a trace, ask "wait, why is that happening?", and chase the answer until something clicks. By the end you should know:

Before we begin, two definitions that will make everything below read better:

You don't usually have to write GPU kernels yourself; when you use a PyTorch operation, it is automatically translated to one or more kernels that do the job on GPU.

With those two ideas in your back pocket, let's start asking questions.

Here is the entire script that we use for the post: 01_matmul_add.py. We recommend opening this script in a separate tab and walk through the code step by step. We use the NVIDIA A100-SXM4-80GB GPU to run the scripts. It is really easy to setup a GPU on the Hugging Face infrastructure and experiment with the scripts using the Dev Mode with Spaces. One could also run the scripts with the Hugging Face Jobs pipeline.(Note: The traces in this blog were generated using PyTorch 2.13. If you are using a different version, some trace details like CompiledFxGraph might differ or be absent.)

As correctly quipped by Dr. Sara Hooker, just as we are primarily made up of water, Deep Neural Networks are primarily made up of matrix multiplies. As fundamental as they are, it would be a shame to start our profiling journey with anything else.

The matrix addition along with the matrix multiplication mimics how weights and biases interact in a neuron. This addition (pun intended) will help us understand how it paves the way for compilation later in the post.

To profile, we will be using the torch.profiler module. The steps involved are:

The profiler exports two distinct artifacts:

Let's see the two in action with our first execution. (Here is the entire 01_matmul_add.py script)

It is recommended to run this script on a machine with a GPU.

If you run the above script (on a GPU machine) you will find a folder traces/01_matmul_add with the two artifacts:

The .txt file holds the profiler table. Upon opening the file, as shown in Figure 1, one would be greeted with a big table with the first column consisting of the events that were triggered inside the scope of profile.

The other columns are related to the time the event takes on the CPU or GPU or any other device(s) specified in activities within torch.profiler.profile. Look at which events take the most amount of time, and try to intuitively understand if that event should in fact take that time. It is also important to look at the column "# of Calls" which dictates how many times the event was triggered.

While we are at it, let's also talk about "Self CPU/CUDA" vs "CPU/CUDA total". The "Self" columns measure time spent only inside the event itself, excluding its children. The "total" columns include the event and all of its children together. So if you look at the "CPU total" of matmul_add, it consists of the time it took on self plus the children events it triggered. This is an important nuance to note.

If you look at the last two lines out of the table you would notice that the profiler tells us that

The CPU time is in ms while the GPU time is in us. To put things in perspective, the time spent on GPUs (the kernel ampere_bf16_s16816gemm...) is less than 1% of the time spent on the CPU (the matmul_add operation). The GPU stays idle most of the time, which is an immediate red flag. The reason this happens is that the GPU can compute a small matmul very quickly, so our code spends most of the time preparing the kernels, launching them on the GPU, sending the data to multiply and gathering the results. This concept is known as an overhead-bound algorithm.

The easiest way to move out of this regime is to use bigger matrix multiplications.

Both times are in ms, which means we have materialized more GPU time just by increasing the size of the matrix multiplications. If you look at Figure 2 you would also notice that the most CUDA time is now taken by the GPU kernel (ampere_bf16_s16816gemm_..) and not by the CPU operation that launched it (matmul_add). This means that we were indeed able to move from overhead bound to compute bound.

We now move into visualising the dispatch chain, which lives inside the .json artifacts. You can upload them to Perfetto UI and see the traces, or you can use uvx trace-util -f traces -b /traces to generate the Perfetto links directly.

In Figure 3, we see the profiler trace for the matrix multiplication and addition. Here the bar width indicates the duration of an event, the vertical nesting is the call hierarchy, the CPU lane denotes the events that happen on the CPU, while the GPU lane shows the actual kernel executions. One might also notice the empty spaces which are the waiting or idle time.

The script was run with default configurations which are:

With Perfetto we suggest using the keyboard for quicker access to the trace. One could use "W A S D" for navigating the trace.

There are two lanes in Figure 4, one for the CPU activity and one for the GPU activity. In the CPU lane one would notice three profile steps (starting from ProfilerStep#2). This comes from the schedule.

The wait skips noisy initializations (ProfilerStep#0), warmup runs through the profiler without recording (ProfilerStep#1), and active is what shows up in trace. One can find the schedule being used in the script here.

Let's put on our detective hats and investigate the trace and ask some questions.

In Figure 5, we notice that ProfileStep#2 takes more time compared to the other steps, and upon looking closely you would see a similar pattern with the matmul_add annotation as well. The smoking gun is inside the annotation, not the annotation itself:

That ~228 µs shown in Figure 6 is the "dead window" between entering record_function("matmul_add") and PyTorch actually dispatching aten::matmul. This can happen for multiple reasons, including workspace allocations, cuBLAS (NVIDIA’s proprietary, GPU-accelerated library for performing fundamental linear algebra operations) heuristics, or lazy module loading. We can either look away or run some more warmup steps before we profile (which is the standard)

In terms of profiling, warmup is when you run the events a couple of times before actually profiling it. The pre-work done by the GPU (including the above pointers) are one time efforts which we do not want to profile. In our example, we have two warmup stages, one where we actually loop over the function before entering the profiler, and two inside the profiler which is achieved by the warmup argument. In this section, we have enabled the actual iterations along with the schedule.

In Figure 7 we see that each profile step takes a similar time, but this does not mean we were able to optimize the one time overheads. We warmed up the runs so that the overheads were not profiled. We think that closing this section abruptly without a hint to solving this would do injustice to the reader, so here is a link to read about further optimizing launch overheads.

In Figure 8, we see that the CPU and GPU lanes have an offset of around 2.5 ms: this is the delay after the CPU submits the CUDA kernels and the time they actually start executing. One might think the warmup stage combined with the schedule's wait and warmup should keep a GPU busy and would diminish the offset.

To uncover what is really happening, let's change our schedule a little:

Figure 9 shows us that there is an Activity Buffer Request in the GPU lane before any operation. Let's zoom in a little more.

Upon zooming into the GPU trace, we notice that the matmul and add kernels for ProfileStep#0 (the CPU trace of which is not visible in the Figure) happen one after the other, while the kernels for ProfileStep#1 have a window in between. The best explanation for this is that there was an overflow of buffers, and another buffer request (a request to allocate some memory on the GPU VRAM) was issued during the kernel execution.

The best way to rule out other possibilities is to profile for more iterations and see whether a similar window appears in other parts of the trace. To do that we run with active=20.

As shown in Figure 11, we see a similar trend in ProfileStep#1. This is aligned with our previous findings, and we can safely conclude that it was indeed another buffer request.

In Figure 12, we see the nested CPU calls. This is an important visualization, where one gets to understand what a chain of dispatch really looks like.

We begin with ProfileStep# which encapsulates the profiling step. Due to us annotating the step, we see the matmul_add row. The matmul_add consists of two aten calls, one for matrix multiplication and one for matrix addition.

The aten::matmul is the ATen-level dispatch that those user-facing PyTorch matmul calls land on. aten::mm is the 2D matrix-matrix multiply backend.

It is very interesting to note how PyTorch calls aten::bmm (batched matrix multiplication) if we add the batch axis to our matrices. Let's take a detour and see the aten::bmm in action.

In Figure 13, upon adding the batch axis to the inputs, aten::matmul now encapsulates a bunch of other prerequisite CUDA runtime calls along with aten::bmm (instead of aten::mm). This also hints at the heuristics that cuBLAS needs to do in order to dispatch the right (most suitable) kernel for the program.

In the rest of the post, we will be working with simple 2D matrices, unless otherwise mentioned.

We notice that for aten::mm there are two CUDA Runtime calls, namely cudaOccupancyMaxActiveBlocksPerMultiprocessor (boxed in Figure 14) and cudaLaunchKernel, while for aten::add there is only the cudaLaunchKernel.

cudaOccupancyMaxActiveBlocksPerMultiprocessor is a planning call and is purely CPU side. It asks: "given a kernel function, a chosen block size, and a chosen dynamic shared memory size, how many blocks of this kernel can simultaneously reside on one SM (Streaming Multiprocessor)?"

This begs the question, why do we need planning for matmul and not for add?

To understand this, we have to look at the kernel's resource footprint. If you click on the GPU kernels, you will be able to inspect the resource footprint for the respective kernel.

In Figure 15, we note that for matrix multiplication the registers per thread and shared memory are dynamic (based on the size of the matrix). cuBLAS ships hundreds of kernel variants, and each has a heuristic-driven launch path that needs runtime information about hardware capacity. The occupancy query is part of that heuristic. Conceptually, we can think of GPU-accelerated matmuls as working on independent tiles: how many tiles we use and how big each tile needs to be depends on the matrices and the hardware. Modern algorithms are way more complicated than that, but this is still a good reference framework.

From Figure 16 we see that the footprint of addition says 32 registers and zero shared memory. That fits trivially. There's nothing to query, because no hardware resource is going to limit occupancy. The kernel is, by design, resource-light.

You can use this as a quick diagnostic when reading any trace. Scan the CPU lane for cudaOccupancyMaxActiveBlocksPerMultiprocessor. Each occurrence flags a "heavyweight, adaptively launched" kernel, usually a GEMM (GEneral Matrix Multiplication), conv, or similar. The kernels without a preceding occupancy query are the elementwise/reduction crowd that PyTorch launches mechanically.

cudaDeviceSynchronize blocks the CPU until all GPU work on this device finishes. The profiler emits this sync at the end of the active window to flush events. Without it, kernel timings would be missing.

A 1.78 ms sync covering 26 µs of real GPU work tells you this run was 98% idle. That's the textbook overhead-bound symptom.

We already know from the profiler table analysis (above) that providing bigger matrices to our algorithm moves it out from the overhead-bound region to being compute-bound.

Let's run the command and dive deeper into the traces.

In Figure 17, we notice that the matmul kernel for ProfileStep#3 takes longer on the GPU than the other steps. This is particularly interesting to note, because the other kernels launched were the exact same, which means there were no cuBLAS heuristics involved. There are no scheduling gaps, the CPU launches are normal, and it is not a profiler artifact.

This trace in Figure 17 makes a useful point that's easy to miss in idealized examples: kernel runtimes are not constants, even on the same hardware environment running identical code on identical data.

Let's make this more concrete by modifying the script a little. We run the iteration 20 times, capturing each of the steps.

Figure 18 reveals a similar finding. While each kernel was the exact same, they time differently. The different compute times can be blamed on a bunch of reasons:

A reader who only saw the average would conclude that a matmul took ~1 ms (mean of 5 = 1084 µs); a reader who looked at the trace would see that the matmul takes ~580 µs except when the GPU throws a fit. Those are very different mental models, and only one of them is correct.

Working with torch.compile has always amazed us. One writes normal eager PyTorch code, but PyTorch tries to capture tensor-heavy regions, turn them into graphs, optimize them, and run generated code. The default backend is usually TorchInductor, and the broad pipeline is:

In this section, we talk about compilation and look at the profiler traces.

The args.compile flag triggers the following code:

In Figure 19, we see the new CPU rows named Torch-Compiled Region: 0/0 which points us to the compiled functions being used.

Looking at Figure 20 we ask the question, did we actually fuse the multiplication and addition operations together into one?

This is operator fusion at the graph level. Inductor took our torch.add(torch.matmul(x, w), b) and rewrote it into a single aten::addmm(b, x, w) call. The important thing to note here is that it did not produce a new fused CUDA kernel. The actual GPU work is still ampere_bf16_s16816gemm_bf16_128x256_ldg8_f2f_stages_64x3_nn, the same cuBLAS kernel eager mode used. So the "fusion" here is at the dispatcher level, not at the kernel level.

PyTorch provides the torch.addmm function that does what we did in two steps, that is multiply and add. We encourage the reader to look at the traces of this function and comment your observations in the comments below!

While we know in theory what happens when we compile our functions it is equally important to see it in action. Let's look at the CPU-side hierarchy which reflects torch.compile's runtime architecture.

TorchDynamo Cache Lookup is where Dynamo checks that the current call still matches what was compiled with the same input shapes, dtypes, devices, and tensor metadata. If anything mismatched, Dynamo would recompile. This cost is paid every call, even after compilation.

Torch-Compiled Region is the wrapper that "enters" the compiled version. AOTDispatcher Runtime Wrapper Prologue is AOT Autograd's runtime wrapper. Even though we don't need gradients here, AOTDispatcher is always in the stack handling tensor metadata, view tracking, and would set up the backward pass if requires_grad were true.

## Call CompiledFxGraph is where the actual generated code runs. The string after "CompiledFxGraph" is the content hash of the FX graph. It's the same across all three active steps, confirming cache hits.

You can find the generated code on disk under /tmp/torchinductor_/fxgraph keyed by this hash, useful when you want to read the Triton/C++ that Inductor actually produced.

Looking at the traces in Figure 21, we were really happy to notice only one cudaLaunchKernel per step. This observation was directly contradicting what we were seeing in the GPU trace. There were still two kernels being launched per step, namely the Memcpy DtoD (Device -> Device) and the GEMM. Going back to the CPU trace, we noticed that we had completely missed the cudaMemcpyAsync dispatch.

addmm computes out = α·A·B + β·C, and cuBLAS's GEMM-with-bias-add epilogue writes into a destination buffer that needs to already contain the bias. An epilogues can be thought of all the operations that happen after a GEMM. In the world of deep-learning we constantly come up with GEMM-Epilogues like activations, bias addition, normalization and many more. This is why there are cuBLAS GEMM-with- kernel variants.

If you use different modes for torch.compile you would notice different kernel variants being launched. You can try it for yourself and add a comment below about your observations!

The result is mathematically still the same. The bias add isn't free, as we pay a memcpy upfront plus a slightly more expensive GEMM epilogue.

The fusion one might have hoped for, where x·w + b (here out = α·A·B + β·C) collapses into a single kernel with no extra memory traffic, isn't what happened. Inductor preserved the two memory-touching operations, it just relabeled the bias copy as a memcpy and the addition as a GEMM epilogue.

A truly fused implementation would skip the memcpy. That's what FlashAttention-style hand-written kernels do, and what Inductor can do via Triton codegen, but for a 4096×4096 bf16 matmul, Inductor evidently decided "use cuBLAS, do the bias via epilogue setup" was the best path.

This is the easiest thing to miss when comparing an eager and a compiled run:

torch.compile is roughly 2× more expensive on the CPU per step. That's because every call walks the full Dynamo > AOTAutograd > Inductor stack, on top of the same aten::addmm dispatch we have anyway. The compile pipeline is built for ML models with dozens of ops where the per-call overhead amortizes (for a single op it's a tax).

torch.compile has a mode argument. It is for the reader to take home as an assignment to read the documentation and come up with a mode that could take the CPU overhead down. 🤗

A quick reference for the patterns we walked through. The idea is: if you see this in a trace, this is what it usually means.

We started with a tiny matmul + add and used it as an excuse to learn how to read a PyTorch profiler. Along the way we picked up a few mental models that travel well to bigger workloads. This was the first stop in the Profiling PyTorch series. In the posts that follow, we will gradually leave this two-op toy behind and walk up the ladder of complexity, looking at larger building blocks and, eventually, real models.

Thanks to Noe Flandre, Suvaditya Mukherjee, and Vidit Ostwal for their reviews on the early draft of the post!

The blog post was polished using an LLM. This in no way means that we have let an agent run in the background and let it generate the blog. Some of us in the team are non-english speakers and think LLMs (which are mostly trained in the English Language) can rectify silly grammar mistakes or rephrase sentences that sound less intimidating and cleaner. Hope this helps with the idea of "why should I read, if this was LLM generated". 🤗

Thanks a bunch for this blog post series -really much needed! Especially the Trace reading cheatsheet sections are very beneficial.

There are some parts I have been thinking about:

Firstly, thanks for the questions. To answer 2 you are right, the context manager should take care of it, but I personally like putting an extra sync to be sure. You can omit it in your own scripts.

Coming to 1, this was really interesting, I had to go back to docs to get more idea. You are right with your observation about cudaMemcpyAsync vanishing and only one kernel launch ..._ldg8_relu_f2f_stages_64x3_nn. It turns out that the new kernels is a relu family kernel, which does the EPILOGUE properly where it falls under the contract of using a bias and broadcasting it across rows. Previously the bias was 2D and did not fall under the correct EPILOGUE contract, and hence there was an extra cudaMemcpyAsync.

Thanks for the kind words! Glad you liked it.

Good read! Helped introduce me to the world of GPUs and lower level stuff. While I understood the shape of things, it made me realise I have a lot of gaps in my knowledge wrt to this aspect of ML.

It would be great if the PyTorch version that was used was mentioned here as well. I was stuck because my trace was not displaying CompiledFxGraph. It worked on Colab but not on my local machine. I was using PyTorch 2.8.0, which does not show CompiledFxGraph in the trace.

Ah! This is an important pointer I missed in the blog. I was using 2.13 throughout the post. Thanks for catching it. Do you mind sending a PR to the blog (github.com/huggingface/blog) and I could merge it! 🤗

#10205. How to Build Conference Talk Slides With AI Without Looking Generic

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Conference talks fail on slides more often than on content. The speaker knows the material and has something worth saying, but the deck is a wall of bullets, or a template everyone in the room has seen before, or forty slides for a twenty-minute slot. AI presentation makers can now produce a complete deck from an outline in minutes, which solves the time problem and creates a new one: the output tends toward exactly the uniform, stock-image, bullet-heavy style that audiences have learned to tune out.

This article explains how conference slides differ from other decks, why AI-generated decks look generic and what specifically causes it, a workflow that uses an AI presentation maker for speed while keeping the talk distinctive, how to handle the slide types that matter most in a talk (the opening, the demonstration, the data, the close), and a checklist to run before the talk.

A conference talk is spoken, timed and performed to a room. That changes the rules compared with a reading deck or a business presentation.

The causes are specific and therefore fixable.

Template uniformity. Every slide uses the same layout family, so the deck has no visual rhythm. Audiences read the sameness as mass-produced.

Bullet default. Given a paragraph, the tool produces three to five bullets. Given twenty paragraphs, twenty bullet slides.

Stock imagery. Icons and photos chosen by keyword match the topic superficially and add no meaning. A talk about database indexing gets a picture of a filing cabinet.

Label titles. “Introduction”, “Background”, “Key Challenges”, “Conclusion”. Titles that name the category rather than make the point.

Flattened emphasis. The tool does not know which of your ideas is the one the audience should leave with, so every slide gets equal weight.

No pacing. Every slide carries the same amount of content, so there is no build, no pause, no payoff.

Each of these is a default that can be overridden, either in how the input is prepared or in a short editing pass afterwards.

Step 1: Write the talk before the slides. Not a script necessarily, but the argument: what the audience knows at the start, what they know at the end, and the four to six moves that get them there. Write the one sentence you want them to repeat to a colleague afterwards. If this is not clear, no deck will fix it.

Step 2: Write the slide titles as the things you will say. Each title is a sentence, in your voice, that states the point of that moment in the talk. “Indexes make reads fast by making writes slower” is a title. “Index trade-offs” is not. Read the titles in order; they should be the talk in miniature.

Step 3: Mark the pacing. Next to each title, note whether the slide is a hold (a key point, stays up while you talk for a minute or more), a beat (a quick slide in a sequence), or a reveal (something shown, a demo, a result). This tells you where to put effort.

Step 4: Generate. Paste the titles with one or two sentences of content under each into an ai presentation maker. Ask for a slide count close to your title count. Pick the plainest theme available; distinctiveness will come from your content, not the template.

Step 5: Strip the bullets. On every hold slide, delete the bullets and leave the title, or the title plus one image or one number. On beat slides, keep at most one short line. The content that was in the bullets goes into speaker notes, which is where it belonged.

Step 6: Replace every stock image. Delete icons. Replace keyword-matched photos with your own material: a screenshot, a diagram you drew, a chart from your data, a photograph you took, a single large word. If a slide has no genuine visual, a title alone on a plain background is better than a filler image.

Step 7: Build the reveals by hand. Demos, before-and-after comparisons, the key chart. These are the slides the audience will remember, and they need more care than a generator can give. See the section below.

Step 8: Break the layout rhythm deliberately. Make the two or three most important slides look different: full-bleed image, a single enormous number, a black slide with one line of white text. Contrast is what makes a moment land.

Step 9: Rehearse with a timer. The slide count will be wrong in the first rehearsal. Cut, merge or split until the pacing matches the time.

The opening. Not a title slide with your name and a logo while you say hello. Open on something that earns attention: a surprising number, a question, a screenshot of the problem, a single provocative sentence. Your name and affiliation can come on slide two, or be said rather than shown.

The problem statement. One slide, one sentence, stays up while you explain why the audience should care. No bullets.

The demonstration. If the talk has a demo, record it. Live demos fail in rooms with unreliable connections and unfamiliar projectors. A recorded demo with the audio off, narrated live, gives the same effect with none of the risk. If you must go live, have the recording ready as a fallback.

The data. One chart per slide, one message per chart, the message in the title. Strip gridlines, legends and secondary series. Highlight the one line or bar that matters in colour and grey out the rest. Label directly. Type large enough to read from the back.

The “so what.” After the evidence, a slide that states what it means in one sentence. This is a hold slide; give it time.

The close. The one sentence you want them to repeat, alone on the final slide. Not “Thank you” or “Questions?”; those can be said. The last thing on screen while you take questions should be your point.

Because the slides are now sparse, two things need handling.

First, the speaker notes must carry what you intend to say, in cue form: the key phrases, the number you must not forget, the transition to the next slide. The generator will have put the stripped bullet content there; edit it into cues rather than prose.

Second, the shared deck. Attendees who download a sparse deck afterwards get little from it. Options: export with notes visible; publish a companion blog post or document; or build a second “reading” version with more text on each slide. Many speakers do the first and link to a post.

For a twenty-minute talk, fifteen to twenty-five slides is typical once hold and beat slides are counted. For a forty-five-minute talk, thirty to fifty. Build-up sequences of several quick beats inflate the count without inflating the time, which is fine. What is not fine is a deck of forty dense slides for twenty minutes; that is a talk that will run over and leave the audience behind.

Rehearse at least twice with a timer, once alone and once with a listener. Cut the content you rush. Nobody has ever complained that a talk finished two minutes early.

Lightning talks (five to ten minutes). Five to eight slides, almost all holds. One idea, one piece of evidence, one takeaway. Cut everything else.

Workshops and tutorials. More slides, more text, because attendees will refer back and follow along. The reading-deck rules apply more here; still, keep each step to one slide.

Panel contributions. Often no slides at all, or two or three for a specific point. Resist bringing a full deck.

Keynotes. Fewer slides, longer holds, more full-bleed images and single sentences. The speaker carries almost everything; the slides punctuate.

Remote talks. The screen is small and the audience is distracted. Larger type still, more frequent slide changes to hold attention, and a recorded demo is essential because screen-sharing a live one adds another failure point.

How much of the deck should the AI tool produce? The structural first draft: layouts, consistency, speaker notes populated. Expect to edit every slide and rebuild the key ones.

Is it acceptable to have slides with only a title? Yes, and it is often the strongest format for a spoken talk. The audience listens instead of reading.

What about code on slides? Short excerpts only, in a large monospace type, with the relevant lines highlighted and the rest dimmed. Anything longer belongs in the companion post.

Should I use animations? Simple builds (revealing elements in sequence) help pacing. Transitions and effects distract. Keep to the former.

How do I make the deck distinctive if I cannot design? Your material is what makes it distinctive: your screenshots, your data, your diagrams, your sentences. Design restraint plus real content beats decorated templates every time.
